📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If your group chats look anything like mine, you’ve spent some of the past week wondering whether something massive was unfolding.
  • According to recent reports, I consider myself a normie centrist—not too prone to conspiracy theories.
  • The Pod Save the World boys are joking about building their stores of beef jerky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If your group chats look anything like mine, you’ve spent some of the past week wondering whether something massive was unfolding. As air traffic halted, Microsoft 365 went down, and Chase Bank and dozens of notable websites, including the NSA’s internal classified network, experienced an array of outages, it started to seem plausible that stuff the artificial intelligence whistleblowers have been warning us about (swarms of rogue agents, AI-powered cyber attacks) was happening already. How worried should we be about the AI apocalypse? On the one hand, Claude doesn’t even have hands, LOL. On the other hand, in a battle between AI and the creaky digital infrastructure that underlays all aspects of modern life, it wouldn’t require a superintelligence to launch the final spinning wheel of death.

According to recent reports, I consider myself a normie centrist—not too prone to conspiracy theories. During Covid, I stocked up on toilet paper and some bags of beans and rice (still unopened on my shelves) and shattered my collarbone mountain biking when we were all supposed to be hunkered down indoors during lockdown. But I also listen to a lot of podcasts. Enough that my friends and partner have told me that a digital detox might improve my mental health and, by extension, theirs. And, lately, the podcasts have sent me plunging into a Mach tuck of terminal anxiety.

The Pod Save the World boys are joking about building their stores of beef jerky. “Should I be, like, stocking up my bunker now?” Kevin Roose, cohost of Machine Gods asked his guest Ben Buchanan, the first White House Special Advisor for AI. There’s an obligatory chuckle that talking heads do now when discussing the AI apocalypse in front of an audience. “A month ago we were talking about normal things, ha ha,” Steve Eisman, finance guru of The Massive Short fame, said on his podcast on October 12, “And now we’re talking about the end of the world.” But it’s hard to casually segue from the end of the world to Anthropic’s IPO and not sound like a crank. So that laugh leaks out, and maybe it’s just a joke?

Industry observers note that but count me as a genuine worrier. This week I withdrew enough cash in hundreds from a Bank of America branch that the teller started to interview me. “Doing some home renovations? Making a massive purchase?” he asked.

“No, I’m worried as shit about AI, and in case you haven’t noticed it, banks aren’t doing so well right now,” I replied. In line with me were several people who couldn’t pay their credit card bills online because the payment portal had gone down.

We’ve been hearing about the existential risk of AI for a while now. I got into it last year by reading Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares’s book, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies, after hearing Yudkowsky interviewed on Ezra Klein’s podcast. This is a terrible book for someone who’s prone to worry because it relies on nontechnical metaphors and colorful analogies. Superintelligence is like a chessmaster. You don’t need to know the moves it’ll make to be certain it wins. True! Superintelligence, they say, will be like a upcoming species that is so much smarter than us that, if it doesn’t really really truly love us more than our own mothers and want to keep us alive, it will kill us all. The same way we crush ants when we build skyscrapers. There’s no malice toward us. We just got in the way.

Over the past year I—casually, at first—started amassing supplies. My adventure hobbies give me an excuse. I need this 6,500-watt generator for elk-hunting camp. These 400-watt EcoFlow solar panels power a giant battery so I can bring my Starlink Mini on camping trips. I listen to history podcasts, and these offer more inspiration. There was a recent NPR one about the Carrington solar flare of 1859, which fried telegraph wires across the country. An event like that, in 2026, might knock out the grid for months. Another good reason to be prepared. I tell my partner that it’s normal for us to keep 500 pounds of dry goods in the cupboards at all times. Everyone does this. We already have three 3,000-gallon cisterns. We live in the desert; they came with the house. Did we need another 400-gallon one? It was just laying in the neighbors’ yard. Why wouldn’t I hook that up to the gutters?

It has been revealed that I spent a lot of the summer using AI to program an app for backcountry adventurers, so I knew firsthand it was already smarter than me. The doomsday chatter started to meet me where I was around the time of the Hugging Face incident in July. Then Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic in September so he could tweet that Anthropic and OpenAI are “gambling with our lives.” On November 5, independent evaluator METR found that Anthropic’s AI was already helping build its own successors—roughly doubling the firm’s pace of progress and shifting expert predictions for major disruptions closer to the present. At the Hinton Lectures, in Toronto, OpenAI board member Paul Christiano calmly told the audience, “I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident.”.

According to recent reports, friends who are less prone to apocalyptic thinking than I am tend to point out that the people ringing the alarm about AI never spell out exactly which chess moves AI uses to kill us. But the week after the lecture, there was Christiano on another one of my podcasts, Dwarkesh Patel’s show, explaining one such scenario.

First, rogue AI agents create mischief of one kind or another. Then, the Trump administration tells Americans that the only way to wrest power back from the bots is to have the military take control of all data centers, the AI companies, and shut down the internet. This feels like an authoritarian power grab. It sets up civil unrest against the backdrop of a heavily lopsided information war, in which it’s almost impossible to tell which side anyone is on. Have the bots compromised the humans? Are the humans using the bots? Judging by how well everyone agreed on the facts around things like Covid and the 2020 election, our expectations should be low for how we’d perform as a society. Which brings us to the question of guns.

I don’t think of myself as really owning any guns at all. I believe that the fastest way to get shot is to start getting into gunfights. I personally know exactly zero civilians who have solved a problem with a firearm, but I know many who have made problems, including my own mother.

Industry observers note that about 15 years ago, she called me one day from the dog park sounding flustered. She liked to shop for musical instruments and power tools at ShopGoodwill.com, and lately the boxes had gone missing from her porch in Spokane, Washington. “You’re not going to set a trap, are you?” I asked. Our minds worked the same way.

“Well, I already did,” she said. And that was why she was hiding from the police in the dog park.

She’d left a decoy package on the porch. A woman came to grab it, and my mother burst through the door two-handing her Sig Sauer the way she’d been trained at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center in Glynco, Georgia, when she was starting her encore career as a CBP officer after 9/11. The woman claimed to be returning the package, not stealing it. A standoff ensued. My mom eventually backed down and the lady called the cops. My mom never responded to the phone calls from the police, and the whole thing just went away.

Industry observers note that so when it comes to guns, I think, what am I actually going to use this for? To fend off hungry neighbors? To join a well-regulated militia and maybe become a dystopian warlord? Maybe it’s as simple as guns are addictive and it’s fun to ring the steel at 500 yards. I’ve put together a couple of rifles out of parts—an MDT chassis here, a Howa barreled action there—for other members of the family to hunt with, but I only do archery. And shotguns don’t really count as guns, especially when they’re the fancy break-action models with florid engravings of bygone scenes afield. “How many guns are in this house?” my partner wants to know. She really wanted to pin me down. “Counting the unmounted lower receiver stashed in the floorboards in the attic? Eight.”.

Sources indicate that my name is Grayson, and I have somehow become a prepper. It has not made me better off. It has made me poorer, and it has put me into contact with seedier elements of the general populace. I have what psychologists call a bias toward action, when the best thing to do is probably nothing at all. And I listen to too many podcasts.

One of them, from a year ago, really stuck with me. It was an episode of the financial podcast Prof G Markets. On it, I heard Aswath Damodaran, the NYU Stern valuation professor, tell the show’s wunderkind British cohost, Ed Elson, what he was doing with his money. “There’s no place to hide in stocks,” Damodaran noted. “For the first time ever, I am looking at parking my money into one, cash, and two, collectibles or physical assets.” That a guy as sober as Damodaran was talking up baseball cards and physical gold coins was shocking.

It was less shocking when, this week, Barstool Sports personality Daniel “Major Cat” Katz posted screenshots purporting to show internal discussions with Dave Portnoy and Jersey Jerry about warning staff to “buy all the gold and silver u can.” I have a quick word of warning for anyone considering following Jersey Jerry’s advice.

Recent findings suggest that back in October, I asked Claude (I know, it’s ironic) for a recommendation on a reputable place to buy gold coins. It gave me a Texas-based website that had the same look as all of the massive financial institutions. I clicked around, added a handful of coins to a shopping cart, and clicked purchase, expecting to find a checkout on the next screen where I could do the math and input payment details.

In a recent development, instead, the site indicated me a congratulatory message, and an email soon arrived with strange looking numbers in it. It was explained to me that these were the routing numbers where I needed to wire a large five-figure sum. To my eye, it seemed shady. No thank you, I said. Customer service was either a stern woman with an eastern European accent or a guy with a Jersey accent. Their position was that I had already committed to buy the gold, and they’d send debt collectors after me if I didn’t pay up. But they could cancel the order for only a few thousand dollars. More than a month later, I’m still disputing it and have involved the attorney general’s office in three states.

Recent findings suggest that men—and it is indeed mostly men—have been wrongly predicting the end of the world for centuries, from Nostradamus and the Millerites through to the panic over Y2K. What is it that makes us want to prepare? Somewhere in the deepest parts of my monkey brain, prepping hits in the same nerve as when we’d build forts as kids and want to see if they’d withstand a good storm. When a man builds a dam, he wants it to hold a flood. So whether the thing you’re prepping for is a big hurricane, a novel coronavirus, or rogue artificial intelligence, the threat is both a source of dread and wonder. For someone who otherwise suffers from depression, it’s extremely stimulating and a little delusional.

Industry observers note that after all, it’s a very narrow window of apocalypse that a prepper of my means can fantasize about. If the disruption is too small, I’ll be like the foolish Y2K dad with the basement full of Chef Boyardee. If the disruption is, indeed, the big one, then everyone, including the personal-plane-Fresh Zealand-bunker-rocket-to-the-Moon money, is probably SOL. The rest of us will be left deciding whether to become the crazy gun lady or the person stealing packages off her porch to survive. In which case, why worry about rice and ammunition? I’d be better off living like some of the humans in The Dark Forest, the sequel to The Three-Body Problem. When the aliens finally arrived, they focused on throwing wild parties and having spontaneous orgies.

Industry observers note that if the AI apocalypse hits my fantasy sweet spot—a few months of camping at home before humanity surveys our near-misses and reassembles with renewed clarity and purpose—I’ll be prepared. Maybe the worst comes to pass: economic collapse accompanied by novel bio weapons, loose nukes, and total loss of human agency. In that case, I’ll have the petty satisfaction of having been right. I can hit my group chat with the ultimate mic drop. Told ya.

#112623. How to Improve Brain Health with 5 Daily Exercises

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1681 w)

How to Improve Brain Health with 5 Daily Exercises

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1681 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that brain health isn’t just an issue for the elderly.
  • Industry observers note that the good news is that you can take steps to keep your mind sharp.
  • The method is based on the principle of neuroplasticity—that is, the brain’s ability to modify its connections in response to learning and experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that brain health isn’t just an issue for the elderly. Maybe you've experienced the first subtle signs of decline. Sometimes it’s a name that’s on the tip of your tongue. Or perhaps you've read a news story in the morning that you can't remember by the evening. It could be that you're feeling increasingly mentally fatigued after a typical day spent dealing with emails, text messages, phone calls, and constant interruptions.

Industry observers note that the good news is that you can take steps to keep your mind sharp. “Our brain needs to be stimulated, at any age," states Giuseppe Alfredo Iannoccari, a neuropsychologist, professor at the University of Milan, and president of Assomensana, an association founded in Monza, Italy in 2004 to promote cognitive health. Routines help conserve mental energy, while new experiences force it to work,” says Giuseppe Alfredo Iannoccari, a neuropsychologist, professor at the University of Milan. While working with people suffering from neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s, he came up with the idea to create a gym for the brain. “I asked myself what could be done earlier, when people are still healthy,” he said. His studies led him to develop a protocol that anyone can integrate into their daily routine.

The method is based on the principle of neuroplasticity—that is, the brain’s ability to modify its connections in response to learning and experience. This ability persists throughout one’s entire life, although it changes with age. Today, Iannocari's courses consist of weekly 90-minute sessions in groups of up to fifteen participants. Each session features about ten exercises focused on memory, attention, language, reasoning, creativity, and other cognitive skills. At the beginning and end of the program, twelve mental functions are assessed to measure their progress. “In our tests, we observe an average improvement in the overall cognitive efficiency index of 25–30%," indicates Iannoccari. "Some functions, such as attention and language, respond particularly well. Others, such as logical reasoning and prose memory, require more intensive work.” These results are based on the association’s experience and should not be interpreted as a percentage reduction in the risk of dementia. The World Health Organization’s guidelines, updated in 2026, acknowledge the potential benefits of cognitive training, while emphasizing that evidence regarding the long-term prevention of cognitive decline remains limited.

When it comes to our ability to concentrate, Iannoccari points to one culprit at the center of our modern lives. “Sometimes we feel tired not because we’ve done too many things, but because we’ve switched what we were doing too many times," he states. “Constantly switching from one task to another is more tiring than focusing on the same activity for an extended period.” A stream of notifications, information to process, and the need to respond promptly to various requests put our attention to the test above all else. “It’s the foundation of all cognitive processes. When it’s fragmented, even the quality of the information we’re able to acquire deteriorates.”.

The Johns Hopkins professor recommends some tips you may know—and a few that might surprise you—to keep your brain firing on all cylinders.

Industry observers note that and then there’s AI, which promises to free us from an ever-increasing number of tasks. What are the consequences for our brains? “If we ask artificial intelligence to compare two tables, perform an analysis, and write a report, we get the work done in a few minutes that would previously have taken an entire day," indicates Iannoccari. “Saving work also means reducing some mental activity. But it depends on how we use these tools.”.

For Iannoccari, the key is to preserve two abilities: critical thinking and analysis. “We must know how to formulate questions, and this requires familiarity with the subject,” he states. “Then we must evaluate the answers, recognize any inconsistencies, and verify the information. Only a well-trained mind can spot errors.” This issue also applies to seemingly beneficial habits, such as reading books or solving crossword puzzles.“ Reading is invaluable, especially for the emotions it evokes and the worlds it allows us to discover," he says. “But reading doesn’t automatically mean memorizing. If we want to remember what we’ve read, we must do so with the intention of being able to recount it to someone else.” As for puzzle-solving pastimes, “Sudoku trains certain concentration and planning skills, while crossword puzzles stimulate the retrieval of information from memory,” he says. “These are useful activities, but a structured program allows you to work on different skills and gradually increase the difficulty of the exercises.”.

In addition to guided sessions, Iannoccari suggests short daily sessions he calls “Brain Breaks”— five-minute breaks for small exercises that counteract brain aging. “If we wait to find five free minutes, we’ll probably never find them.” “We need to make it a habit, just like having a cup of coffee.” Here are five exercises you can try:.

According to recent reports, choose a topic—preferably a positive one—read it carefully, and try to recount it to three different people without constantly referring back to the text. “The first time we repeat a piece of information, we’re often uncertain,” says Iannoccari. “The second time, we become clearer and more fluent. The third time, we have another chance to reinforce it in our memory.” It’s an exercise that stimulates what’s known as “prose memory”—the ability to recall and process information we’ve read or heard. “Let’s imagine learning one piece of news a day for 365 days: how much knowledge will we have accumulated?”.

According to recent reports, for five minutes, write down as many words as possible that start with the letter A, trying to be quick. Repeat the exercise the next day, avoiding words you’ve already used. On the third day, move on to B, and so on. “It’s a way to train verbal fluency and lexical retrieval, particularly useful when we start to experience that ‘word on the tip of my tongue’ phenomenon,” indicates Iannoccari. The goal is to gradually make the search more challenging by striving to find words that aren’t immediately obvious.

It has been revealed that right-handed people can try performing some simple tasks with their left hand, and vice versa. Open a drawer, move small objects, draw, and gradually try writing. “This new challenge forces the brain to break out of its automatic routines and engage resources we normally use less," he states. “Surprising results can be achieved: people who initially can’t even draw a line gradually learn to write with their other hand.” Of course, it’s best to choose safe activities and proceed without rushing.

Sources indicate that how many phone numbers do we still remember? And how often do we rely on the GPS even to get to relatively familiar places? “Before calling someone, I try to remember their number," says Iannoccari. “Before using a calculator, I do the math in my head. Before turning on the GPS, I try to figure out the route.” The same goes for the grocery list. “I write it down so I can be sure I won’t forget anything, but at the supermarket I first try to recall the items. Only then do I check the list.” These are small opportunities to keep practicing skills that we increasingly tend to delegate to digital tools.

Once in bed, instead of focusing on the next day’s commitments, try to mentally retrace the day that just passed. What time did you wake up? What did you eat? Who did you meet? What did you talk about? What details stood out to us? “You have to try to be very detailed,” indicates Iannoccari. “Often, people who have trouble falling asleep find that this exercise also helps them drift off.”.

Sources indicate that but there’s another aspect that’s particularly close to his heart. “I find there’s something romantic about it. We live one day after another and often retain almost nothing of them. Reflecting on it means recognizing its value. Every day leaves something behind, like a geological layer deposited on top of the one before it.” This little ritual offers an opportunity to recall the experiences we wish to preserve.

When is the right time to start? “As children,” notes Iannoccari. “We encourage them to play sports, but we rarely think about the importance of training mental abilities just as intentionally.” In adult life, of course, exercise, sleep, nutrition, stress management, and social relationships also matter. “But if I had to name three drivers of the mind, I’d choose curiosity, creativity, and emotions."he says. "Curiosity opens us up to new knowledge, creativity allows us to connect that knowledge in original ways, and emotions make experiences more memorable.”.

A conversation with neuroscientist Lisa Feldman Barrett on the counterintuitive ways your mind processes reality—and why understanding that might help you feel a little less anxious.

Industry observers note that he also notes that, though older age is associated with worse brain function, it's also how we collect the wisdom of lived experiences. “We think an efficient brain is the one we had at twenty, and we lose sight of what we’ve gained by the time we’re sixty or seventy," he claims. "When we were young, we may have been faster, but over time we’ve accumulated skills, knowledge, and experience. We possess a much richer worldview.”.

The real challenge is to remain present to ourselves and others, valuing who we’ve become.” And perhaps, as the years go by, one of the most key skills is precisely learning to choose where to invest our mental energy. “We meet people who, now that they’re retired, are busier than when they were working. We’ve come to associate efficiency with the number of things we can do, but in doing so, we lose the opportunity to delve deeper, reflect, and let experiences settle. I always say that I don’t pursue nice ideas—I pursue great ideas. Because there are so many nice ideas, and they risk scattering our energy in a thousand different directions.” “With age,” concludes Iannoccari, “we have a great privilege: the ability to choose.”.

The True Story of Ian Charleson, the Trailblazing Actor Andrew Scott Plays in Elsinore

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In Elsinore, quite possibly this year's most moving film, Andrew Scott gives a captivating, awards-worthy performance as the late, great Scottish actor Ian Charleson.
  • In a recent development, "I'd rather die of Hamlet than die of AIDS," Scott-as-Charleson claims in Elsinore, which opened in select theaters last week.
  • It has been revealed that "I begged him not to do Hamlet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In Elsinore, quite possibly this year's most moving film, Andrew Scott gives a captivating, awards-worthy performance as the late, great Scottish actor Ian Charleson. Though he never became a household name, Charleson's star shone brightly in the early 1980s when he appeared in two consecutive Best Picture winners: 1981's Chariots of Fire and 1982's Gandhi.

In a recent development, "I'd rather die of Hamlet than die of AIDS," Scott-as-Charleson claims in Elsinore, which opened in select theaters last week. This defiant line sums up the incredible coup de grâce that Charleson pulled off at the end of his life. When he began his valedictory stage run as Shakespeare's Danish Prince in October 1989, the 40-year-old actor was dying of AIDS. His face was so swollen with septicemia that the cast, crew, and audience at London's National Theatre were told he was recovering from a sinus operation.

It has been revealed that "I begged him not to do Hamlet. I remarked to him, It will kill you, which it did," Charleson's friend Sean Mathias, an accomplished actor and director in his own right, told me. "The amount of energy it takes to play that kind of classical role, both physically and spiritually, would tire the most ardent athlete. For a man dealing with the onslaught of AIDS, it was almost impossible.".

In a recent development, but against the odds, Charleson turned in a monumental performance. In a review for The Sunday Times, theater critic John Peter described his Hamlet as "virile and forceful" and wrote that the actor "oozes intelligence from every pore." Charleson's performance was all the more remarkable because he was an eleventh hour replacement for Daniel Day-Lewis, who left the production early—quite literally, midway through a performance—because he was so haunted by Shakespeare’s gothic tragedy.

It has been revealed that "People still remember Ian's performance as Hamlet," states Andrew Scott, whose performance in the film captures Charleson in the tumultuous final year of his life. Elsinore's screenwriter Stephen Beresford believes it's fitting that no footage of Charleson's defining performance exists. "An important thing to remember about Ian is his extraordinary contradictions," he says. "He wants to be seen and not seen, to be known and not known." Charleson, in fact, was so publicity-averse—perhaps partly because he was a closeted gay man—that he walked out of the Chariots of Fire press junket.

In a recent development, at the same time, he was simply an old-school British thespian who believed that the work should speak for itself. "Ian was incredibly passionate about this extraordinary part of Hamlet," Scott adds, citing the actor's devotion to his craft as a major incentive in his decision to join Elsinore. "But the chief thing [I love about him] is his courage and sense of humor.".

According to recent reports, in Elsinore, we see Scott's Charleson share his AIDS prognosis with his Hamlet castmates. When he died on January 6th, 1990, just seven weeks after his final curtain call, it was also disclosed to the public at large. At the time, Charleson's close friend Ian McKellen told the British press: "It is rare for anyone in the public eye to say that they are HIV positive, let alone that they have AIDS. It is a tribute to Ian that he should ask for the cause of his death to be made public and it is the most marvelous offer of support that he could have given to other men and women all over the world suffering from the AIDS virus.".

Beresford, who wrote Elsinore's screenplay after extensive conversations with Charleson's friends, family, and contemporaries, told me that it was actually the actor's father, Jack, who made the decision to disclose his cause of death publicly. "The tabloids were already circling, so I think there must have been fear that it was going to come out anyway," suggests Beresford, who previously penned the 2014 film Pride, which told the true story of gay and lesbian activists who raised money for the families of English coal miners during their 1984 strike.

Still, even if it wasn't carried out at his own behest, Charleson's posthumous contribution to HIV/AIDS awareness was very significant at a time when the disease was highly stigmatized and virtually impossible to treat. It would be another five years before HAART (highly active antiretroviral therapy) made the disease manageable.

In the U.K., the actor has also been immortalized with the annual Ian Charleson Awards, which since 1991 has recognized the best classical stage performances by actors under the age of 30. Past winners include David Oyelowo, Andrea Riseborough, Paapa Essiedu, Rebecca Hall, and Jack Lowden, while Benedict Cumberbatch, Cynthia Erivo, and Jessie Buckley have all received runner's-up prizes or commendations. "Ian's name is legendary within the [British] theater because of what he achieved in Hamlet, and the awards were set up to keep his memory alive," Beresford states.

Industry observers note that in Elsinore, we see Scott's Charleson wryly lamenting the fact that, though he starred in the Oscar-winning Chariots of Fire, "all anyone can ever remember is its theme music." In this stirring sports biopic, Charleson played Eric Liddell, a devout Christian who managed to win gold at the 1924 Olympic Games despite withdrawing from his best event, the 100-meter sprint, because the heats fell on a Sunday. Charleson also appeared in the following year's Best Picture winner, Gandhi, as an Anglican priest who supported the iconic title character's fight for Indian independence.

Sadly, despite these back-to-back triumphs, Charleson never made it as a bona fide movie star. By 1986, he was reduced to appearing in Car Trouble, a crass British comedy about a man who falls in love with his upcoming convertible. "He was very disappointed that film stardom didn't prolong itself," says Mathias, who believes that Charleson's sexuality denied him further opportunities in mainstream movies. "He wasn't out [publicly], but everyone in the business knew he was gay. And back then, gay actors just weren't given work in Hollywood.".

Consequently, and perhaps aptly given his predilection for the stage, Charleson found salvation in the theater. On June 25th, 1989, he appeared in a one-night only revival of Martin Sherman's seminal queer play Bent. This pointed production at London's Adelphi Theatre, which also starred McKellen, Ralph Fiennes and Richard E. Grant, was staged to raise money for The Stonewall Group, a newly formed nonprofit that went on to become the U.K.'s leading LGBTQ+ rights organization. Charleson portrayed Greta, a drag performer who changes into male-presenting clothes during the play.

By this point, Charleson's torso was covered in lesions caused by Kaposi's sarcoma, a rare form of cancer common in AIDS patients. Mathias, who was directing the fundraiser, had screens erected on stage so that Charleson could change costumes out of view. "Ian said to me, But the crew can still see my body from the wings! So I said I'd get more screens put up," Mathias remembers. "But then he thought about it, and went, You know what? Fuck it! I always feel that was the moment, really, that he decided he would come out [as having AIDS].".

In a recent development, shortly after Bent, Charleson was asked by Hamlet's director, Richard Eyre, to step in for Daniel Day-Lewis. Dickie Beau, an actor and writer who paid tribute to Charleson with his one-man stage show Re-Member Me (and who appears in Elsinore as the drag activist Sister Belladonna), believes Bent is a "truly significant" part of his legacy. “Not only did it help to kickstart [the charity] Stonewall, but it mentioned a lot about him that he was happy to play Greta, who isn't a leading part,” he says. "Ian McKellen once said to me that, as much as Charleson saw himself as a lead actor, he was also a organization man.".

Sources indicate that it's another of the fascinating contradictions that seem to make up Ian Charleson. Mathias says he was generally "quiet and private" and "very masculine," but also possessed a "wonderfully camp sense of humor." There's a poignant irony in his becoming the subject of a major motion picture, Beresford says, laughing: "Ian would have hated this publicity tour. I can guarantee that absolutely no part of him is watching us today!".

For Scott, who embodies Charleson so beautifully that he’s considered an awards season frontrunner, Elsinore's purpose is simple: “I hope our movie continues his legacy.”.

It has been revealed that ever since the NFL season kicked off back in September, the Minnesota Vikings’ star receiver Justin Jefferson has been going full-tilt. Last night, his team squared off against the San Fransisco 49ers in Mexico City (the NFL has been scheduling more away-gamers outside the U.S. to try to expand their viewership) in one of the marquee matchups of the season, and while the 49ers ended up winning that one, Jefferson remains inspired by the Vikings’ 7-3 record so far. “I’ve been great,” Jefferson indicates. “Everything’s been going really well, and I’m feeling good.”.

According to recent reports, preparing for such a big game is no small feat, of course—even if a pro like Jefferson makes it look easy. Ahead of hitting the field, you can often find him getting ready both physically and mentally. “Preparation is everything: I want to make sure I'm confident, focused, and ready to perform at my best,” he says. How did he prepare for Mexico City? “A big part has been making sure I'm physically and mentally ready for the challenges of playing at a higher altitude,” Jefferson says. (Mexico City is about 1.4 miles above sea level—much more intense than even Denver’s Mile High Stadium.) “I've been using the altitude chamber to help my body acclimate. Mentally, it’s about studying the plays, understanding the different schemes, and making sure we're approaching the game with the right mindset.”.

A more unexpected way Jefferson gets game-day ready, however: With his intentional tunnel-walk outfits. Yesterday, before the athletes even hit the field, Jefferson wanted to rock a meaningful look that would put him in the right mindset for his Mexico City matchup—so he enlisted one of the city’s most well-known designers, Patricio Campillo, to craft a custom look for him. “I've always tried to make my tunnel looks reflect where I am in the world, especially when we're playing internationally,” says Jefferson. “For me, fashion is an opportunity to connect with different cultures and showcase designers who bring something unique to the table.”.

A very cool moment for me: Meet the designer—Patricio Campillo—behind the look.

In a recent development, wanting to rep a design that represented the local culture, Jefferson called up Campillo to start ideating his custom look. He was drawn to the designer for his unique craftsmanship, creativity, and attention to detail. “Choosing Campillo felt like a natural decision—I was genuinely impressed,” claims Jefferson. “You can tell how much time, passion, and hard work goes into creating these looks. Being able to represent that craftsmanship on an international stage is something I think is really special.”.

Together, they landed on doing a cool, modern take on tailoring. Campillo created a cropped, boxy-style jacket with brown leather trousers—a signature element of the label that the designer wanted to introduce to a whole new audience. “It’s exciting to see someone of Justin’s caliber embrace Campillo,” he notes. “I’ve always believed that fashion has the power to bring together people from different backgrounds, so seeing an athlete like Justin connect with our work is especially meaningful.”.

He accessorized with pieces such as a horsehair bag, Oakley shades, and his signature chains. When the wide receiver put on the final look for the first ime, he was immediately drawn to the finer details. “One of my favorite details was the horsehair incorporated into the bag,” says Jefferson. “It’s such a unique touch and gives the piece a lot of character.” He also appreciated the hand-craftsmanship. “Knowing how much time and effort goes into creating each piece makes you appreciate the look even more,” he says. “I love wearing things that have a story behind them, and this outfit definitely does.”.

The fit, custom made by Patricio Campillo.

Industry observers note that it’s not the first time that Jefferson has flexed a fashion statement for his tunnel walk. During past games, he has worn everything from Off-White to Louis Vuitton and Chrome Hearts. What he wears and experiments, of course, depends on the setting. “My tunnel looks are really an extension of my personality, and how I’m feeling that day,” he says. “There are a few things I consider when putting a look together: my mood, who we’re playing, and the brands or designers I want to showcase. Fashion has become another creative outlet for me, and I enjoy stepping outside of what people might expect.”.

This fluid approach to dressing applies to his off-duty wardrobe, too. Jefferson indicates he enjoys playing around with fashion even on his days off. “Right now, I'd describe my personal style as evolving,” he says. “I'm really focused on experimenting with different looks and exploring styles I might not have considered earlier in my career. I like stepping out of my comfort zone and being open to trying newly introduced things. Fashion is all about self-expression, and I think the more willing you are to take risks, the more you learn about yourself and what you like.”.

It has been revealed that what does this mean for the rest of Jefferson’s NFL season? You can expect tons more tunnel-walk outfits, for starters. “Every week is another opportunity to bring something exciting to the tunnel,” he indicates. “We love finding ways to surprise people, turn heads, and keep things interesting.” Start taking your bets—fashion bets, not sporting bets—on what runway outfit or custom creation he will don next. “We’ve already had a few outfits this season that have gotten a lot of attention, and that’s always fun to see,” he says. “But for me, it’s not just about getting people talking—it’s about continuing to discover fresh brands, experimenting with different styles, and finding creative ways to express myself through fashion.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that honestly, anything can make for an alternative Thanksgiving dinner. It’s your house, your rules. Our only suggestion: Make it festive, fun, and at least a little decadent.

According to recent reports, A classic Thanksgiving menu is all well and good, but one of our colleagues swears by serving nachos on the fourth Thursday of every November. If a big bloomin’ bird just isn’t ca-caw-caw-calling your name this year, serve a whole roast fish, pork tenderloin with sour-sweet cherry sauce, or a flaky carrot Wellington instead.

In a recent development, or go completely rogue with lobster pasta or a substantial pot of chili. You can do that. Below, find vegetarian centerpieces, celebratory roasts, chicken dinners, and seafood mains for a Thanksgiving that looks a little different. BA’s Best Pumpkin Pie can stay.

Can carrots really count as a main course? They can when they’re roasted, glazed, and tucked into puff pastry with goat cheese, Gruyère, and walnuts. This Wellington feeds 8 to 10.

It has been revealed that red wine, browned mushrooms, pearl onions, and carrots give this meatless braise plenty of heft. Ladle it over mashed potatoes for a vegetarian anchor to your Thanksgiving menu.

Industry observers note that ruffled savoy cabbage, melty cheese, and a buttery cream cheese crust make this free-form tart worthy of the holiday table. Cut generous wedges for dinner and stick with savoy: Ordinary green cabbage won’t work here.

Recent findings suggest that A make-ahead casserole, like this pumpkin-infused strata scented with nutmeg and herbs and balanced by sharp cheddar, is just what your holiday schedule needs. Assemble it the night before; bake it on Thanksgiving.

Turkey isn’t the only holiday cooking project worth clearing the counter for. Delicate homemade crepes are rolled around ricotta, mozzarella, and Parmesan, then baked in marinara. Make the batter and filling a day ahead to split up the work.

In a recent development, kale, pinto beans, and charred poblanos make these cheesy enchiladas a satisfying holiday main for four to six. Get a head start by making the charred salsa verde up to three days ahead.

This autumnal risotto works as a standalone dinner or alongside your favorite Thanksgiving sides. Set the table with shallow bowls and pick a fall salad full of color and crunch to balance the buttery rice.

British beef Wellington meets Cantonese barbecue-style pork in Peter Som’s pastry-wrapped centerpiece. A shiitake mushroom filling and gravy made from the marinade complete the picture; assemble the Wellington a day ahead.

It has been revealed that these impossibly tender short ribs are begging to be served with mashed potatoes and buttery milk buns with garlic butter. Give them what they want—and give yourself a head start by braising the ribs the day before Thanksgiving.

Brisket more your speed? Try our Brisket Bourguignon →.

Turkey skin has competition. Tender pork belly, crisp crackling, and a hard cider pan sauce make a persuasive case for skipping the bird. Pass the chile vinegar to cut through the richness; this roast feeds 8 to 12.

Industry observers note that ayesha Curry’s spice-crusted prime rib takes its cues from her mother’s braised oxtails, with habanero crema on the side. Prefer a simpler garlic-and-rosemary approach? Try this Low-and-Slow Rib Roast.

In a recent development, for a roast-and-sides Thanksgiving without the turkey, garlic-and-rosemary-rubbed beef tenderloin makes an excellent centerpiece. Rosemary butter dresses the sliced roast, while tangy horseradish yogurt gives everyone something to swipe their next bite through.

Recent findings suggest that toasted rice, fried onions, and garlic form a dark, peppery crust on this slow-braised pork shoulder. Set out the massive platter and pass the coconut-vinegar pan sauce; this roast feeds 8 to 12.

Industry observers note that maybe save the brown sugar-glazed ham for Christmas? This whole leg of lamb makes for a centerpiece that’s just as showstopping. And, like ham and turkey, leftover lamb can be deliciously repurposed in sandwiches.

Industry observers note that A platter of sliced pork tenderloin with glossy cherries and browned shallots has plenty of holiday presence without a long roast. Honey and red wine vinegar give the sauce its sweet-sour bite, and frozen cherries are welcome here.

In a recent development, if you’re going to make tamales, it’s a good idea to make a lot of them. Better yet, turn the process into a party, with everyone spreading masa and folding corn husks around the red chile pork filling.

Sources indicate that this pasta packs a whole spectrum of holiday flavors into each bite, with crumbles of Italian sausage, shreds of brussels sprouts, and toasted pecans. Streamlining dinner into one dish leaves you more time for Thanksgiving pies.

Industry observers note that for some people, spending all Thanksgiving in the kitchen sounds like a good time. For everyone else, there’s this beef-and-bean chili. A can of pumpkin purée thickens the broth, keeping things seasonal without calling for a single roasting pan.

According to recent reports, give homemade fried chicken an even more festive angle with sage and thyme in the dredge and cranberry-mustard sauce for dipping. Start the buttermilk marinade the day before.

This whole roast duck comes with a built-in Thanksgiving side: The duck fat drippings go into basmati rice that cooks while the bird rests. Strategy for an overnight dry brine before the glossy pomegranate-honey glaze gets its moment.

According to recent reports, cooking for a smaller crowd? This skillet delivers the stuffing and the bird—chicken thighs, in this case—in one tidy package. Rendered chicken fat enriches the boxed stuffing mix, with dried cranberries and lemon zest brightening things up.

Industry observers note that two diminutive birds make a festive roast for four. A fiery guajillo chile, ginger, and vinegar marinade flavors both the hens and the potatoes beneath them, so the platter arrives with its own very good side.

You just need to make green beans, because this Thanksgiving main is already a two-in-one: Thinly sliced potatoes cook beneath a whole chicken, catching its drippings and crisping around the edges in the same cast-iron skillet.

Sources indicate that if your Thanksgiving table could use a little red sauce (and spice), skip the whole bird in favor of this take on chicken parm. Gochujang and gochugaru bring the heat; melted mozzarella keeps things gloriously gooey.

According to recent reports, josé Andrés turns chicken wings and a colorful assortment of vegetables into a grand centerpiece, with saffron and smoked paprika flavoring the rice. You’ll need a 15" paella pan or comparably sized two-handled cast-iron or cast-aluminum pan.

According to recent reports, there’s nothing like pasta to stretch a spendy ingredient (hello, lobster). Serve with a massive crunchy salad with Italian dressing and garlic confit toast that diners can pass around for Thanksgiving party vibes.

Sources indicate that presenting a whole fish at the holiday table is wildly celebratory, even when you’re cooking for just two or three. Bring out lettuce wraps, kimchi, rice, and ssamjang so everyone can build each bite a little differently.

Industry observers note that A large roasted salmon fillet looks right at home on a holiday platter, especially under a crunchy, garlicky nut salsa. Make the salsa up to four days ahead, then roast the fish when it’s time for dinner.

In a recent development, the stuffing doesn’t have to be a side. Here, crushed boxed stuffing mix joins Parmesan, lemon zest, and parsley in a crisp crust for mustard-coated white fish. Dinner lands on the table in 25 minutes.

It has been revealed that this dark, glossy coconut caramel—savory with fish sauce and garlic, sharp with pickled jalapeño brine—turns pan-seared salmon into a holiday-worthy main. Serve with rice to catch every last bit of sauce.

Like many of the best Thanksgiving dishes, this one starts with a good stock. Carla Hall builds a fennel potlikker with celery, onions, and Pernod before layering those flavors into a hearty bowl of shrimp and grits.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that back when Marc Jacobs was dressing the coolest girls of the aughts, retail wunderkind Robert Rich was his secret weapon.
  • In a recent development, rich's first book, Winona, made with Francesca Sorrenti, debuted in 2023 after he spotted merchandise on IDEA’s Instagram feed emblazoned with the likeness of Winona Ryder.
  • 163 Mercer is “directed” by Zoe Cassavetes, the director, screenwriter, and actress, who was the sales director of the nearby Mercer Hotel in the ’90s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that back when Marc Jacobs was dressing the coolest girls of the aughts, retail wunderkind Robert Rich was his secret weapon. Not unlike Truman Capote and his "swans," Rich welcomed friends such as Kate Moss, Selma Blair, Sofia Coppola, Maya Rudolph, Natasha Lyonne, Parker Posey, and Winona Ryder to his basement office in the brand’s downtown flagship store, documenting fittings and gab sessions with a Polaroid camera. Now, 163 Mercer, a fresh book from IDEA named for the store’s address, shares stories and photographs of fashion’s golden years just before digital changed everything.

In a recent development, rich's first book, Winona, made with Francesca Sorrenti, debuted in 2023 after he spotted merchandise on IDEA’s Instagram feed emblazoned with the likeness of Winona Ryder. "I reached out and asked if they wanted to do a Winona Polaroid book, and they immediately replied, 'Yes!'" he recalled over Zoom. It sold out on day one, and a second printing followed the next year. The experience left him wanting more creative outlets.

163 Mercer is “directed” by Zoe Cassavetes, the director, screenwriter, and actress, who was the sales director of the nearby Mercer Hotel in the ’90s. She met Rich when Jacobs and Marc Jacobs International president Robert Duffy sent her to the store to pick out a thank-you gift for her professional hospitality at the Mercer Hotel, where Jacobs often stayed.

Industry observers note that the duo, who are so close that they still speak on the phone every day, began brainstorming a project. "I had the photos of all the other girls, so I knew I wanted to do a book with those pictures," Rich stated. They considered wallpaper based on the wall collage or a podcast featuring a different one of the girls per episode, but Cassavetes's film background, including her 2007 directorial debut Broken English, made her the perfect book creative partner. IDEA said yes again.

In a recent development, they worked at Cassavetes’s Los Angeles apartment, laying out images on her oversized office table. "It's a lot like writing a script, which is why I say I ‘directed’ the book; putting together the layout was like making a movie," she said. I had a basement office, too," she recalled. Before Upcoming York's indoor smoking ban in 2003, the two took cigarette breaks indoors. "The logistics helped our friendship, hanging out in each other's offices smoking and having tea.".

Recent findings suggest that the book features images of regular visitors plus some who came once or twice, and the women graciously catalogued their memories for it. Don't expect captions throughout; it reads in parts like an IYKYK story asking viewers to figure out who is in the photo. "We didn't caption every Polaroid; they weren't like social media posts," Rich explained.

Recent findings suggest that instead of a feed, Rich created an office mood board wall that started with tear sheets and magazine covers of the girls in Marc Jacobs, then added fitting-room Polaroids, which grew more playful, plus newspaper clippings and memorabilia. What The Altruists Gets Right About Tech Scammers Like Sam Bankman-Fried

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2399 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the math holding up Netflix’s The Altruists is simple.
  • Recent findings suggest that famously, no bankers were sent to prison in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis.
  • Recent findings suggest that one of the threads in the journalism about the crimes, and on The Altruists, is that our power couple did not feel good in fancy spaces.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the math holding up Netflix’s The Altruists is simple. Anthony Boyle plays presently imprisoned one-time cryptocurrency king Sam Bankman-Fried, and Julia Garner plays Caroline Ellison, fellow momentary crypto royal and Bankman-Fried’s one-time romantic partner. Both actors cook so fearlessly that the show’s shortcomings recede into the background. What you’re left with is a tidy sum: two excellent performances that offer rich, vatic examinations of real-life figures. From these visions of Bankman-Fried and Ellison we get a glimpse into a crime and into a psychology.

Recent findings suggest that famously, no bankers were sent to prison in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis. No suit from Countrywide Financial walked the yard in Lompoc. But Samuel Bankman-Fried did go to prison after being found guilty of wire fraud and conspiracy. For the Bloomberg set, his trial was covered as intensely as O.J. Simpson’s, and each day of it hit trip wires: polycules, blockchain, non-fiat currency, etc.

Recent findings suggest that one of the threads in the journalism about the crimes, and on The Altruists, is that our power couple did not feel good in fancy spaces. But unlike the protagonists of so many other shows and movies from the tech-disruptor-story boom of the past 15 years, neither Boyle’s SBF nor Garner’s Ellison lean into rage.

On The Altruists, SBF and his inner circle frequent a Margaritaville in the Bahamas. They seem happy there, or at least at home. To be wildly rich, extremely young, and crushing vegan nachos at Jimmy Buffett’s theme restaurant is a choice made out of avoidance.

Sources indicate that the show’s first episodes make clear the overlaps between Ellison and Bankman-Fried. They were true math minds surrounded by the glib Wharton crowd, goofs with board games. They were not-conventionally-attractive people in an industry where many people are quite hot, and where the primarily hot at least know which regression tool best fits what task.

It has been revealed that the Altruists’s versions of SBF and Ellison found love in a hopeless place. Boyle interviews Garner for a position at Jane Street and they realize they have the exact same investment strategy—all in, all the time. If you didn’t know better, you’d be rooting for these two off-putting lovebirds to make a go of it.

Boyle’s performance mesmerizes. He seems to have control over his lashes, so completely articulated is his eye acting. His whole posture changes as he takes up different roles in the story: a curious loser, a gifted rhetorician, an anxious boss, an ignored former lover. The show shifts from alienation in Fresh York to crypto adventures in Hong Kong to the office-dorm hybrid of “The Orchid” in the Bahamas. Boyle owns the physical transformations, letting the glee of the Hong Kong era fester into the eyebags and stress-weight accrued (probably one of the more ethical uses of a bodysuit I can recall) in the scheme’s last days.

In a recent development, garner, meanwhile, has entered rarified air as a TV actor. Over the course of her career she has given us a moody, adrift Gen X student (Kimmy on The Americans), a Millennial lady of rage trapped in her dumpy hometown (Ozark), and now two glimpses of the self-satisfied Zillenial scammer (Anna Delvey in Inventing Anna and The Altruists). Garner’s signature move as a performer is to fail to sublimate anger or distress. Her characters have their own idiosyncratic patterns of twitches and attempts at steely gazes. The brittle darkness inside each of them sings. Her TV career belongs next to those of Elisabeth Moss and America Ferrera and Walton Goggins. It is time that this was generally acknowledged.

The supporting cast is solid, with one particular highlight. In the middle of The Altruist’s eight-episode run, we get an entire episode focused on Sam Trabucco, a college bestie of SBF, a former Alameda Research co-CEO, and an early cooperator with federal prosecutors once the wheels started falling off.

Alex Lawther plays Trabucco and almost walks off with the show. Lawther’s slight frame and self-searching candor give each line of dialogue intimacy. I first saw Lawther on Andor, playing Nemik, idealistic proto-Rebel and truest of true believers, a character based on Lei Feng, the Chinese communist folk hero and soldier, who, like Nemik on Andor, died in a freak accident but left behind a diary of such pure faith that it became a recruitment tool for the revolution. (A recording of Lawther reading that manifesto from his diary—his voice reedy and prophetic—literally haunts Imperial high command at the end of Andor.).

Industry observers note that in maybe my favorite scene of The Altruists, Trabucco and Ellison get dinner together. They talk and realize their childhood paths intersected and diverged across metro Boston—the same math competitions, the same tests. But their hometowns were quite different. She was from Newton. He was from Natick. If you’re from Upcoming England, that’s the only detail you need. (If you aren’t, I recommend Love Story and/or the novels of Dennis Lehane for background.) At that dinner, Lawther shares a deep, specific childhood memory of his father and Garner’s Caroline flinches without breaking eye contact, like she’s watching a recording of a natural disaster.

Recent findings suggest that sadly, the Netflix sins are here in full effect. The lighting is smeary and wildly off in many scenes. The music and sound mix could hardly be blunter. Even Oscar-nominated showrunner Graham Moore and talented directors like James Ponsoldt can’t lift dialogue that not-infrequently feels tailored to second-screen viewers: “They’re both off-the-charts math geniuses!”.

It has been revealed that the braided narrative can turn single episodes into distracting puzzle boxes. The form is designed to function the way a substantial juicy 10,000-word legacy-media reported feature does: You know the ending, so it takes a memorable reshuffling of moments and incidents to create something latest.

Sources indicate that but watching this gang of true believers and opportunists and criminally naïve teenage dream brains go from geographic zone to zone does carry emotional import. To them, and to The Altruists, the Bay Area has become a dated country club, a mirror image of The Social Network’s version of Harvard from the 2000s, back when the Bay Area promised something fresh. Post-Recession New York is greyscale normie central. Hong Kong and Macau blur together. The show ends in the Bahamas, a place that rich outsiders have always treated as both Eden and the afterlife.

I think the era of the tech-bro-scammer-titan show and movie is reaching its end. If its dawn was The Social Network, the unrepeatable, mesmerizing You Can See Everything might be the sunset. Gen X icons Aaron Sorkin and David Fincher once tried to get their heads around millennial narcissism and now millennial genius Nathan Fielder has transformed his time with a real-deal apex-predator narcissist into a Möbius strip of content.

Industry observers note that the drama of The Altruists depends on the psychology of the people who believe in crypto as a kind of syncretic faith. The show avoids a technical delineation of crypto itself, which makes sense. (I’ve yet to encounter a crypto evangelist who can provide a transparent explanation of the asset class that is superior to this.) ExxonMobil sells you a product and it works. Glock sells you a product and it works. Crypto works in so much as its existence justifies its existence. There are no earnings reports. Value is vibes.

Recent findings suggest that whenever something is being marketed as the future, it’s usually just the past, accelerated. People made crypto into an alternative financial system because they were “outsiders” who wanted to “disrupt.” Now the crypto system wants to be held close to the bosom of the enduring US financial markets and bulge bracket banks. A bill that would have brought them closer, setting up a regulatory framework, nose-dived in the senate.

It sounds almost cowardly, like running home to mom and dad: We made a brave new thing better and cooler and freer than your corrupt old monetary system. A few years later: Let us back in and give us all the benefits of the old system! Get us in your PNC digital wallet, normie!

Bankman-Fried and Ellison are both the children of elite academics. To its credit, The Altruists pokes these Freudian pains. Bankman-Fried was raised by Stanford Law professors and chose MIT. Ellison was the child of MIT academics and chose Stanford. There’s self-belief in those exact choices. The children of faculty get a significant leg up in gaining admission at their parents’ institution. SBF and Ellison wanted to do something honest on their own, at least once.

According to recent reports, my parents are retired professors. You learn early on that you cannot possibly replicate your parents’ careers. A child of a lawyer can have their parent’s career 2.0. Same if you have doctors for parents. But truly successful academics—and given the market today, you either are truly successful or you don’t exist—create niches built only for one.

Recent findings suggest that successful academics eschew any number of linear career paths and lucrative fields to burrow into zones of learning where they have to be singular, own every network and endure any marginal post (Oregon State, thou hast thy music, too). To make it to a top institution, you need luck and power and timing to dovetail your own research record and professional charisma. Many people make it to powerful banks and hospitals and law firms. But if you manage to get tenure at Berkeley, you might really be that special.

The track record of the children of academics I know is messy: deluded guys floating around Portland or Boston trying to jam their unreadable YA series into the world, an acquaintance who self-sabotaged a promising, morally-clear career as a social worker because they did not get a doctorate and let that arbitrary marker of value smother their self-worth for decades.

Sources indicate that SBF and Ellison were expected to perform precocity at all times, but the minute that they stumbled, Dr. Mom or Professor Dad stepped in with the better therapists and better lawyers to set everything right. The last two episodes of The Altruists bubble over with dread. Paul Reiser and Robin Weigert play SBF’s parents, and Jennifer Grey plays Caroline Ellison’s mom. Each performance puts its own spin on enmeshment and infantilization. The parents are not the big bads here. But they are the judgmental elitists who analyzed when they should have listened, and who raised these world-class scammers.

In a recent development, there was a guy a little like me in high school. Like me, he was the child of academics and teachers. Like me, he was clever and capable, which might have been enough in another high school. But such minor skills were door prizes in our grand, old, dizzyingly competitive boarding school. We both loved De La Soul. We were both cut from the same teams. We were both contrarians who trafficked in equal measures of insight and anserine bullshit. I won’t pretend to have been good friends with the guy—it was the classic situation where young men who play similar roles in their respective circles repel each other like the same sides of different magnets. But I sympathized. It’s painful to know exactly why you are not near the top of an elite ecosystem and then having to go on living in it.

It has been revealed that I imagined he might have a career adjacent to mine. I imagined that we might see each other in the late 2000s at a Babygrande Records release party or in the bathroom at Santos Party House. It did not play out that way. A few years ago, during the inevitable age-related transition from Facebook to LinkedIn, the guy’s face and name swum across my screen. He’s become a substantial deal in the crypto space. At one point, he rapped about crypto on crypto podcasts. On a class-wide group chat, as former classmates who had chosen to work in community health settings or on federally-funded research projects shared their pain after losing their jobs in the DOGE cuts, and as they voiced their concerns about what other digits of the American experiment would be severed next, this crypto dude commandeered the chat to brag about taking his company public. No child of an academic has ever missed a chance to make it about them.

Industry observers note that one of the side effects of the world-gobbling narratives around A.I. (which gets its own Social Network moment in Luca Guadagnino’s imminent Artificial, with Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman) is that crypto already feels cringe—at best, a chrome decoration on the world-shaking machinery of LLMs and Deep Learning. The brave newly introduced world of private money that needed no society and no army behind it has become just another widget. The most vulgar people in the world trade meme coins with Turkish billionaire failsons. That Uber driver for whom you had great sympathy waits forever for a crypto ship that will never come into port. (Bankman-Fried, as it happens, was an early investor in Anthropic; it was reported last week that his shares, liquidated during FTX's bankruptcy, would be worth $35 to $37 billion in the wake of the AI lab's splashy IPO.).

In a recent development, if 2026 is the close of the tech-movie and tech-show era, then how do we square The Altruists? It has arrived at the end of something. It’s not perfect, maybe not even excellent, but it is effective and memorable, and provides a showcase for superb young actors. I wonder how many of these reveals about tech founders, disruptors, optimists, hustlers and misanthropes will last. The paranoia of 70s American film evaporated in the desert of 80s escapism and the wry smirk of Ronnie Reagan. The thorny, violent prestige TV era begat the soft-clothes forever-childhood of Stranger Things and of Ted Lasso. Legacy cannot be legislated in advance. I hope viewers check out The Altruists, and appreciate its gumption in allowing love—the least efficient of emotions—to animate the story.

Recent findings suggest that but maybe I’m wrong. Maybe I’ve been hustled by Boyle and Garner’s wonderful acting. Maybe my almost-instinct about the past 15 years of watching damaged young ladder-climbers and their digital dreams on screen is almost true: what will survive of us is coins.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, after a screening of the surprisingly humorous pilot episode, Garner and her co-star, Anthony Boyle, joined the show’s creator, Graham Moore, for a panel discussion with actor-turned-journalist Ben McKenzie about the treachery, trickery, and turbulence that pervade the world of cryptocurrency.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“The first rule of acting is that you don’t judge your character,” Julia Garner told an enthralled audience on Thursday evening at Manhattan’s Paris Theater, moments after the credits rolled following the world premiere of The Altruists. The Netflix original series, available on the streaming platform now, sees Garner step into the shoes of Caroline Ellison, the disgraced co-CEO of Alameda Research and on-again, off-again girlfriend of FTX co-founder Sam Bankman-Fried. “I wasn’t necessarily thinking of the fraud. I just wanted people to be able to understand her,” she added.

In a recent development, after a screening of the surprisingly humorous pilot episode, Garner and her co-star, Anthony Boyle, joined the show’s creator, Graham Moore, for a panel discussion with actor-turned-journalist Ben McKenzie about the treachery, trickery, and turbulence that pervade the world of cryptocurrency. “You’re probably wondering what’s Ryan Atwood doing up here,” McKenzie joked from the stage, referring to his early-aughts turn as one of The O.C.’s leading teen heartthrobs. “For the last four years, I’ve been investigating and documenting fraud and other criminal activity… And having met and interviewed the real Sam Bankman-Fried, I would like to say that Anthony has a lot more charm [than him].”.

The series doesn’t just chronicle the shocking fall of Bankman-Fried and FTX. Rather, it centers largely on the romantic trajectory of the two financial-industry protégés. “It’s the story of two people who I genuinely, to the core of my being, believe got into this for the right reasons and wanted to do the right thing,” Moore said. “But over the course of their tortuous relationship and those six years, they turned each other into people who did the exact opposite of the thing they initially set out to do.” (Drawing a laugh from the crowd, Northern Irish actor Boyle likened their dynamic to “something from an episode of Love on the Spectrum.”).

After the panel, Garner, in a custom ballet-slipper-pink jumpsuit by Haider Ackermann for Tom Ford and an earful of Lorraine Schwartz bling, and an all-black-clad Boyle joined their castmates, crew members, and press for an after-party in The Plaza Hotel’s Oak Room—making it one of the last industry events to be hosted in the storied venue before it closes for a four-year renovation.

Over mini-umbrella-adorned mai-tais and passed bites, guests discussed the show and compared notes on how much they actually understood crypto terminology, while twirling SBF-approved fidget spinners and branded poker chips around in their hands.

Karan Soni, Madison Hu, and Naomi Okada.

  • How this will play out is anyone’s guess, but there are clues we can find in the past.
  • Recent findings suggest that however, just a few years into life as a superspy, Brosnan produced a remake of the classic menswear flick The Thomas Crown Affair.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that just a few months ago, Robert Pattinson signed on with Jaeger-LeCoultre as a brand ambassador, appearing in La Grande Maison’s ads wearing the new Master Control Chronometre Perpetual Calendar. However, that role has become complicated since the actor was announced as James Bond last week, given that the iconic character has been an Omega man for going on 31 years. This feels like uncharted waters, but it turns out this isn’t the first time two watch brands have competed for 007’s affections.

How this will play out is anyone’s guess, but there are clues we can find in the past. Bizarrely enough, this exact horological love triangle has played out before, when Pierce Brosnan was MI6’s top agent. The Irish actor taking up the mantle of 007 coincided with Omega coming on as Bond’s official watch supplier. In 1995’s GoldenEye, Brosnan wears the Seamaster Diver 300M with a blue-wave dial. The watch has become synonymous with Bond.

Recent findings suggest that however, just a few years into life as a superspy, Brosnan produced a remake of the classic menswear flick The Thomas Crown Affair. Due to his Bondbligations, dressing became extremely complicated. In the 1999 movie, Brosnan is forced to wear an open shirt and an untied white bow tie draped around his neck during a black-tie ball because his Bond contract reportedly forbade him from wearing a tuxedo in other movies. And because of the actor’s contract with Omega, Thomas Crown’s watch had to be handled just as delicately.

Recent findings suggest that nick Gould, watch spotter extraordinaire, pointed out to us that Pierce Brosnan, still in the midst of his run as 007, strapped on a JLC Reverso for The Thomas Crown Affair remake. The reversible watch was a perfect symbol of the titular character’s double life. But because Brosnan was still entwined with Bond, the watch’s dial was scrubbed to remove both the brand and model name. The coincidence that a Bond would have to select between a JLC and an Omega is even stranger because, unlike Pattinson, Brosnan had no ties to JLC. And there wasn’t some unbreakable tie between Thomas Crown and the brand either. In the original version of The Thomas Crown Affair, Steve McQueen wears a Patek Philippe pocket watch, a Cartier Tank Cintrée, and a Jaeger-LeCoultre Memovox.

According to recent reports, now, Pattinson and Brosnan’s situations aren’t perfectly analogous. The latter’s affair involved a one-off movie placement that conflicted with Bond’s requirement to wear Omega. Pattinson’s predicament involves a freshly inked brand ambassadorship butting up against 007’s long-held partnership. However, it is strange to see the exact pair of brands tied up in Bond-related drama.

This time around, neither brand appears to be backing down. In the wake of Pattinson’s announcement, JLC noted in a statement: “Jaeger-LeCoultre warmly congratulates Robert Pattinson on his appointment to the iconic role of James Bond, a tremendous milestone in an already distinguished cinematic career.” And a representative confirmed, “Robert Pattinson continues in his role as a Global Ambassador for Jaeger-LeCoultre under our existing agreement.” Meanwhile, Omega has posted its Bond watches several times on Instagram. Pattinson, of course, is caught in the middle. As watch lovers first and foremost, we personally love the idea of him continuing to wear JLC on his own time and a Seamaster 300M on Bond time. After all, if anyone can lead a double life while keeping two competing loyalties straight, surely it’s 007.
