Chipotle’s Thanksgiving Eve BOGO Returns For One Night Only—Here's How To Get It

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (356 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanksgiving is practically an Olympic event for eating, but there’s nothing wrong with a little warm-up the night before.
  • Sources indicate that the deal runs Wednesday, November 25, from 5 to 9 p.m.
  • But, as expected, there’s some fine print worth reading before you get in line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanksgiving is practically an Olympic event for eating, but there’s nothing wrong with a little warm-up the night before. Chipotle is bringing back its Thanksgiving Eve BOGO deal, giving you a perfectly good excuse to grab a burrito with an old friend before the turkey, stuffing, and inevitable food coma take over.

Sources indicate that the deal runs Wednesday, November 25, from 5 to 9 p.m. local time at participating U.S. restaurants, with the usual buy one entrée, get one free format we all know and love.

But, as expected, there’s some fine print worth reading before you get in line. You’ll need to be a Chipotle Rewards member, order at the restaurant, and scan your Rewards card at checkout. The free entrée must cost the same as or less than the one you're buying, and you can claim up to five free entrées per check. Kids’ meals don't qualify, and ordering ahead through the app, online, or for delivery won't work.

The timing has changed a bit from last year, too, when it ran from 4 p.m. all the way until closing. This time, you've got a four-hour window, so make sure that one friend you have who’s perpetually late gets the memo.

“The response last year showed us how much our guests embraced the occasion,” Stephanie Perdue, Chipotle's senior vice president of brand marketing, said in a statement. According to the chain, the promotion ended up being its biggest sales-driving campaign of 2025, so a return trip was probably inevitable.

And if you’re stuffed and don’t feel like leaving the couch the next day, there’s a little something for the post-Thanksgiving crowd as well. From Friday, November 27, through Monday, November 30, Chipotle is waiving its delivery fee on eligible orders placed through its app or website with code CYBER26. You’ll need to spend at least $10 in the U.S. or $12 in Canada, and delivery menu prices may be higher, with other fees still applying.

If nothing else, it’s a convenient excuse to take a break from the annual challenge of finding increasingly creative ways to eat leftover turkey.

#112596. Latest Update: Setting Up Shop in Istanbul

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3383 w)

Latest Update: Setting Up Shop in Istanbul

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3383 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in Istanbul, hosts encourage guests to stay as long as they like — even in luxury department stores.
  • According to recent reports, the store is located in Galataport, a cultural and shopping district adjacent to the Bosphorus, the strait separating Türkiye’s European and Asian sides.
  • Sources indicate that beyond luxury retail, Istanbul and Türkiye are widely renowned for their role in the textile and leather industries, home to a large portion of the major clothing manufacturers used by Western brands, including Isko Denim, Kipaş and Bilsar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in Istanbul, hosts encourage guests to stay as long as they like — even in luxury department stores. “We want our client to spend time here, to sit here, to play backgammon, to chat, to have a drink,” notes Sebla Refiğ Devidas, chief merchandising officer at Communité, a new concept-department store hybrid, first opened in April of this year, with two outposts on the European side of the city. “We wanted to give a homey, warm feeling,” she adds, guiding me through the retailer’s second location, opened in May. Unlike many of Istanbul’s retail spaces, the store features windows throughout, letting natural sunlight fill the curving, geometric shop-in-shops, clean furnishings, and marble plinths. We pass rails of brands including Martine Rose, Simone Rocha and Auralee, as well as a warmly lit Mayfair-style restaurant, a glass-paneled red-light therapy salon and box vitrines of jewellery by Turkish jewellery designer Sevan Bıçakçı.

According to recent reports, the store is located in Galataport, a cultural and shopping district adjacent to the Bosphorus, the strait separating Türkiye’s European and Asian sides. Galataport is also home to a number of luxury players. Beymen — Türkiye’s answer to Bergdorf Goodman — has an outpost. There’s also a Vakkorama, the luxury retailer Vakko’s accessible, contemporary store. And Turkish design-focused luxury chain Gizia Gate. Together, these four names (Communité, Beymen, Vakko and Gizia Gate) define the Turkish fashion landscape, taking the lion’s share of a relatively small fashion retail market.

Sources indicate that beyond luxury retail, Istanbul and Türkiye are widely renowned for their role in the textile and leather industries, home to a large portion of the major clothing manufacturers used by Western brands, including Isko Denim, Kipaş and Bilsar. Value-seeking shoppers also enjoy the region’s stores specializing in factory seconds — lightly defective branded apparel sold at a discount — and counterfeit luxury goods available in the historic Grand Bazaar, where sellers are naturally averse to photography.

Sebla Refiğ Devidas (left) works as the chief merchandizing officer at Communité.

According to recent reports, istanbul has a population of more than 15 million people, while Türkiye has over 86 million. According to data from Euromonitor, Türkiye’s market for luxury goods delivered steady growth in 2025, recovering from continued macroeconomic pressures. High-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) remained a core driver for growth, while inflation — exacerbated by the Middle East crisis — dragged on discretionary spending for middle-income groups. The report also cited Gucci, Hermès, Prada and Louis Vuitton as some of the leading international brands in the personal luxury goods category. In 2026, Euromonitor forecasts luxury sales to reach almost $28 billion in 2026, over double the revenue in 2021.

“Istanbul sits at the heart of this opportunity, supported by growing domestic wealth alongside its strength as an international shopping, hospitality and cultural destination,” states Fflur Roberts, Euromonitor International’s head of luxury. Tourism is becoming particularly vital, she adds, noting that international visitors now account for 29% of personal luxury goods spending in Türkiye, up from 20% in 2019. “Wealthy Russian travelers have contributed to this shift, as geopolitical developments redirect travel and luxury spending toward markets including Türkiye and the UAE.”.

Outside Communité’s new location in Galataport.

Sources indicate that currently, Roberts reports, online channels account for 21% of personal luxury sales in Türkiye — which is more than double the share in 2015. “Yet physical retail remains important, giving Istanbul an opportunity to combine global luxury brands with Turkish fashion, craftsmanship, hospitality, gastronomy and culture as consumers increasingly blend shopping with travel and experiences,” Roberts affirms.

Within this relatively small retail pond, luxury retail competition is fierce.

And competition is heating up. Communité will open two more stores on the European side and one on the Asian side in 2027, complementing a strong online presence. The retailer is owned by Boyner, which originally founded Beymen in 1970. Beymen has now changed ownership: since 2015, the Qatari fund Mayhoola has been investing in the retailer, eventually taking control in 2019.

Inside Communité, clients can inquire about buying the furniture.

Devidas was a merchandising lead at Beymen, but in August 2024, following a five-year non-compete clause, she and many of her former colleagues from Boyner jumped ship to the newly founded Communité. “We didn't want to repeat what we had done,” she notes. “But we wanted to create something upcoming from scratch.” During the research stage, the team traveled the globe, informing their objectives for clienteling, product assortments and dwell time. Hospitality will prove integral to its value proposition, she says.

Sources indicate that insiders respect it, too. Cemre Bosnalı Zeydanlı, Vogue Türkiye’s strategy editor, pinpoints the retailer as exemplary of Türkiye’s retail development: “With its locations at İstinye Park and Galataport, the concept goes beyond traditional multi-brand retail by bringing together fashion, beauty, design, culture and lifestyle.”.

It has been revealed that on my visit to Communité, Devidas tells me that much of the furniture in the store is available to buy. There are Turkish brands — Lug Von Siga, for example — alongside mega international brands, including Japanese streetwear giant A Bathing Ape (Bape), which Devidas indicates is a Communité exclusive in Türkiye.

Taking a more traditionally luxe approach, Beymen Group is ramping up its retail presence across the country. The retail giant owns 290 stores in various formats across Türkiye and Egypt (a small operation): 25 multi-brand, 60 franchise stores with leading designer brands, and three of its own brands. The expansion is in progress.

During my stay in the city, Beymen underscores its luxury ambitions with a ritzy event program, built around a fresh exhibition, Timeless Treasures — an homage to traditional Anatolian envelope bags through the lens of contemporary Western and local designers — at its flagship location in the wealthy shopping and hospitality district of Tersane. The exhibition coincides with the OMA-designed store’s first anniversary and intends to bridge a gap between the Turkish and global fashion landscape.

Toasting the occasion, Beymen invited industry authorities and fashion designers Giuseppe Zanotti, Giuseppe Santoni and Antonin Tron to a black-tie gala. During the evening, brand execs rubbed shoulders with Beymen group’s senior leadership team as group CEO Elif Çapçı outlined her vision for Beymen and the future of Türkiye’s fashion landscape. Diana Ross performed afterwards.

High-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) typically lead consumer spending for Beymen, and the manufacturer — thanks to Mayhoola’s investment — is courting this, enhancing its store experiences and private-shopping service. Beymen has no prepares to expand globally and will focus almost entirely on Türkiye.

Beymen’s Tersane location was designed with the Office for Metropolitan Architecture (OMA).

The reason for Beymen’s focus on the home market? It needs to feel rooted in the location. “The department store is more like a house that you bring people to,” indicates Rachid Mohamed Rachid, Mayhoola CEO and chairman for Valentino and Balmain. “People have to be comfortable with the culture, with the DNA, with the approach.” This fiscal year, the group is close to making €1.5 billion, growing at 15% in the first nine months.

According to recent reports, while Communité’s footprint doesn’t quite compete with Beymen, Vakko’s — opened first as a small hat shop in 1934 — does. As of March 31, the manufacturer has 150 stores and remains a household name in Türkiye. The company offers a variety of categories, own-brand goods and store formats including Vakkorama, Vakko Couture (a fashion-forward boutique) and the original Vakko luxury stores.

Tarik, 28, a sales adviser in Vakkorama.

Industry observers note that tarik, 28, works in Vakkorama’s Galataport location. He explains that customers engage with the retailer for its fashion-forward choice of brands evidenced in the V2K Designers range — Marni, Thom Browne, JW Anderson, for example — as well as unique pieces from brands, such as Adidas, that can’t be found elsewhere in the country.

“I think multi-brand stores such as V2K Designers play an notable role in Istanbul’s fashion ecosystem,” claims Zeydanlı. ”Being able to explore collections from different designers in one place brings a more curated perspective to shopping.”.

Vakko — which own sub-brands V2K, Vakkorama, and Vakko Couture — is one of the massive four in the Turkish retail market.

For local Turkish designers, landing one of the significant four wholesalers can be hard, especially if you’re an emerging voice. When Gul Agis, the designer behind established Turkish brand Lug Von Siga, started out 17 years ago after studying in Italy, she actually focused on reaching stores across mainland Europe, taking part in fashion weeks and trade demonstrates in Berlin, Paris and Milan. “It was quite challenging for me because where Milan was quite professional in prêt-à-porter, it was almost the beginning here [in Istanbul],” she remembers. “Most of the fashion houses or designers used to do more haute couture or made-to-measure pieces.”.

At the time, she states that the major Turkish retailers tended to focus on foreign brands. Fast forward to now, and a lot has changed. Lug Von Siga has since been stocked by Beymen and Gizia Gate, although those partnerships have now ended. Today, she works with Vakko and Communité, plus a myriad of European stockists including Harvey Nichols, Farfetch and Harrods.

Vakkorama’s Galataport location faces a waterway used by cruise ships.

Istanbul’s retail landscape is substantial on malls, comprising key fresh-build districts such as Tersane, Galataport and Zorlu Center. Shoppers take their time while purchasing, sipping coffee or Turkish tea, and store advisors provide discretion and advice where necessary for private clients. The shopping experience is slower and more relaxed, compared to fashion hubs like London and New York.

Consumers in Istanbul rely on malls such as Zorlu Center on the European side.

In a recent development, beyond these purpose-built complexes, Istanbul is also home to an even more easygoing, hilly, open shopping district, Nişantaşı, on the European side of the city. Here, Prada, Chanel, Beymen, Vakko, and other major players have stores, as well as a substantial number of concept stores. Turkish fashion photographer Fırat Koçak, who joins me on the journey, describes Nişantaşı as a trendier district, with many editors, stylists and photographers living here. National treasure designer Ozgur Masur’s showroom is here, as well as Agis’s.

Nişantaşı’s Shopi Go is a perennial hangout for cool kids. Opened in 2012 in a former Chinese food joint, complete with exposed-brick walls, the cozy two-story store is arranged with coffee-table books, knick-knacks, and niche fashion apparel. Y-3’s cleat football sneakers, Wales Bonner x Umbro designs, and pieces from underground Turkish label Doomster fill the space. It’s charmingly dingy, and the product assortment is esoteric, clearly aimed at a more niche Turkish consumer.

Shopi Go is a Chinese-food-spot-turned concept store.

Shopi Go is aimed at the more directional Turkish consumer, offering Wales Bonner x Umbro through to local brand Doomster.

According to recent reports, A few blocks away, two smiling buyers — Emir Akdogan and Dylon Kader — sit outside the streetwear store Wunder’s largest location. They’ve agreed to show me around. Inside, the architecture is restrained, cold and contemporary — a far cry from the more luxe DTC stores peppered elsewhere in the area. Wunder’s first store opened in 2015 in Kadikoy, a district on the Asian side, and quickly capitalized on the sneaker boom. In 2021, Wunder opened the Nişantaşı store. Today, it continues to push anticipated sneakers from Nike (including Jordan) and Salomon, as well as streetwear from brands including Stüssy, Carhartt and Stockholm Surfboard Club.

“I assume we are the only super-contemporary store, rather than a department store [in Istanbul], which makes us slightly different,” claims Akdogan. “Still, sneakers are a huge part of the business,” says Kader. “We were one of the stores that had camps — first come, first served. People put tents in the streets. It was so new to the Turkish community, and the Turkish market, so it was not done before.”.

It has been revealed that in Istanbul, stray cats are treated with reverence and free neutering. They’re not typically allowed in stores, though.

In a recent development, akdogan and Kader describe the Turkish market as a little slower to catch on to hot European market trends. The pair tells me that they had to convince the Salomon global team to come to Türkiye. When Salomon agreed, two to three years ago, Wunder began selling the brand. “The first three or four seasons, it didn’t sell at all — even with discounts,” remembers Kader. “Then last season, something happened. People started to ask for Salomons, and we started to bump up our orders.”.

The buyers want to set trends and be global, but contend that does involve some business sacrifice as the national market catches up with global trends. That stated, the most loyal consumer for Wunder is an educated shopper, the pair confirm.

Emir Akdogan and Dylon Kader are buyers at Wunder, one of the original streetwear stores in the city.

Recent findings suggest that “Türkiye is a dynamic market for fashion and luxury, but one shaped by its own economic and cultural nuances,” notes Zeydanlı. “One of the most interesting aspects of the Turkish market, in my opinion, is the consumer’s interest in both global fashion houses and local designers.” Zeydanlı encourages brands looking to enter the Turkish market to understand local consumer expectations, developing the right pricing strategy to handle growing price sensitivity among consumers.

Beymen’s chief merchandising officer, Ahmet Öcal, explains that the firm’s buying strategy is rooted in a deep understanding of their clients’ lifestyles. “We serve a diverse and increasingly sophisticated customer base through Beymen’s extensive brand curation and personalized service approach, ranging from established luxury clients who value heritage, craftsmanship and timeless elegance, to younger, fashion-forward consumers who are looking for newness, individuality and self-expression,” he explains, noting that the core consumer base is local, while 15% are international tourists.

Industry observers note that “Occasion wear, elevated casualwear, luxury handbags, jewelry, cosmetics, and beauty are particularly relevant categories for our market,” says Öcal. “Resort wear is another vital area, reflecting the lifestyle of our customers and their connection to destinations like Bodrum.”.

“When it comes to clienteling, I believe the emphasis should be on genuinely understanding the customer: their personal style, preferences and shopping habits,” notes Zeydanlı. “Curated product selections, early access to upcoming collections, private shopping appointments, and invitations to exclusive brand experiences all play an notable role.” This chimes with the kind of customer engagement strategies Beymen employs, maintaining close and enduring relations with top spenders, many of whom have shopped there for years.

Across the board, luxury players cite millennials as a strong consumer in the Turkish retail landscape, particularly those within the 30 to 40 bracket. Beymen’s target consumer is roughly 35-plus. That said, players should ensure they speak to younger generations. For Zeydanlı, Gen Z might not have the strongest purchasing power yet, but they remain a key consumer group shaping the future of luxury. “Gen X, meanwhile, remains an crucial segment, particularly among high-net-worth consumers, thanks to more established luxury shopping habits and stronger brand loyalty,” she states.

The city of Istanbul is relatively young in the global luxury retail market, despite its strong manufacturing heritage. “However, on the design side, we are lacking certain components that would make our designers global names and successful on a global scale,” says Mayhoola’s Rachid. “The visibility is not there.”.

In a recent development, setting up shop here as a local independent designer remains risky, although it’s improving. Across the board, international household names rule the market.

In a recent development, however, as the market grows, tastes could shift. While Beymen might choose to focus its efforts on the local demand, the Istanbul region still has plenty of white space. “We see an important distinction between generations,” says Öcal. “While our more established customers tend to prioritize quality, exclusivity and long-term value, Gen Z and younger millennials are more experimental, trend-conscious and open to discovering emerging designers and brands.”.

The importance of physical retail in Türkiye is another advantage. Euromonitor’s findings revealed that brick-and-mortar stores dominated personal luxury goods distribution in the nation last year.

Beymen’s Tersane flagship location opened last year.

“The importance high-net-worth consumers place on personalized service and exclusive shopping experiences makes physical stores indispensable for luxury brands,” argues Zeydanlı. “I believe independent designers and local brands are becoming increasingly visible. Consumers are looking beyond global fashion houses and are also interested in discovering brands with a distinctive design identity, more limited production and a unique creative perspective.”.

Communité is an experiment in the market. Prospective competitors will be watching closely to see if it lands or if it’s just too soon.

Recent findings suggest that matt, 45, a firm owner based in Istanbul, is trying on a Beymen Club (the group’s own brand) knit in Beymen’s Galataport location. He opts for brands that aren’t “too vulgar”, preferring what he calls “silent luxury”. “I don’t like clothing with huge brand [logos] on them,” he says. “This is one of the places you can find the stuff that [I’m] looking for.” Annually, his typical clothing spend sits at no more than around $5,000 per year. “I don’t shop very often to be honest with you,” he says. For Matt, the country’s luxury sector isn’t especially different from other countries, although he does note a preference among consumers for more visibly branded clothing.

Originally from Germany, Ayliz, 22, owns her own brand. Her store is around the corner. She’s posing for a photo in Nişantaşı when I stop her to ask what she makes of the Turkish fashion landscape. “I think Türkiye follows world trends. So, people my age, we wear things that are viral now on social media,” she says. As a shopper, she’s drawn to high luxury, citing Loro Piana and Chanel, and she prefers physical retail. “100% in-person. I have to feel the texture, and see how it looks on me.” She sees Türkiye as a place where you can shop “everything you want”, offering far more stores than her home country.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Inspired by the iconic egg and sausage sandwich on a pancake bun, this breakfast casserole is cheesy and just a smidge sweet from the brushing of maple butter at the very end. Destined for holiday brunch tables everywhere and best enjoyed while you’re still in pajamas, this cozy bake will feed a full house. (Don’t be surprised if you find yourself making it again long after the last guest leaves though!).

More high-protein breakfast recipes here.

Sources indicate that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Lightly coat a 13x9" baking dish with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Whisk 2½ cups (313 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ cup (50 g) sugar, 2 Tbsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Set aside.

Cook 2 lb. breakfast sausage, casings removed if needed, in a large skillet set over medium-high heat, stirring and breaking into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until browned and cooked through, 10–12 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer sausage to a small plate, leaving fat behind. Pour fat into a heatproof measuring glass. You want ½ cup fat; spoon out any excess or pour in vegetable oil as needed if you don’t have enough. Stir 2 large eggs and 2 cups whole milk into fat. Let sausage cool slightly, then crumble into small, even pieces with your hands.

Recent findings suggest that pour fat mixture into reserved dry ingredients and stir until just combined and no large dry pockets of flour remain (batter may be thin and lumpy; it’ll be fine). Set aside ½ cup sausage and ½ cup cheese from 8 oz. sharp yellow cheddar, coarsely grated (about 2 cups), for topping, then add remaining sausage and cheddar to batter and stirring until evenly distributed.

Industry observers note that scrape batter into prepared baking dish and evenly scatter reserved sausage and cheese over. Bake casserole until top springs back when gently pressed with your finger and a tester inserted into the center comes out with just a few moist crumbs attached, 20–30 minutes.

Just before casserole is done, heat 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a small skillet over medium, stirring occasionally, until butter is melted, about 2 minutes.

According to recent reports, brush maple butter over casserole and let cool 10 minutes. Cut into squares. Serve with more maple syrup and butter alongside.

#112594. Breaking: Doing Crime Barely Covers My Menswear Habit in GTA VI

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1399 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gq ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Doing Crime Barely Covers My Menswear Habit in GTA VI

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1399 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When GTA 6 came out at midnight last week, I played it for eight hours straight, all in the name of real, boots-on-the-ground journalism.
  • In a recent development, most people will have spent their first-ever session getting through the missions, exploring the map, and finding out what Jason and Lucia have got themselves into.
  • Before we get into it, you should know: Your in-game clothes matter more than ever compared to other entries in the Grand Theft Auto universe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I am still slightly delirious. When GTA 6 came out at midnight last week, I played it for eight hours straight, all in the name of real, boots-on-the-ground journalism. Well, there was a quick power nap somewhere around 5 a.m., but otherwise I've been working very hard. I have a new wardrobe and some concerns about the price of digital jorts.

In a recent development, most people will have spent their first-ever session getting through the missions, exploring the map, and finding out what Jason and Lucia have got themselves into. Not me. My main goal was to visit as many shops as possible. It's been 13 years since GTA 5; I wanted to see what had happened to the menswear.

Before we get into it, you should know: Your in-game clothes matter more than ever compared to other entries in the Grand Theft Auto universe. As I wrote last week, the latest “heat” system lets cops remember what you were wearing, so losing them doesn't necessarily mean you're in the clear. Changing your hat or sunglasses won't clear the clothing clue, either. You need a full fit change. So technically, all this shopping could help me get away with something. That's my justification, anyway.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, even virtual shopping requires cold, hard cash—and early on, that takes considerably more effort than I'd hoped. You start with almost nothing, spending much of the opening stretch around Key Lento in swampy Mariana County. I'd gone in expecting to buy loads of clothes. Instead, I was checking what I could afford.

My first opportunity came in a random gun shop that also sold some workwear. I had a quick browse then went straight for the camo shorts. Back in August, British GQ's senior style editor Mahalia Chang declared that “camo shorts are fucking back, baby,” having watched Jason spend much of the trailer wearing them. Who was I to argue?

In a recent development, nearby, in Hamlet, I found a few thrift shops and picked up a battered chore jacket with more than a little Carhartt Detroit about it. It looked properly used, which suited both my budget and the general condition of my pickup. I bought a watch, too, but more on that another time.

I was already getting quite into it. I was comparing pieces, checking prices, and deciding what could wait. There were clothes I wanted and clothes I could afford. Annoyingly, the game understood the difference.

I bought a trucker cap at one point and was very happy with it. Over the summer, I wrote about wanting to give them another go despite having a head my mates call “a sniper's dream.” Jason doesn't have that problem (in a metaphorical sense, anyway), so I thought I'd let him enjoy one. Shortly afterwards, a gang of lads picked a fight with me, punched me, and knocked it off his head. I fled, only realizing once I was safely away that I hadn't picked it back up. I'd barely had a chance to enjoy it. I hope one of them's wearing it at least.

Industry observers note that after a few missions, I finally had enough money to justify another shopping trip. I got into my beaten-up pickup and headed downtown, where the prices started getting a little more serious. Denim jackets were around $120. A pair of dark wash jorts I really liked cost $45, which was slightly more than I wanted to spend.

According to recent reports, I appreciate that this is a game in which you can steal a car, and I was still having a small financial discussion with myself about the price of shorts. For a game called Grand Theft Auto, I'd done surprisingly little car stealing in the time I'd been playing.

Sources indicate that the map is absolutely massive, and there almost 70 clothing stores to work through, so visiting everything was never gonna happen in one sitting. Cars now use fuel, too. Driving miles out of your way to look at a jacket comes with an additional expense, and I had to leave enough money to get home.

According to recent reports, there was a reason to keep exploring, though. I went into another shop expecting more of the same and realized the stock was different, so now I wanted to check the other shops before buying anything. Apparently, I'd waited 13 years to recreate how I spend my Saturdays.

Naturally, I decided to drive to Ocean Beach, a more expensive part of the city where I had very little business shopping. Inside Nola, the person at the till looked me up and down in my shitty workwear and asked, “Eh, are you looking for somebody?”.

Sources indicate that it was an impressively efficient assessment of my finances. Nola felt a little like Casablanca, the French-Moroccan label known for colorful prints, sportswear, and clothes that suggest a considerably nicer holiday than the one you're on. I'd previously called Hawaiian shirts “the unofficial uniform of Vice City.” Here, joining in cost about $330. Blazers were about $430. I could look, provided I didn't get any dirt on anything.

Sources indicate that then I accidentally punched the shop assistant; I'm still getting used to the controls. At least, I think it was an accident. Either way, I had to flee before I could give the blazers much consideration. When I came back later, the store was temporarily closed. I hope it wasn't due to staff injuries.

Recent findings suggest that other boutiques were even less accommodating to my balance. Italian house Ferruccio Tucci (probably a GTA-ified Emilio Pucci) had $3,000 suits and $1,200 horsebit loafers. I went in to browse and accidentally bought a pair of $350 shades, which was a very expensive way to learn which button does what. The annoying thing is that they looked genuinely sick—exactly the sort of thing I'd wear IRL, which made it much easier to justify keeping them. Well, that was fuel and dinner gone for the day. At least I could look good while walking home.

Later, driving past Waxman Island, I came across Vice City's Eris flagship. Obviously, I had to go in. For anyone who hasn't spent the past few months staring at fictional trainers, Eris is basically GTA's answer to Nike. Nike takes its name from the Greek goddess of victory; Eris is the goddess of strife and discord. The shoes are often just as recognizable as the joke.

The store kinda reminded me a little of Niketown in London—presently closed for refurbishment—with neon lights and big statues and enough footwear to keep me occupied considerably longer than was sensible. There was the Rise Low, an Air Force 1 lookalike that I ended up getting in two colourways; the Strife 360, with its very Air Max 97-ish shape; and the Rook 1 High, which follows the Air Jordan 1 High. I own more than 400 pairs of sneakers IRL—I probably should've known that going in here would be a problem.

According to recent reports, and Eris is only one option. There are alternative sneaker labels, beach shops, souvenir shops, and smaller, DIY-looking streetwear brands all dotted around the city. I'd barely begun working through them. Every time I thought I'd seen enough to stop, there was another shop worth going into.

In a recent development, the most expensive-looking thing I acquired didn't come from a boutique at all. Slight spoiler: A naked man offered to give me his “Crowex” watch after pulling a plastic egg out of his own ass. (Yes, you read that right.) You'll know him when you see him. I'm not gonna go into any more detail, partly because I'm tired and partly because I'd like you to experience that transaction yourself.

Recent findings suggest that eight hours in, I'd hardly scratched the surface. What surprised me most was how long the expensive stuff felt like it would take to earn. Those suits and loafers were sitting there, available to try, while my balance suggested another few missions first. There's a lot of city left to explore, quite a few shops I want to revisit, and a pair of jorts I'm still thinking about.

Recent findings suggest that for now, though, I need some sleep. And Jason needs to earn back that $350.

A version of this story originally appeared in British GQ.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

In a recent development, whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

It has been revealed that toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

In a recent development, heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Recent findings suggest that add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Christmas might get the lights, presents, and monthlong buildup, but Ina Garten has a few thoughts about which holiday really deserves the fuss. And if a certain Thanksgiving side dish comes up in conversation, the Barefoot Contessa’s face might tell you everything you need to know.

Industry observers note that during the November 18 episode of her Happy Hour with Ina Garten podcast, the cookbook author asked guest Rose Byrne about her first Thanksgiving in the United States. The Australian actress recalled attending a Friendsgiving, with everyone contributing something to the meal, and Garten immediately wanted to know whether the whole thing had been organized in advance or “if everyone just showed up with string beans.”.

Things got even funnier when Byrne mentioned candied yams topped with marshmallows, something she found “pretty weird.” Garten visibly grimaced at the mention of the dish, chuckling before describing them as “very American." Judging by that expression alone, I wouldn't expect to find the dish making an appearance at her next dinner party.

Garten's feelings about Thanksgiving itself, however, are considerably warmer, especially when compared to Christmas.

"Thanksgiving is just quiet. It's all that one day and it's all about the food," she explained, pointing out that Christmas comes with gifts, parties, and a whole lot more going on.

It makes sense coming from someone who’s built an entire career around bringing people together over a good meal. And we already know Garten’s enthusiasm for Thanksgiving extends beyond what’s on the plate. Last year, she shared her favorite wines to serve with Thanksgiving dinner, including Morgon, a lighter French red from the Beaujolais region, and white Burgundies like Meursault or Montrachet to accompany the turkey. She also likes a Sonoma Valley Pinot Noir, giving the American holiday a little hometown representation in the wine department.

At least now I know that if I ever get invited to Thanksgiving at Ina’s, I'll gladly let her handle the wine—and I know to keep the marshmallow-topped yams at home.

Is This Department Stores’ Significant Comeback Christmas?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1749 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gone are the days of the branded luxury Christmas window.
  • In an era where department stores need to work harder than ever to get a holiday shopper into their store — rather than them shopping online, directly with a brand, or at the department store up the road — many retailers are branching out beyond the monobrand Christmas window strategy that’s dominated recent holiday seasons.
  • Last week, stores from Bergdorf Goodman to Bloomingdale’s made a splash with their holiday window unveilings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gone are the days of the branded luxury Christmas window.

In an era where department stores need to work harder than ever to get a holiday shopper into their store — rather than them shopping online, directly with a brand, or at the department store up the road — many retailers are branching out beyond the monobrand Christmas window strategy that’s dominated recent holiday seasons.

Last week, stores from Bergdorf Goodman to Bloomingdale’s made a splash with their holiday window unveilings. Saks followed suit on Monday, November 23. The weather was unseasonably warm, with attendees clad in light jackets, rather than the usual fur and puffers for this time of year. Bergdorf made up for the tepid temps with fake snow. Bloomingdale’s had Sienna Spiro sing a rendition of “Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas”.

Industry observers note that by going the multibrand route, stores can put themselves at the center of their holiday storytelling, and appeal to a wider range of consumers by displaying merchandise across a host of different price points. Utilizing existing merchandise is also a lower lift than the logistical and financial burden of staging a full brand takeover. “I’m anticipating highly creative windows with a variety of merchandise. The general sentiment as of the last several months is that the customer shops high and low, where two years ago it was all about the big labels,” states luxury consultant Robert Burke. “So I think you’re going to see a variety of merchandise displayed in creative ways.”.

It’s panning out. Nordstrom is partnering with David Bowie’s estate to celebrate what would be the star’s 80th birthday — and is Nordstrom’s 125th anniversary. Included in Bowie80 are collaborations with designers including Paul Smith, Marc Jacobs and Undercover’s Jun Takahashi. Bergdorf Goodman’s windows are a vignette inspired by a Upcoming York winter, celebrating 125 years with an array of capsules from brands including Michael Kors, Brunello Cucinelli and Valentino. Saks’s windows offer up a tour of the festive period in the city. Over in London, Liberty is leaning into storytelling around holiday rituals and routines, and Selfridges is, like its peers, celebrating wintertime in the city (New York City, that is).

Bergdorf invited a host of designers to participate in its holiday window unveiling.

Industry observers note that not all of the players are going wide, though. Bloomingdale’s Friday window unveiling was in partnership with Ralph Lauren. Partnering with Ralph was a no-brainer, states Kevin Harter, VP of integrated marketing. “Ralph Lauren is synonymous with the traditions, nostalgia and timelessness that makes the holidays so special,” she says. The evening included a festive Ralph cocktail in the store — with teddy bear sweaters aplenty — and David Lauren was onstage to celebrate the unveiling alongside Bloomingdale’s CEO Olivier Bron. Inside, though, there are an array of brand activations — over 50 — from Barbour’s Tea & Sympathy pop-up to Ugg’s takeover of the Bloomingdale’s restaurant — and famed froyo destination — Forty Carrots. (There’s an Ugg-exclusive flavor, of course.) Ralph Lauren is the anchor, Harter says.

In a recent development, overall, this multibrand, amped-up storytelling logic extends to the in-store experience itself. Department stores this season have built out their holiday strategies around curation, with the view of inspiring their customers with the creative while making their lives as easy as possible. “One of the biggest opportunities for retail at Christmas is getting the balance between inspiration and ease right,” claims Lydia King, managing director of retail at Liberty.

Industry observers note that this is especially crucial this year, after department stores weathered quieter holiday seasons amid the upheaval of recent years. 2026 started with a bang, as Saks Global declared bankruptcy in January and, since summer, has been pushing its comeback as Exemplar Luxury Group. Bloomingdale’s, too, has spent 2026 pushing upmarket, making the most of a moment in which many of its contemporaries are struggling to meet the moment. This festive period, the stakes are high, capping off a year in which US department stores sought to regain lost magic.

Here’s how department stores are meeting the moment for this all-vital holiday season.

Recent findings suggest that this season, retailers are placing emphasis on their curation for the holiday period. The single-brand focus made sense a few years back when luxury was at its peak, Burke says. But now, he argues, department stores are looking to be more democratic in price point and product. “Compared to a few years ago, I’m seeing a lot of interest in smaller brands and independent brands,” he says. “The luxury customer today, even at the highest level, their mindset is very open to not having to only have major luxury branded merchandise.”.

According to recent reports, department stores are curating more than just product, though. Across the board — and in keeping with Gen Z’s desire for shopping experiences that offer meaning and excitement inaccessible via social media — they’re placing emphasis on the unique experiences offered in-store throughout the holidays.

Nordstrom’s holiday facade is an embrace of Bowie.

In doing so, they’re putting themselves at the center of the narrative. Bergdorf Goodman is doing this literally, placing the store in the middle of its New York-themed holiday campaign and window display which, this year, literally leads shoppers inside. “After the sidewalk introduces you to the narrative, it continues through the main doors into a Zhivago-esque wintry snow-laden forest hung with rock crystal chandeliers and a flock of white geese overhead,” says Linda Fargo, SVP of Bergdorf’s fashion office and store presentation.

“This year we’ve put much more emphasis on the whole experience of Christmas at Liberty, beyond the product offering,” says Liberty’s King. The store’s campaign, The Liberty Christmas Chronicles, follows the rituals of the season — preparing, dressing, traveling, gathering, unwinding and eventually resting — with gifting running throughout, of course. “We know customers increasingly value curation, personalization and expertise,” she says.

This comes in via mini in-store experiences, from wreath-making with Diptyque (Liberty’s hero partner in its Atrium section) to build-your-own hampers in the Liberty Food Hall. Other activations include personalized bows with Moët & Chandon, lipstick engraving with Lisa Eldridge and makeup bag embroidery with Westman Atelier.

According to recent reports, selfridges is taking a similar multibrand approach with tailored, ‘only available here’ experiences. With Canada Goose on Duke Street, for instance, the retailer has constructed an Arctic-inspired research outpost with hot chocolates and personalized luggage tags, and the ultra-buzzy Vice City GTA VI pop-up kicked off the retailer’s holiday activities.

According to recent reports, “These partnerships help create a Christmas that feels distinctive to Selfridges,” indicates marketing and experiences director Rebecca Warburton. “We know that people are looking for experiences, opportunities to connect with others and to create memorable moments,” she says, noting that Selfridges looked to offer more reasons for customers to spend time at the store this season.

Saks is leaning into these in-person experiences more than ever. For the first time, L’Avenue at Saks will host breakfast with Santa throughout the season and will transform into Le Chalet, with festive menu programming, on holiday season weekends.

Sienna Spiro performed at the Bloomingdale’s x Ralph Lauren window unveiling.

According to recent reports, this curation extends to stores’ gifting options. Beyond offering a smart selection of brands, stores are also thinking more deeply about their non-fashion gifting options, so that customers will shop with them not just for shoes, but for stocking stuffers, too.

Sources indicate that bergdorf Goodman does this well, Burke says, noting the store’s “tremendous” holiday season in 2025. “Bergdorf’s home floor is a very good example of it being a tourist destination with fun Christmas merchandise, because they sell all of these Christmas ornaments, candies and candles. It takes over the entire seventh floor,” he says. In celebration of its 125th anniversary, Bergdorf is upping the ante this year with an Assouline legacy book, Very Bergdorf, ‘Very Bergdorf’ specialty ornaments, plus a snow globe featuring the Bergdorf Goodman facade. “Every part of the store has something uniquely made for us, and it all adds up to a very Bergdorf holiday,” Fargo says.

It has been revealed that this year, Nordstrom is partnering with toy companies including FAO Schwarz and Jellycats. “You think about a retailer being relevant and having all the things customers want to buy — particularly at the holidays — partnerships like that help, in addition to carrying the best brands in the world,” says Deniz Anders, EVP, chief marketing officer. “Being able to check off their list for everyone across the family, that’s something that we’re really focused on.” Nordstrom has also invested more in consumables this year, and has a partnership with fashion-favorite Flamingo Estate.

Industry observers note that this season, department stores are thinking more than ever about ease. Saving customers time and effort, execs believe, is the way to capture their hearts — and their spend.

Industry observers note that nordstrom has expanded its gift shops in common areas throughout the store. “It’s really not something that we used to do, but we want customers to know this is a place that you can buy gifts at broad price points,” Anders states. The retailer tested the cross-store setup last year and has expanded the size of the shops this season. “We want to make it easy and fun for customers to buy gifts.”.

Liberty’s largest holiday season development is the introduction of its Gifting Curator service, King indicates. “For the first time, customers can book one-to-one appointments with Liberty experts who can guide them across the whole store, rather than within a single category or brand,” she says. “The idea is to make discovering the right present feel as special as giving it.” To round out the experience, Liberty has introduced a gift-wrapping experience with wrapper Roxy Wraps.

Stores have also been planting seeds to get their customers in the shopping mindset. Though all of the major, splashy window displays were unveiled at their usual time, just before Thanksgiving, the communications around the holiday season started far earlier. Nordstrom sent out its holiday catalog a week earlier than usual, Anders claims. It’s the retailer’s biggest catalog ever. “We’ve been bringing in gifts a lot earlier,” she says. “Holiday is a marathon and you’ve got to have the gifts early and be ready to serve customers and bring a little joy and fun.”.

Latest Update: The Tucson Restaurant Turning Cactus Into Fine Dining

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat.
  • Gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake.
  • Recent findings suggest that don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat. Plants armed with burs, barbs, and spines all but scream “do not touch.” For chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee, however, this prickly, dusty landscape stocks a pantry of possibility. The married co-owners of Ursa see the Arizona desert as a rich ground for foraging.

Gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake. Dusty, sage-colored salt bush, when hung to dry, takes on an intensely umami, aquatic saltiness like seaweed. The sweet buds of the Seussian-green palo verde tree become briny, like olives, when suffused with lye.

Recent findings suggest that don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year. The restaurant processes the young and mature paddles, fruit and their seeds, buds, and flowers, which are then grilled, poached, cold-smoked, juiced, dehydrated, nixtamalized, or preserved into jam, wine, and vinegar.

In a recent development, there are hundreds of edible plants in the Sonoran Desert. Ursa strives to showcase their potential, one 10-course meal at a time.

Industry observers note that “We treat Ursa as an art showroom, demonstrating to people what these plants can do, what sustainable means, and what was here before it got easy,” indicates Lopez. The idea was inspired in part by his Sonoran grandfather, Hector Lopez, who died in the spring. “He was the first person I ever heard say they’re proud to be from the desert,” the chef said.

Ursa began as a pop-up in California in 2023. Lopez and Chee moved to a historic brick building in downtown Tucson, re-opening their doors in October 2025. It’s a homecoming of sorts for the couple, who are both from the Sonoran Desert borderlands. They met in Hawaii, where Chee was working in clean energy and transportation. Lopez, meanwhile, spent roughly 18 years cooking in fine dining and modern progressive restaurants like Redbird and Orsa & Winston in LA, and Pai Honolulu. But he was longing for the desert.

After helping a friend open a restaurant and hosting a few popups in Austin, Lopez and Chee bought a desert foraging guide, packed up their two dogs and began driving around the Southwest. It made sense to settle in Tucson, which was recognized by UNESCO in 2015 as a Creative City of Gastronomy for its continuous 4,000-year agricultural history and deeply rooted Sonoran Desert food traditions.

“That’s a unique thing about being here, the connection from seed to plant to restaurant that we hadn’t been able to grasp before,” Chee indicates.

In a recent development, consider a recent course that Ursa built around tepary beans, in which the ancient, nutty bean is refried and topped with h:al squash that’s been lactofermented. The squash’s leaves are fermented to make Japanese-style kosho and its flowers are pickled, dried, crushed with dried saltbush, then tossed with barrel cactus seeds for a desert furikake. It’s served with grilled coins of chorizo made from Lopez’s great-grandmother’s recipe and housemade flour tortillas, to all be washed down with an amazake drink made from fermented wheat and goat fat. Don’t get too attached, however. Riffs owing to finicky ingredient availability occur here almost daily.

It has been revealed that running a restaurant using only ingredients foraged and farmed from within about eight to 10 miles means abiding by pretty intense guardrails. The only wheat used is pima club, an ancient soft white variety cultivated for centuries by the Akimel O’odham (Pima) people. Ursa does not use cucumbers, radishes or citrus.

It has been revealed that “We’re not trying to substitute anything, like, ‘How do we achieve cucumber? Let’s grab a cactus,’” Lopez states. “We have to throw everything out, really strip it down. Sometimes we have to let the ingredients be bitter or spicy. We have to put our egos aside and let the ingredient be the star.”.

For staff who didn’t grow up or learn to cook here, the learning curve at Ursa can feel a little like alighting on a new planet, even if certain flora happen to resemble prickly weeds in their own backyards.

“We have these really cool moments in the restaurant where people are like, Oh! I have lamb’s quarter just growing in my yard!” Chee says of the spinach-like desert green that appears all over Ursa’s menu.

A young Aaron Lopez with his grandfather Hector Lopez.

Ursa’s approach isn’t always easy for customers to understand, so the couple came up with a more down-to-earth option. This fall, the restaurant debuted a four-course, family-style Lineage menu for $75, alongside the existing 10-course Harvest menu ($150). There’s now a pozole course inspired by the family’s annual springtime tradition of roasting goat in agave leaves, barbacoa-style, and shredding it for soup, and a red masa tamal with glazed quail and yucca blossoms in mole made with burnt mesquite bread, a technique Lopez remembers from childhood.

The idea took shape during Ursa’s extended summer break, as Lopez recovered from foot surgery and reflected on the loss of his late grandfather, the tenacious keeper of family traditions.

Sources indicate that “I feel so much closer to my ancestors and the land; we want Ursa to be less esoteric and more soulful,” he notes. “The story of Ursa is partly of the desert, partly my family. Now we’ve advanced to the point where they’re symbiotic, and I can't tell them apart.”.

The Real-Life Wardrobe of Michael Bennett, Who Traded the NFL for Furniture Design

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When you’ve won a Super Bowl ring, made three Pro Bowl appearances, and played a key role on one of the most dominant defensive squads ever—the Seattle Seahawks’ 2010s-era Legion of Boom—what do you do next?
  • It has been revealed that after completing his 11-year NFL career in 2020, the 41-year-old enrolled at two institutions—the University of Hawaii and Seattle’s Heritage School of Interior Design—to study architecture and interior design, respectively.
  • Through his design practice Studio Kër, Bennett debuted an 11-piece collection of avant-garde furniture inspired by the African diaspora in 2024, which was well received by critics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When you’ve won a Super Bowl ring, made three Pro Bowl appearances, and played a key role on one of the most dominant defensive squads ever—the Seattle Seahawks’ 2010s-era Legion of Boom—what do you do next? For Michael Bennett, the answer was to head back to school.

It has been revealed that after completing his 11-year NFL career in 2020, the 41-year-old enrolled at two institutions—the University of Hawaii and Seattle’s Heritage School of Interior Design—to study architecture and interior design, respectively. “I’m a student of whatever I do,” Bennett tells me. “My best quality—and probably my worst quality—is that the things I love to do, I try to become the best. I play tennis five days a week. I’m trying to go to Wimbledon. And design and architecture are like that.”.

All that effort is paying off. Through his design practice Studio Kër, Bennett debuted an 11-piece collection of avant-garde furniture inspired by the African diaspora in 2024, which was well received by critics. He’s now hard at work on his sophomore line, alongside a spoken-word album and the occasional bespoke garment.

That last side quest should come as no surprise, because Bennett has some of the most distinctive personal style I’ve ever seen on a pro athlete–current or former—with a particularly clean headwear and accessories game. Here, Bennett tells me all about the skills he carried over from football into his newly introduced career, what fatherhood has taught him about masculinity, and the song he listens to every day.

Michael Bennett: I’ve been playing football my whole life, man. After winning so much, I dug deep. I had already conquered the body. How do I conquer the mind? At what point am I being selfish? I’m missing so much of my kids’ lives. I’ve already been to the highest of the high. Am I going to leave my family with a broken man? That was really the question. Am I chasing ego or am I chasing something else? In reality, a lot of us are just chasing the ego, to be remembered, scared of the death of what [your life] was rather than [embracing] the growth that can be.

It has been revealed that people want to keep others in a certain box because that’s the way that they understand them. That’s in any relationship. If you started to date somebody when they’re 20 and you turn 40 and they start to change, you’d be like, “You used to like your eggs like that.” People don’t allow others to transition; won’t allow people to actually experience growth. Often you’re meeting people in a time where they’re just starting to learn who they are. Over time you start to really develop who you are.

Sources indicate that the truth is it doesn’t matter if people take you seriously, [as long as] you take yourself seriously. What are you doing to practice your craft? Artists are like, “Oh, my practice, my practice.” I never really understood what that meant until I started doing my own practice. I practiced on the field and I can practice the body. But really, if you want to be taken seriously intellectually, then you have to practice the mind. Sometimes practicing the mind is also connected to the body. In football, yeah, you are connected to the mind in a certain way. But it isn’t always like learning to be a lawyer or an architect or an artist—to be a thinker, you’re doing something completely different. And it’s just allowing yourself to transition. Man, truthfully, you got to say fuck everybody.

I think it’s one of the most intellectual sports in general. Tennis is one of those sports where it’s about the angle, the quick twitch. You’re by yourself. With football, it’s the amount of moving parts. People overlook the amount of detail that it takes to run a team—practicing and going through a play 3,000 times before you actually get it. The best players I ever met were the smartest when it came to the sport. They were the PhDs of their craft.

Recent findings suggest that it’s taught me vulnerability. It made me a better human. In some ways, my daughters have allowed me to mature. The sport of football requires so much masculinity. I’m not saying that all masculinity is toxic, [but] it’s more about, how do you hunt but still be gentle? The true samurai doesn’t strike, but knows he can.

What my daughters have allowed me to do is develop my whole humanity. To have a daughter is so special—women are very special. As an athlete, people come back from injuries, but to see a woman come back from giving birth is a whole other level of love. My daughters have been my greatest accomplishments in my life. I never made a Super Bowl trophy. There’s always another winner. But there’s only one Peyton, there’s only one Blake, and there’s one Ollie. As a maker, those are the most special things that I could make.

In 2019, I was really into Booker T. Washington and W.E.B. Du Bois and [their debate over] the “Talented Tenth.” [Booker T. Washington believed that] intellectualism should never get away from the idea of making. I got into design because I’ve always been involved in politics, and politically, I started to realize that everything came down to design.

Recent findings suggest that shirt and pants by Studio Kër. Shoes by Collegium.

Whenever I spoke out about police brutality or on critical issues in America, that was really where I started to think about design as this language—this form of resistance. How can I change the system? It starts with design. Where I grew up, a non-gentrified area that was low income, it’s like you could see that there was no empathetic way of thinking about design. The definition of architecture for me is empathy for space. That’s what led me to this idea of these African diaspora forms and languages that I will use as my form of resistance.

Industry observers note that I’m working on a new collection of furniture. The first collection I did was called “We Gotta Get Back to the Crib,” which to me was really about getting back to the essence of Blackness. A lot of times we talk about Blackness and it’s always connected to traumatic experience. But to me, it was more about how can I connect to these true levels of love, these things really shaped my culture, my family, my mother, my grandmother, and everything that was beautiful about being Black? This next collection is about African brutalism. How can I bring these things that are seen in the ghetto in America and in West Africa and then turn those into ideas about furniture? A lot of times what I’m dealing with as a designer is this idea of abstraction. How can I pull and reference something in such a sweet way? Like how Virgil designed shoes with references, leaving crumbs to this unspoken past. As a designer, that’s what I’m trying to do.

Yeah, I got a spoken word project.

Recent findings suggest that as an athlete, if you talk about your cars or you talk about your jewelry, the way that you gained it doesn’t have that kind of Jay-Z effect—you didn’t hustle to get that. You played to get that, which is different from somebody hustling to get that. With spoken word, I think about Gil Scott-Heron or The Last Poets. They’re talking about critical issues. My perspective is really about humanizing the Black experience and the Black man. My stories and what I’m trying to tell with this music, E-Nigg-Ma, is so much about Black culture, Black design, Black features, this idea of what America is trying to suffocate about Blackness and not let it breathe.

According to recent reports, cuff by Dries van Noten. Ring by Olithica. Watch by Patek Philippe.

Industry observers note that music. When I’m designing, beautiful sounds are really notable to the way that I think. My number-one song that I always listen to is Miles Davis’s “Flamenco Sketches.” It’s my daily listen. Those are the sounds that I need to hear: the horn, the riffs, the in-between.

Recent findings suggest that my studio inspires me, just the way light hits. It’s the simplest things. Seeing my family movies. My wife inspires me with what she’s designing.

Industry observers note that my great-grandpa, Hall Mack, everybody talked about his fashion. People still talk about his style. He was the first person I saw dry cleaning everything. His style was impeccable. When I look back at a period of style that I liked, it’d be the years of the Birth of the Cool. People like Miles, Sidney Poitier, everybody was just fresh.

I’ve always been connected to style. People always call me “Runway Mike.” They say, “Bro, you wear more Margiela than anybody I know.” I design my own clothes. [Style] is a part of who you are. I love the idea of fashion. I want to design a fashion show. Yo, Wales Bonner, let me design something for you! I want to be backstage.

Over time I just found me. That takes so much time. I feel like one of the most beautiful things is Instagram and this ability to share things, but one of the worst things is Instagram and the ability to share things. Because there’s a part of us that starts to mimic [what we see] in a way that isn’t true to us. We start to judge ourselves on other people’s experience.

It’s cool to see things, but it’s also cool to experiment with what you feel good in. “Yo, this is what I look good in. I don’t care what nobody claims, I feel good.” That’s what true fashion is. I buy Prada because I actually like it. That’s the development of who you are and your taste—when you buy things for the love of it. Like, “Man, I really love the shoulder on this.” I’m not buying anything to be seen in it. I’m buying it because I respect the process.

Jumpsuit by Studio Kër. Shoes by Prada.

Recent findings suggest that I think it was something from Acne, even though Acne was that middle kind of brand. Acne now has gotten too expensive.

According to recent reports, two things. I bought this striped Prada sweater. It was just a nice, beautiful brown. It was quiet, but it was super nice. And I just designed the blue shirt [from my second look]. Even making something like that is expensive.

I just sketch it, and then I make it in LA.

Yeah, or show a picture of something and break it down like, “Cut this out. I need the arms to be like this.”.

I’m also going to do it for my studio. My goal is to have studio attire that I produce. This year I’m dropping four shirts. If you’re a designer and you want a beautiful shirt, here’s four of them. I’m only making a hundred of them. Keep it very simple.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a traditional Thanksgiving meal, mashed potatoes are a seemingly simple side dish that does a lot of heavy lifting. They're the perfect vessel for a puddle of gravy, and they’re a creamy complement to everything else on your plate—yes, even your aunt's questionable green bean casserole.

Mashed potatoes prove you can transform even the humblest ingredients into something magical. And yet, we've all somehow still eaten bad ones. With a recipe this basic, even the smallest mistakes have nowhere to hide.

In a recent development, thankfully, those mistakes are 100% avoidable. We rounded up the most common ways to mess up mashed potatoes so that yours turn out as delicious as possible this holiday season.

It doesn’t matter if you cut your potatoes into a fine dice or rough chunks. Whatever size you pick, stick with it. Making sure your potato pieces are roughly the same size will help them all cook at the same rate. If your knife work is haphazard, you may end up with some pieces that are perfectly cooked, others that are waterlogged and mushy, and some that are still firm in the center.

Like pasta, potatoes need a good amount of seasoning to really shine—which is why salting the cooking water is so key. You can be generous with the salt, since much of it stays in the water and ends up going down the drain. When you start seasoning early in the cooking process, it’s easier to build flavor and adjust as you go.

It has been revealed that in the hustle of cooking all of your Thanksgiving dishes, you may be tempted to boil your potatoes ahead of time and mash them later in the day. But it’s always better to work with potatoes while they’re still hot and easier to mash. Waiting until they’re cool will likely require far more elbow grease—and you’ll still end up with uneven chunks.

A smooth, creamy mash is the height of decadence. To make sure the potatoes are lump-free, some people may reach for a blender—but this is one of the most consequential mistakes you can make. Potatoes are naturally starchy, and the more you work them, the more starch gets released from their cell walls. Breaking out the blender may be well-intentioned, but it can leave you with potatoes that are gummy and gluey. Instead, opt for the right tool, like a hand masher, food mill, or potato ricer.

Another notable thing to consider is that potato starches continue absorbing moisture as mashed potatoes sit. They can soak up the milk you’ve added, leaving your potatoes dry and dense. Don’t be afraid to add more liquid—or at least keep some extra on hand to loosen up your mash before serving.

Recent findings suggest that anthony Bourdain famously pointed to generous amounts of salt and butter as part of what makes restaurant food taste so good. That’s especially true for mashed potatoes. You may be scared to add more than a light sprinkle of salt, but don’t forget to taste and adjust the seasoning before serving. A little extra salt can make all the difference for your Thanksgiving dinner.

According to recent reports, whether you’re feeding your immediate family or a small army, you should always make a substantial batch of mashed potatoes. This side is one of the most popular components of a Thanksgiving menu, so it never hurts to make extra. It’s also one of the most versatile dishes for repurposing leftovers. You can transform them into gnocchi, shepherd’s pie, or crispy fried croquettes. It may require more mashing in the moment, but your future self will thank you.

It has been revealed that A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

According to recent reports, place 1–1¼ lb. boneless Latest York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

It has been revealed that heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.).

Sources indicate that uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

According to recent reports, combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.
