📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

In a recent development, add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

Some handbag trends come and go, but the bucket bag has proven its staying power. Somewhere between a slouchy hobo and a structured tote, the cylindrical style has long struck a balance between practical and effortlessly cool.

Recent findings suggest that part of the silhouette’s enduring popularity is its versatility. What began as a utilitarian design (one of the earliest iterations was a Louis Vuitton bag from the 1930s, originally intended to transport Champagne bottles) has become grounds for experimentation, with designers playing with proportions, materials, and distinctive details. This season, in particular, the bucket bag is enjoying renewed attention, with everything from cinched drawstring closures and sculptural top handles to unexpected hardware giving the classic a fresh look.

When shopping for a bucket bag, consider more than just the looks. Think about how and where you’ll carry yours: A spacious style can double as a work tote, while a mini version can add a touch of whimsy to evening looks. Fortunately, there’s no shortage of choices, whether you’re looking to invest in a luxury piece or discover something at a more accessible price point.

It has been revealed that while preferences are unique to each shopper, the best options combine quality craftsmanship with functional details, from comfortable straps to secure closures and interiors that accommodate everyday essentials. Ahead, we’ve rounded up bucket bags to shop now, from understated versions to modern interpretations of the timeless silhouette.

It has been revealed that few materials make a handbag feel as luxurious as suede, particularly in wintertime. In rich shades of chocolate brown, navy, and burgundy, the tactile surface exudes sophistication. Just remember that suede requires care, particularly when water is involved.

Industry observers note that for anyone who carries their entire life in their handbag, oversized bucket bags offer a stylish alternative to traditional work totes, with enough room for a laptop, water bottle, and whatever else the day demands. Supple leather designs have a relaxed, lived-in appeal, while sturdier versions offer a professionally glossy finish. Look for a wide strap, a secure closure, and an organized interior to make the most of the extra space and keep it gentle on your shoulders during the commute.

There’s something undeniably charming about a drawstring closure, which gives bucket bags their signature gathered appearance (and helps keep belongings secure). The cinched opening creates visually impactful folds that look particularly elegant in buttery leather, soft suede, or evening-ready satin.

If your wardrobe leans minimalist, a structured bucket bag may be the perfect match. Unlike softer iterations that collapse when set down, these styles maintain their architectural structure thanks to firmer leather and well-constructed bases; longer straps also allow for crossbody wear. Their shape makes them feel more like design objects than everyday accessories, especially when finished with distinctive hardware.

Good things really do come in small packages, and mini bucket bags are proof. These scaled-down versions trade generous storage space for playful proportions that are ideal for evenings out, weekend aims, or occasions when you only need the essentials. Choose a style with a detachable strap for added versatility, or carry it by hand for a more dressed-up effect.

Sources indicate that woven bags have moved beyond their beach-vacation beginnings. Intricately interlaced leather lends the bucket silhouette an artisanal quality, while tightly bound raffia in darker shades is appropriate for city dressing. Look for details like leather handles and tonal finishes that give these textured designs a more elevated, winter-ready look.

For a ladylike approach to the bucket bag, consider a top-handle silhouette. Short, sculptural handles give the otherwise casual shape a more refined appearance. Some feature rigid circular handles, while others have softly curved leather straps that sit comfortably in the crook of the arm.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Skyler Gisondo is getting soaked.

It’s a wet, quasi-Floridian November afternoon in Carroll Gardens, Brooklyn; the sidewalks are plastered with layers of translucent brown and gold leaves. We’ve just met at a cafe for a bite; our plan is to walk to Brooklyn Bridge Park. But the second we step outside, we’re pelted with rain. Gisondo is dressed more for a sunny Southern California boardwalk than these soggy Brooklyn streets: white vintage-ish T-shirt (“Norwalk Seaport’s Oyster School”), canvas pants, brown boots, and the usual Rolex Submariner on his wrist. No hat to cover his thick auburn hair, no jacket, and, crucially, no umbrella.

Sources indicate that jacket by Celine. Shirt by Banana Republic Vintage Archive. T-shirt by Paul Smith. Pants by Raimundo Langois. Watch by Cartier.

We promptly unite in a single mission: to locate and purchase one. “I have a good feeling about Park Natural,” the actor says optimistically, gesturing to the health food store across the way. We splash over to check, and an employee redirects us to a CVS down the street, prompting a nine-block journey under my single umbrella. Gisondo is a supportive partner on the scavenger hunt. He is patient as I lead us the wrong way, carefully holding the umbrella over us both while I look at my phone to course-correct, and takes the lead only with my permission. He matches each of my questions with his own, seemingly determined to maintain the cadence of a conversation, rather than that of an interview. As we walk, the rain gets even heavier, saturating the cuffs of our pants. Gisondo draws a few excited looks of recognition from people on the street, before two passersby attempt to recruit him to their church. “Oh, that’s all right—thank you,” he responds politely.

By the time we finally arrive at the CVS, I’m worried the trek was a mistake—not the type of thing you subject a Hollywood actor to, no matter how easygoing they may seem. But when I offer to buy Gisondo a $20 drugstore umbrella and charge it to GQ, his pale-blue eyes light up and a substantial smile breaks across his freckled face. “Hoo-ley smokes,” he claims, his voice rising in astonishment. “Thank you.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Heck yeah,” he continues as I navigate through self-checkout. “You know what’s funny? The real ‘pinch me’ moments are this stuff.” He explains with complete earnestness how he grew up reading GQ. “Being a boy, being a young man, I was like, ‘I want to look like these guys.’ It’s almost like Stranger Than Fiction, where you hear the narration in your head or something.”.

Recent findings suggest that when we step outside, it’s stopped raining almost entirely. Still, Gisondo thanks me again. “Spanking brand-new umbrella,” he declares with childlike awe, as if he’s holding the key to the city.

This is how Gisondo moves through the world: present, content, unflappable, well-mannered. An all-around good sport. It’s why, in a 4/20-themed Jimmy John’s campaign transparently angling for virality, he seemed not just willing to play ball but really, truly stoked to be eating a Jimmy John’s sandwich. It’s why the persistent memes that imagine Gisondo as a ’90s kid with a peanut allergy who got “hyper as fuck at recess” feel spiritually, if not always factually, accurate. And it’s those same wholesome qualities—and his ability to wield them in increasingly dark scenarios—that have turned the steady, subtle drumbeat of his acting career into an infectious stomp-clap over the course of a year.

Recent findings suggest that in 2026 thus far Gisondo has appeared as a deadbeat but emotionally literate surfer bro boyfriend in the Apple TV series Brothers, made a charming cameo in a Phoebe Bridgers music video as one of its titular adventure-seeking “Lost Boys,” and received a seven-minute standing ovation at the Venice Film Festival for his absorbing role as a sex offender decoy in Primetime. The day before Thanksgiving he’ll complete his sprint with Focker-In-Law, the latest Meet the Parents sequel, in which Gisondo plays Greg Focker’s well-intentioned but avoidant grown-up son. Next up, he’s got two lead roles in projects tentatively slated for next year: a return to the DC universe of James Gunn’s 2025 Superman, as the unwitting ladies’ man and journalist Jimmy Olsen in the true-crime mockumentary The People vs. Gorilla Grodd, and an A24 comedy called Goblin, where he stars opposite a talking puppet, in a film whose script Gisondo calls “probably the most batshit crazy thing I’ve legitimately ever read.”.

In a recent development, though these projects take place in wildly different worlds, Gisondo’s characters have one thing in common: They’re nice guys in fraught situations. In a cultural moment where dark, morally slippery antiheroes dominate entertainment as well as real life, Gisondo has carved out a lane as a sincere, scrupulous bright spot. “He reminds me of Michael J. Fox in Back to the Future,” says Danny McBride, who cast Gisondo as aspiring stuntman Gideon, the grounded eldest grandchild of the dysfunctional evangelical family empire in The Righteous Gemstones. “There’s something about him that hearkens back to a simpler time and an innocent time, and it makes you root for him.”.

For a guy with an IMDB credit page almost as long as the CVS receipt that came with his umbrella, the blitz of red-carpet events, late-night TV spots, and awards season buzz for his role in Primetime has been especially surreal. “For the first time, at 30, I’m engaging with the part of this job I haven’t before, in a heightened way,” he says.

Now, with his first real shot at an Academy Award nomination, People magazine calling him the “internet’s boyfriend,” and a 2027 stacked with high-profile parts, Gisondo appears poised to prove that, even in the darkest of timelines, nice guys don’t necessarily finish last. And since his role in Primetime, he’s never been more locked in. “It lit a fire under me that I didn’t know I had before,” he says. “I heard actors say stuff like that in the past, ‘I want to do stuff that scares me,’ and I never got it. And now, light bulb. That’s it. That’s when you feel alive. That’s the point.”.

According to recent reports, up until about age 12, Gisondo wanted to be one of three things when he grew up: an actor, a professional hockey player, and/or a professional basketball player. “I was imagining playing both seasons somehow,” he tells me with a grin at Mister Cheeks, the cafe where we first meet. “I held on to that dream for too long.”.

He recalls really “tearing it up” in the 9-to-10-year-old hockey league—until he moved up to the next age bracket, which widened to include older kids, ages 11 to 14. “That’s the first league where full-contact was allowed,” he states. “I was 11 and the size of an 8-year-old, and there were dudes who were shaving.” This mismatch in size and ability culminated in a wake-up call on the ice: “All I remember is getting hit, and then the next thing I’m on my back, opening my eyes with my parents over me. The game had stopped and that was the day that dream died,” he says—before adding, with a laugh: “Thankfully, the acting thing kept working out.”.

Recent findings suggest that the acting thing included fewer instances where one might be bodychecked by a pubescent teenager, at least in the literal sense. And by that point, Gisondo was already pretty experienced in the craft. Growing up in Palm Beach, Florida, he was “obsessed with movies,” watching West Side Story on repeat until he’d memorized the entire script. Gisondo got it in his head that he could be an actor. His parents, who are process-oriented oceanic engineers, were skeptical. But when a work project brought his family to the Los Angeles area, his mother finally acquiesced and took him to an audition: a hundred-child call for a national Pizza Hut commercial. Gisondo, a precocious blue-eyed cutie pie with bangs and an underbite smile, landed the part. At the time, his dad was convinced his family was the victim of some kind of scam. In actuality, Gisondo had secured his first professional acting gig—and a Screen Actors Guild card—at the tender age of six, a whole 17 years earlier than his character Dan Plum in Primetime. Fans have since dug up and posted evidence of his acting debut, delighting over “TINY GISONDO.”.

Thus began a string of small roles—as “Chris,” “Ryan,” or “Boy #1”—on a handful of family-friendly TV sitcoms. Gisondo’s parents relocated to Southern California and began homeschooling him to support his budding career. As Gisondo tells it, his mother specifically forbade any Disney and Nickelodeon auditions, in order to keep him far away from child stardom. “You get one childhood, so I think she wanted to preserve as normal of a childhood as she could for me,” he indicates. “And I’m really grateful that she did that.”.

That freedom to be a kid helped him play one so well that he has since become a folkloric avatar for carefree adolescence—and the subject of one of the modern media landscape’s few truly benevolent memes. Captioning an old photo of Gisondo (from the press cycle for 2015’s Vacation), fans have imagined him enjoying all manner of nostalgic ’90s-kid activities—doing crazy tricks on trampolines, playing with Nerf guns, buying a Guinness Book of World Records at a book fair.

Industry observers note that “Some of them I’m like, Oh my God. This is uncanny,” he claims excitedly. “These people tap into something.” Gisondo and his friends did, in fact, shoot Nerf guns at each other “point-blank” during sleepovers. As a kid he was “ecstatic” to be on a trampoline. And he keeps a copy of The Guinness Book of World Records on his coffee table to this day.

Industry observers note that “At a certain point, with the memes,” he says, “I feel like they transcended and it became about something else, like it’s not about me anymore. It’s become a vessel for something.”.

Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, these posts have been passed around long enough that even his girlfriend—rumored to be Sterling Point’s Ella Rubin—seems to have internalized them. “There’s one that’s like, I just know his ass has a peanut allergy or something,” he claims. “I don’t have a peanut allergy, but I’ve been with my girlfriend three years, okay? We’ll be at dinner. I’ll go to take a bite from her plate and she’ll very seriously go, ‘Oh no, peanuts.’ And then she’ll go, ‘Why do I always think you have a peanut allergy?’ That’s been happening for years.”.

Recent findings suggest that to Rachel Brosnahan, who starred alongside Gisondo as Jimmy Olsen’s Daily Planet colleague Lois Lane in Superman, the memes speak to a larger appetite for Gisondo’s wholesome qualities. “It feels so in line with something that we were pleasantly surprised and excited by when the first Superman movie came out, which is that being earnest and caring a lot and loving really hard can also be cool,” she says. “It’s been awesome to watch a world that feels sometimes increasingly cynical and apathetic embrace that. And it’s not surprising to me that Skyler has become the face of that.”.

Even if Gisondo managed to have plenty of good old-fashioned fun as a kid, being homeschooled for nine years left him with a lasting identity as an outsider. He’d show up to camp each summer, trying to figure out what kids who’d spent the year in school together were into. “And I remember that feeling of exclusion,” he states; the older he got, the more apparent it was. “I remember being 15 and getting auditions for high school kids, and they were at a house party. And I was like”—here Gisondo shifts into a blissfully clueless impression of 15-year-old him— “‘I don’t know what the fuck this is about.’”.

Recent findings suggest that that was around the time Gisondo enrolled in traditional high school, in pursuit of some quintessential experiences. But by then the kind of parts he was booking made even the most prototypical occasions extraordinary. He attended his senior prom—and brought a date he’d secured by filming a prom-posal video on the set of Night at the Museum: The Secret of the Tomb with the help of his costars Ben Stiller and Robin Williams. (Stiller even paid for his limo the night of, as a “wrap gift.”).

Gisondo would chase his dream of a normal life all the way to University of Southern California’s film school, where he pledged a frat for all of three weeks before dropping out. He managed to attend at least one real-life college party before finally accepting his fate as a full-time actor. “It was not my vibe per se,” he notes, as we stroll through a dank tree-lined block of brownstones. “It’s like Lord of the Flies.”.

You could argue that only tip-toeing past these young-adult rites of passage has helped Gisondo preserve a certain old-world aura—untouched by keg stands, gravity bongs, or double-digit daily screen time. “Something about Skyler reminds me of actors from the ’30s or ’40s, who had a real personality and a kind of street smarts about them,” Stiller notes via email. “I could see him in a movie playing one of the Dead End Kids in the ’30s, like these kind of Fresh York street kids.”.

Recent findings suggest that gisondo did manage to collect enough real-life memories to call upon in future standout supporting roles like the rich-kid hypebeast nerd in Booksmart or Cooper Hoffman’s smarmy child-actor nemesis in Licorice Pizza. He now measures his life milestones by the types of roles he’s being called to audition for. “I remember when I got sent Fockers, I think it was my first time being a fiancé, and I was like, Oh my God, I’m a kid,” he claims. “And then it hit me like, Wait a minute, most of my friends are engaged. I’m not a kid. I’m not a child bride. This is a completely appropriate age to be doing this.”.

Those years as an outsider have made Gisondo especially attuned to social dynamics. He indicates he senses when someone is quiet in a group and will be the one to go talk to the person standing alone in the corner of the party. “A lot of my friends and people I respond to are people who are, I don’t know, weirdos in some way, who maybe do have a more difficult time,” he says. “It’s funny, there’ll be moments with my girlfriend where I say something. And she’ll be like, ‘Oh my God, I forget you were homeschooled for nine years.’”.

In a recent development, but after turning 30 this past July, he states that he feels more self-assured than ever. “I think you spend a lot of your 20s posturing, trying to find your place, find your lane. And I almost feel like I sprung into consciousness two years ago. At 30, I feel very much like myself for the first time. You know what you like, you know who you are. It becomes almost harder to fake it. You become less interested in faking it. I guess I did always feel that, but there’s an immediacy to that feeling now.”.

That self-assuredness has only grown with time, notes Beanie Feldstein, who worked with Gisondo on Booksmart and then again, seven years later, on Focker-In-Law. “Skyler has always been very pure and truthful and rooted and that has never changed, but of course we are older and have lived more life,” she notes via email. “He feels like a more settled-in version of the same person I’ve always known.”.

Recent findings suggest that that Gisondo has always felt more at home with the out crowd has made him all the more surprised by his current buzzy moment—much of which can be credited to Primetime and what he calls “the most challenging” role of his life. The propulsive film fictionalizes the lurid early-aughts reality series To Catch a Predator, hosted by former Dateline NBC correspondent Chris Hansen. Gisondo plays one of the decoys Hansen and his team used to lure sex offenders inside a sting house, an impressionable musical theater fan named Dan Plum—a.k.a. Decoy Dan—who’s so eager to kickstart his acting career that he’s initially oblivious to the toxic workplace and mission he’s joined.

Recent findings suggest that unlike Plum, of course, Gisondo was already a known quantity when he auditioned for Primetime, but he desperately wanted the part. As he tells it, Lance Oppenheim offered it to him within the first 10 minutes of their introductory call. “I was used to singing for my supper,” he indicates. “But he was so certain. And I remember asking him, ‘What have you seen of mine that makes you so certain?’” Oppenheim, who says he “bookmarked” Gisondo when he saw Licorice Pizza, was drawn to what he describes as “this particular combination of sweetness, humor, and slightly awkward, boyish earnestness.” The director also liked that Gisondo had experience as a child actor, but from the perspective of an older, wiser adult. “I was drawn to the idea that Skyler had spent so much of his life navigating the strange machinery of the entertainment industry himself, and what he might bring to a character who was also trying to find his place within that world,” he told me via email.

According to recent reports, gisondo recalls trying to explain the part to his father, the oceanic engineer, after he signed on to the film. “It was the most exciting opportunity of my career by far,” he claims. “I remember telling my dad all of these things: So, it’s an A24 movie, starring Robert Pattinson, this guy Lance Oppenheim. And I would play a guy who’s an aspiring actor who’s used as bait to catch pedophiles in the decoy operations. And I’ll never forget, my dad was kind of quiet and he goes, ‘So this is something you’d be excited about?’”.

Sources indicate that as Dan, Gisondo parades through rented homes in puka shells and tie-dye T-shirts, directing unknowing predators toward a variety of snack foods with a high-pitched, exuberant naivete that manages to both brighten the film’s depraved subject matter and make it feel that much more sinister. (These scenes, too, were GIF’d and memed by the Gisondo hive.) But as we watch Hansen (Robert Pattinson) and his producer Andie Bender (Merritt Wever) plunge deeper into a shameless pursuit of higher ratings, Dan recoils, gradually becoming the closest thing this story has to an ethical center.

“He plays it absolutely honestly, absolutely straight-faced with absolute sincerity,” claims Wever, who calls Gisondo’s performance “perfect and undeniable.” “So when there’s comedy to be had—even if it’s uncomfortable or squirmy comedy or cringey comedy or comedy that is uncomfortable because you’re laughing because you can see the heartbreak inside somebody, the true ouch of the vulnerability and the unknowingness—it’s there because he’s not winking at the audience. He’s really inside that part. It has so many colors because he’s playing it so truthfully. That’s a sign of a very smart actor.”.

Sources indicate that I point out to Gisondo that this isn’t the first time he’s played a character who becomes the sneaky moral compass of the story. He had something similar going as Gideon in The Righteous Gemstones, where he served as a relief to the over-the-top antics of a completely insane evangelical empire. Considered alongside all those memes about his imagined childhood, a single through line becomes obvious—in the parts he plays, but maybe also on a human level, he seems to remind people that good still exists in the world.

Sources indicate that “What’s funny is hearing you say that—it’s my first time bumping up against perception, in a way. Being perceived on that scale,” he notes, slowing down to sort through his words for the first time in our otherwise free-flowing conversation, his eyes widening a little. “I think all any of us want is to be seen. I think to be loved is to be seen, in a way. People thinking that about me is the most gratifying possible thing. To me, it communicates I’m doing something right in my life.”.

According to recent reports, but even as he’s astonished by the public feedback loop about his persona, he also can’t help but feel a little unnerved by it. “Usually, I feel like, only at your funeral are you meant to see so many people talking about what they think of you.”.

In a recent development, by this point Gisondo and I have made our way down through Brooklyn Bridge Park, looking out at the Manhattan skyline from a waterlogged pier and then wandering along a few wooded paths to arrive on the edge of Dumbo, where we’re idling as our conversation winds down. Behind him, the Brooklyn Bridge is enveloped in rain clouds. I remind him that people are saying good things.

Industry observers note that “Everybody wants to read nice things about them, whether it’s a review, whether it’s a meme,” he notes. “There’s no doubt it feels good. I’m not sure I want to feed the part of me that likes how good that feels. That’s the gremlin in all of us.”.

According to recent reports, with that, we say our goodbyes and I turn to make my way to the subway. “Thanks for my umbrella,” he indicates. I have no question he really, truly, earnestly means it. ✦.

BA's Best Lasagna

📅 07 Feb 2018 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1433 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this lasagna recipe has “rainy Sunday cooking project” written all over it.
  • Recent findings suggest that the secret weapon is the meat sauce.
  • One step you can skip: boiling the noodles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this lasagna recipe has “rainy Sunday cooking project” written all over it. Layers of slow-cooked pork-and-beef ragù, silky Parmesan béchamel, and pasta bake into a rich, creamy lasagna Bolognese with a browned top and crisp edges. Make the sauces ahead to break up the work, or settle in for a day of very good kitchen smells.

Recent findings suggest that the secret weapon is the meat sauce. Why make meatballs only to break them apart? Searing the meat in large balls leaves room for moisture to escape, so you get deep browning instead of a potful of steam. After a long, gentle braise, a potato masher turns them into ragù. Whole canned tomatoes, crushed by hand, give you control over the sauce’s chunky texture.

One step you can skip: boiling the noodles. In side-by-side retests, regular dried lasagna noodles (not no-boil!) produced similar results whether parboiled or layered straight from the box. The ragù and béchamel provide enough moisture to cook the pasta in the oven—as long as every noodle is covered. Spread the sauces to the edges, leaving no dry patches, and making sure the sauce totally covers the top layer of noodles before baking. Round it out with homemade garlic bread and a Caesar salad.

Do I need to buy no-boil lasagna noodles?

No—use regular dried lasagna noodles, preferably De Cecco. Skipping the boiling step isn’t the same as using noodles labeled “no-boil.” In our original tests, those absorbed too much sauce, leaving the finished lasagna drier than we wanted.

De Cecco Lasagne No.1 Pasta, 16-oz.

Why doesn’t this lasagna have ricotta or mozzarella?

This is a lasagna Bolognese, built around meat ragù and Parmesan-enriched béchamel rather than a separate cheese filling. The béchamel supplies the creaminess, while Parmesan brings salty, nutty flavor. For a less involved version with a cheese filling, try our Cottage Cheese Lasagna.

What’s the best way to split up the work?

Make the ragù one day, then tackle the béchamel, assembly, and baking the next. For an even lighter second day, make both sauces ahead and refrigerate them separately; rewarm the béchamel just enough to loosen it before layering. The ragù can be refrigerated for up to 4 days or frozen for up to 3 months, while the béchamel can be refrigerated for 1 day.

Watch Chris make BA’s Best Lasagna.

Recent findings suggest that save recipes and blueprint every week with confidence. Download the app.

Saving this cooking project for another day? We tasted nine brands to find the best frozen lasagna.

Preheat oven to 225°. Mix 2 lb. ground pork and 1 lb. ground beef chuck (20% fat) with your hands in a large bowl; season generously with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper, then mix again. Form into about 18 large meatballs (they don’t need to be perfect—you’ll be mashing them later).

Warm 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high heat. Working in 2 batches, cook meatballs, turning occasionally and reducing heat if bottom of pot looks in danger of scorching, until browned all over, about 6 minutes per batch. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet as they’re done.

Sources indicate that reduce heat to medium. Add 2 oz. pancetta (Italian bacon) or slab bacon, chopped, to pot and cook, stirring often, until lightly browned and beginning to crisp, about 5 minutes. Add 1 medium onion, finely chopped, 1 celery stalk, finely chopped, 1 medium carrot, peeled, finely chopped, and 6 garlic cloves, sliced, and cook, stirring occasionally, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until paste is darkened in color, about 2 minutes.

It has been revealed that add ¾ cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until almost completely evaporated, about 5 minutes. Add one 28-oz. can whole peeled tomatoes, crushing with your hands, and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, stirring occasionally, until liquid is jammy and reduced by about half, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 cup low-sodium chicken broth and 1 cup whole milk, then return meatballs to pot. Bring to a simmer. Cover pot partially with a lid, transfer to oven, and cook, checking every hour or so to ensure liquid is at a low simmer and adjusting oven temperature as needed, until meatballs are falling-apart tender, 3–4 hours.

According to recent reports, using a potato masher, break meatballs apart and incorporate into liquid (you should have about 8 cups ragù; transfer pot to stovetop and simmer gently to reduce if needed). Taste and season with more salt and black pepper if needed.

Do ahead: Ragù can be made 4 days ahead. Let cool; cover and chill, or freeze up to 3 months.

Melt 7 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in ¼ cup plus 3 Tbsp. all-purpose flour and cook, whisking occasionally, until mixture smells slightly nutty, about 4 minutes. Whisking constantly, add 6 cups whole milk. Increase heat to medium-high and continue whisking until mixture comes to a simmer. Reduce heat to maintain a simmer and cook, whisking occasionally, until béchamel thickens, about 4 minutes. Continue cooking, whisking occasionally and adjusting heat as needed to maintain a gentle simmer, until béchamel is smooth and velvety, 8–10 minutes more. Remove from heat and whisk in 4 oz. Parmesan cheese, coarsely grated (about 1 cup), a pinch of cayenne pepper, and a pinch of ground nutmeg. (You should have about 6 cups béchamel.) Season with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper. Transfer to a large bowl and press plastic wrap directly onto surface; let cool slightly.

Sources indicate that note: You can skip the following boiling step (and save yourself a pot to wash!). In side-by-side retests, the BA Test Kitchen found that regular dried lasagna noodles (not no-boil) produced similar results whether parboiled or layered straight from the box. To use them uncooked, spread the ragù and béchamel all the way to the edges, covering every noodle completely, and make sure the sauce blankets the top layer of noodles before baking.

Sources indicate that if parboiling: Cook 1¼ lb. dried lasagna noodles in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally and separating them so they don’t stick together, until just starting to soften but still snap in half rather than bend when folded; 3 minutes is the magic number. The noodles will be so firm it will just seem all wrong. Using tongs, transfer noodles to a large bowl of cold water to cool. Drain and lay flat in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet, separated by parchment or wax paper.

Lightly coat a 13x9", 4–6-qt. glass or ceramic baking dish with extra-virgin olive oil. Spread 1½ cups ragù in dish. Lay a single layer of noodles over ragù (cut or break noodles as needed to fill any gaps). Spoon 1¼ cups béchamel over noodles, spreading in an even layer with a small offset spatula. Top béchamel with 1½ cups of meat sauce. Repeat layering noodles, béchamel, and ragù 3 more times. Top with a fifth layer of noodles and the remaining 1 cup béchamel.

Note: For more pasta in every bite, build six layers instead of five. Start with the same 1½ cups ragù on the bottom of the dish, but use 1 cup béchamel and 1¼ cups ragù between the pasta layers. Finish with a sixth layer of pasta and the remaining 1 cup béchamel.

Cover with a lightly oiled piece of aluminum foil and set lasagna pan on a rimmed baking sheet (just to catch drips). Bake lasagna until bubbling gently around the edges, about 1 hour. Remove from oven. Increase oven temperature to 425° and carefully place rack in top of oven. Remove foil from lasagna and continue to bake until top is browned and crisp around the edges, 10–15 minutes longer. Let sit 10 minutes before serving.

According to recent reports, do ahead: Béchamel can be made 1 day ahead; keep chilled. Rewarm just enough to loosen before using. Lasagna can be assembled 1 month ahead; let cool, then cover with plastic and freeze. Let frozen lasagna thaw overnight in fridge before baking.

Editor’s note: This recipe first appeared in our February 2018 issue as part of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen’s definitive takes on iconic dishes. It has been updated with clearer assembly instructions and guidance from additional BA Test Kitchen testing, including the option to skip parboiling regular dried lasagna noodles. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a massive, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

It has been revealed that heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.).

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Industry observers note that remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

Recent findings suggest that thanksgiving asks a lot of us (and our ovens!). From making the turkey to all of the casseroles and sides, don’t even get me started on dessert. You’ve got a lot on your plate, so we’re trying to make the major turkey day a little easier. Appetizers are my favorite part of the meal: little bites that pack so much flavor and fun into the start of the big feast, so you’ve gotta make them count. Recent findings suggest that whether you’re looking for quick and easy last-minute options or want something more elaborate, we’ve got something on this list for you. Need more Thanksgiving hosting ideas? Check out our favorite Thanksgiving side dishes and Thanksgiving cocktails!

Pumpkin Spice Hot Honey Brie Bites.

Sweet and savory with a kick of heat, these pumpkin, Brie, and hot honey bites are the perfect fall appetizer to serve during the holidays. The honey provides the perfect balance for the sweetness of the pumpkin and the savory, melty Brie. Add a bit of fresh thyme and some roasted pecans, and you’ve got yourself a certified crowd-pleaser.

There is nothing better than a soft, homemade dinner roll. These rolls use sweet potatoes to make them even softer and fluffier, similar to our classic potato rolls. These would be a fun alternative to biscuits or Parker House rolls at Thanksgiving or another big family meal.

Having multiple Thanksgivings this year? Want to transform your leftovers from one into something incredible for the next? Look no further than this stuffed bread ring—it's gorgeous and super easy, thanks to store-bought crescent roll dough.

With all of the elements of stuffing plus the added flaky and butter benefits of biscuits, this pull-apart stuffing bread just might start a tug-of-war situation at your table when you grab for a slice.

It’s a tail as old as time: It’s right before Thanksgiving dinner, and your guests don’t want a full meal but are feeling a little peckish. Try a bird of a different feather this year, and serve this festive and impressive fruit and cheese display as the centerpiece of your holiday app table.

Recent findings suggest that these Thanksgiving potato skins are piled high with leftovers, but they’re so good, they just might deserve a place in your holiday spread. Preparing these potato skins is simple; all you need for this recipe are Thanksgiving leftovers and a few additional pantry staples: potatoes and cheddar cheese.

It has been revealed that it’s hard to find a party appetizer that’s more beloved than a cheese log—or its alternate form, the cheese ball. Here, dried sweetened cranberries, walnuts, and fresh thyme conjure a holiday feeling, while a little honey complements the sweet-tart fruit.

These are a fan favorite every fall. They always disappear within minutes, probably because the combo of salty, creamy brie, sweet-tart cranberry sauce, and crunchy pecans is PERFECT.

Fall desserts may get all the attention once autumn comes around, but I'm here to say that seasonal appetizers deserve their share of the spotlight—especially these adorable pizza-stuffed pumpkins. Stuffed with creamy ricotta, these biscuit-based bites are baked to golden perfection before being brushed with a flavor-packed garlic butter.

Just like our famous cranberry brie bites, these little guys are hard to put down! They're the perfect amount of sweet and savory, so you can serve them before or after the major meal.

Sausage Stuffing Bites With Cranberry Sauce.

It has been revealed that stuffing, inside the turkey or out, is a Thanksgiving staple. The only thing better? MORE. STUFFING. Enter this bite-sized, stuffing-centered appetizer with a tangy, three-ingredient dipping sauce (just cranberry sauce, honey, and Dijon).

In a recent development, even if you're not serving turkey this Thanksgiving doesn't mean you can't get in on the theme. Enter: this adorable cheeseball. We used carrots, pecans, pretzels, and bell peppers to create the iconic look, but feel free to substitute them with different ingredients for what you have on hand. Serve it with crackers and use the decorations as dippers too!

In a recent development, these sweet potato bites have a crunchy, herbaceous crust, with a sweet, silky inside that, when topped with a light drizzle of honey, will have you craving them again and again. Once you bite through the crust, the sweet potato mixes with that melted, nutty Gruyère for a dream flavor combination that works SO well.

Cranberry Brie Jalapeño Poppers.

According to recent reports, cranberry brie bites are by far one of our favorite appetizers for the holidays, but jalapeño poppers also have place in our hearts too... So why not combine them? The spice of the jalapeño goes so well with the tart cranberries.

In a recent development, to make these, we stuff baby bella mushrooms with garlicky, herby breadcrumbs and plenty of cheese. Stuff them ahead of time and bake them off when you're ready for the most Thanksgiving-friendly appetizer ever.

Cranberry Brie Pull-Apart Bread.

Pull-apart bread reaches a whole new level, thanks to brie and cranberry sauce. Use your favorite homemade sauce recipes, but store-bought works too if you're short for time.

Caramelized Onion & Goat Cheese Bites.

Little puff pastry squares get topped with caramelized onions and a little crumbled goat cheese for an easy appetizer that always wows. The final step is a light drizzle of honey for that salty sweet combination everyone will love.

It has been revealed that if you’re a fan of our cranberry brie bites, we’ve got news for you: There’s a upcoming app in town, and it’s inspired by another fan fave, baked feta pasta. These features the flavors you know and love, all nestled into bite-sized cups of golden crescent roll dough.

There's something very classic about the crescent roll dough flavor, so we tend to gravitate toward it, but puff pastry or even biscuit dough should both work here, too.

Think this sounds like a strange combo? You've gotta trust us on this one. If the aroma of toasted puff pastry, roasted apples, and nutty cheddar cheese doesn’t wake up your spirit… we're not sure what will.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Netflix’s The Beast in Me brought Claire Danes back to TV and reunited her with creator Howard Gordon, with whom she spent eight seasons working on Homeland. That combination was already exciting enough, but the cast also included Matthew Rhys and Brittany Snow, and Conan O’Brien and Jodie Foster were among the producers.

Sources indicate that danes stars as Aggie, a successful author grappling with the grief of losing her son. Her fragile sense of stability is shaken when Nile (Rhys), a wealthy real estate figure once accused of murdering his wife, moves in next door. With just eight episodes, the series left viewers wondering whether Aggie’s story could continue beyond its initial run. Here’s what we know so far.

Sources indicate that yes. In September 2026, Variety confirmed that The Beast in Me would return for a second season on Netflix.

According to recent reports, “We always told ourselves we’d only do a second season of The Beast in Me if we found a story that was worthy of the first—and I’m thrilled to say we found it,” Gordon said in a statement. “We loved making this show and our audience seemed to love watching it, so we’re enormously grateful to Jinny Howe and Netflix, and to Karey Burke and 20th Television for giving us the chance to get the band back together and do it again.”.

According to recent reports, variety’s report confirmed that Danes would return to her role for The Beast in Me season 2. In October 2026, Deadline reported that John Goodman (Righteous Gemstones, Digger) would star as “Aggie’s dad, believed to be a long-time con artist.”.

On November 3, Deadline revealed that Lili Taylor (Outer Range, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping) joined the cast in a series regular role as Fiona, Aggie’s stepmother.

On November 19, Netflix revealed that Riley Keough (Daisy Jones & The Six, Under the Bridge) and Lorelei Olivia Mote (They Know, The Rescue, Daisy Jones & The Six) will join the show as series regulars for season 2, while Aaron Paul (Breaking Bad, Fallout), Taip Ceman (Cupertino, The Families Stone), and Matthew James Thomas (Accused, Summer of Rockets) join as recurring guest stars.

Gordon discussed the ending of season 1 with The Wrap and what it made him consider for season 2.

It has been revealed that “I think that to the extent that Aggie is a writer who has been delivered to this next stage of her life, whatever that stage is,” he shared at the time. “If there is a story, there might be more. I am tempted by the character of her grifter father in some way. We’ll see how the show does and if an idea comes. But I think they’d be open to more.”.

#112558. What Is GTA VI Trying to Say About the Manosphere?

What Is GTA VI Trying to Say About the Manosphere?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1883 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that what’s a man allowed to like these days?
  • We asked a physical therapist, developers, and other gaming obsessives for the best tips to help you highjack garbage trucks in Leonida for as long as humanly possible.
  • Grand Theft Auto VI, these men assert, is emasculating because it asks players to role-play a man that respects his partner and do mundane tasks she would appreciate, like repaint their bedroom or get her a nice necklace.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that what’s a man allowed to like these days? Not the Super Bowl, or Christopher Nolan movies, it seems, each of them guilty of sins against masculinity. Now there is a latest offender: Grand Theft Auto VI. Over one brief weekend, Rockstar’s long-in-the-works, exorbitantly expensive opus has given us a rare monocultural moment and elicited a wounded reaction from a slice of gamers steeped in the streams and podcasts of right-wing figures like Steven Crowder, Zack “Asmongold” Hoyt, and Braden Eric “Clavicular” Peters.

We asked a physical therapist, developers, and other gaming obsessives for the best tips to help you highjack garbage trucks in Leonida for as long as humanly possible.

Grand Theft Auto VI, these men assert, is emasculating because it asks players to role-play a man that respects his partner and do mundane tasks she would appreciate, like repaint their bedroom or get her a nice necklace. For others, it is less that the game is offensively woke and more that its wokeness is getting in the way of their fun. “You can’t kiss anyone other than your strong female Latina partner,” complains Crowder, his cohosts all lamenting that video games ought to be a vehicle for their every base fantasy. These men object to what they see as politics encroaching on what they think ought to be a politics-free space, “shut up and dribble” but for violent video games. But there’s a delicious irony to this because the game genuinely has a bone to pick with these unfortunate figureheads of the manosphere.

The manosphere, it should be noted, is a (shitty) state of mind. Less a formal designation than a collection of people who promote similar sexist, racist, and/or fascist ideals, a loose web of podcasters, streamers, and influencers who all preach a gospel of grievance in which men are victims of women withholding sex, liberals withholding power, and other men for not performing masculinity correctly. They can run the gamut from disgraced influencer Andrew Tate (currently in jail awaiting trial for a litany of alleged crimes) to the comedians and podcasters orbiting Joe Rogan’s massive audience. But they all have one thing in common: These men and the people who pay rapt attention to them are the targets of Grand Theft Auto VI’s satire.

Some background here: While yes, Grand Theft Auto VI casts players as modern Bonnie and Clyde Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, their story is only one reason to play the game. Another is the incredibly dense setting of Leonida, a feverish and astonishingly lifelike take on Florida, chock-full of weirdos and wildlife to take in. Layered on top of that is a whole media ecosystem: a fake Instagram to scroll named Snapmatic, a news feed app, a suite of radio stations with robust programming including two talk radio stations, three TV networks with entire reveals, and magazines and books you can read in excerpts.

It has been revealed that it’s in all this background material that Grand Theft Auto VI really tears into the modern grievance grift of the manosphere. The game’s decade-plus gestation means it’s had a lot of time to amass a shooting gallery of noxious conservative male influencers that the algorithm has elevated and buried, ranging from flat-earth conspiracy theorists to MAHA-adjacent cronies. On the Weazel TV network, you can find these views as the punchline of entire Adult Swim–esque cartoons like Right Wing, about a patriotic superhero horrified to learn that a straight pride parade has been transformed by a gay superhero called the Flamer. “All these years suppressing who I was, but now I’m free!” shouts Right Wing’s colleague Great Uncle Sam after the Flamer has liberated him. “Isn’t that what America is all about?” “No,” Right Wing retorts. “America is about guns, and lots of them!”.

Scroll through Snapmatic, and you can find a clear analogue of Liver King—the content creator who promoted an “ancestral lifestyle” that involved consuming raw animal organs—posting under @paleoprimal. In one of his faux influencer videos, he advises his followers to “start beating your meat,” before dropkicking a hunk of raw flesh. “I don’t eat anything unless I’ve conquered it first.” Ashes of Glory, a sendup of historical war fiction that sits by Jason’s bed, is drowning in overly reverent prose that also happens to note that its war heroes are psychopaths. One passage: “'You’ve been charged with murdering civilians, violating every law known to God and man, calling your enemies rude names, and uncontrollable teabagging,’ mentioned the General. 'Which is exactly why we need your help.’”.

According to recent reports, A lot of these blows are glancing, more about attacking attitudes than people, give or take a Liver King. But turn the in-game radio dial to WKTT, Grand Theft Auto VI’s conservative talk radio station, and the targets sharpen. Hosts Richard Bastion (Jason Sudeikis) and Dominic “The Brick” Brizzolato (Stavros Halkias) do pastiches of Alex Jones and Nick Fuentes, spouting racist and sexist takes. Ponytails are “the hairstyle of someone who’s about to suck your dick,” per Brizzolato, who also maintains local football team the Manatees have problems to do with “culture” and “not race.” Every so often they are undercut by callers who ask how performance-enhancing drugs and hair implants don’t count as gender-affirming care. Of the many items they hawk—Flaming O’s snacks, Sprunk soda, and Patriot beer—the most absurd and on-the-nose is a special playing card set with “no queens.”.

Sources indicate that in its blunt re-creation of the conservative male media ecosystem, Grand Theft Auto VI plainly states what Rockstar thinks of these guys: They’re really fucking stupid. They are stupid in ways that are true to life and moronic in ways that Rockstar exaggerates, but only just so. They drive home this point by underlining the pathetic loneliness subtextual in all these real-life broadcasts, with Richard Bastion asserting that he doesn’t have friends but is building “a fraternity with a mission to save America” and that friends “let you down” and “tell the papers that your wife sleeps in a separate bed and sometimes house.”.

After 13 years, and a budget rumored to rival that of Dubai’s Burj Khalifa skyscraper, the new Grand Theft Auto is finally here. Our critic's verdict? It's a tour de force that reimagines what a video game can be.

The message hits cleaner than past iterations of the game not because Grand Theft Auto VI is any less lowbrow than before—it is still awash in dick jokes, memes about shitting your pants, and South Park–esque lambasting of White America—but because this more richly detailed, lifelike version of Grand Theft Auto means the cartoonish aspects stand out all the more. What’s a joke and what is not is clearer than it has ever been.

Despite the protests from fans who say the latest iteration of Grand Theft Auto betrays the spirit of the franchise, there was always evidence that the game hated these hypermasculinity-obsessed tryhards, even before they had a manosphere to inhabit. While early games in the series did not have much in the way of plot or characters, they were tongue-in-cheek caricatures of gangster epics and the ambitions of men within them, a touch of arch Scottish humor (Rockstar’s lead Grand Theft Auto team is based in Edinburgh) keeping them from being sincere homages.

According to recent reports, nearly 20 years ago in Grand Theft Auto IV—a series turning point, where the games started to have stories with intentional thematic interests—Rockstar Games incessantly lambasted the pursuit of the hypermasculine. Its protagonist Niko Bellic served as a stoic counterpoint to many of the jacked-up weirdos of the faux Latest York dubbed Liberty City, arriving in the United States during the game’s opening credits with nothing but the clothes on his back and his cousin Roman’s lies about his own success in his ear. Through Niko’s journey, Grand Theft Auto IV posed the arguments that this country’s obsession with the unfettered pursuit of power and wealth makes people unwell and that culture afflicts men in ways that render them uniquely delusional. It gives his cousin Roman a fantasy of a success that will never come, causing him to submit to the intimidations of two-bit enforcers. It makes men like Brucie Kibbutz, a supplement-obsessed fitness freak, deny his own obvious interest in men in favor of a nonstop stream of homophobic jokes and crude sexual banter. It makes Niko, a soldier who thought he was escaping his criminal past, find himself immediately becoming a different kind of criminal at the behest of men who believe the world is theirs to take. And that’s just in the first few hours.

Grand Theft Auto IV’s skewering came at the expense of others—namely the women and queer people who are the butt of nearly every joke in the game. Seven years later, Grand Theft Auto V would course-correct by being hateful to everyone in its fictional version of Los Angeles: the acai-and-granola liberals and the asshole conservatives alike. It mires itself in the desperation of male entitlement, as three characters—the middle-aged Michael De Santa, the young striver Franklin Clinton, and Trevor Philips, the lewd loose cannon—adjust poorly to a world they cannot dominate. De Santa, arguably the protagonist of the three characters the player can inhabit, sees the world as out to emasculate him, either through his wife’s affair, his deadbeat son, or his daughter, who he must rescue from TV producers that he assumes are predatory. Michael’s world is much simpler when he’s holding a gun, and Grand Theft Auto V is eager to get one in his hands. In this, it feels like the game wants you to agree: Isn’t this more fun than dealing with all that? And it is, because Rockstar made it that way.

Sources indicate that yes, there are missions. But have you seen the kicks?

It has been revealed that there has always been a have-it-both-ways nature to Grand Theft Auto’s satire. Rockstar is happy to facilitate the same American male id it’s lampooning, and the staggering number of copies sold suggests that even conservative commentators out there appealing to incel logic are logging right onto their PlayStations the moment they stop posting. But despite what critics may claim to their audiences, Grand Theft Auto VI’s manosphere parodies are not a huge departure for the series, because the problems with toxic masculinity remain woefully consistent, as do the grifters who seek to profit from it. Insecurity is both a massive business and a renewable energy source.

It has been revealed that what’s left out of all these complaints about Grand Theft Auto VI being a game where you embody a simp man is that you do not have to do any of the loving behavior these clowns rail against in the video game. You can ignore Lucia when playing as Jason, let your relationship grow distant and decay. You can leave the walls unpainted, never pick up flowers or groceries, not press the button to hold Lucia’s hand, keep your distance on the dance floor. The game just makes clear what the real world does not: That’s a good way to end up alone. And that’s the one thing the parodied blowhards of GTA VI’s in-game manosphere broadcast loud and clear: that they’re alone.

#112557. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (406 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior.
  • More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.
  • Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

Apple Juice Bread

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level.
  • I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal.
  • In a recent development, take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

In a recent development, take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard.

In a recent development, mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

According to recent reports, set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Sources indicate that transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Industry observers note that place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Industry observers note that bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

Sticky Miso Chicken and More Recipes We Made This Week

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1457 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work.
  • My husband and I recently took our 3-year-old daughter apple picking.
  • Industry observers note that armed with a fresh trio of cumin, coriander, and turmeric from Diaspora Spice Co., I decided to make Alison Roman’s Chicken Tikka Masala.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

My husband and I recently took our 3-year-old daughter apple picking. As expected at the tail end of the season, the only apples left were Granny Smith. A perfect apple for baking, I decided to peruse our new app to see what fit the bill and found Zaynab Issa’s Caramel Apple Snacking Cake. After scanning the instructions, it seemed like a fairly straightforward one-bowl situation—the perfect pace for my lazy Sunday. I grated the apples right into a large bowl, and mixed it with the dry and wet ingredients before baking. The cake is elevated with a quick caramel that gets drizzled on top, which makes it feel fancy. —June Kim, executive editor.

Industry observers note that armed with a fresh trio of cumin, coriander, and turmeric from Diaspora Spice Co., I decided to make Alison Roman’s Chicken Tikka Masala. It’s a bit of a project, but the payoff is worth it. The spice-rich sauce takes 30 to 40 minutes, but let it go closer to 40 for something thick, concentrated, and luxurious. Broiling is a genius move: Set on a wire rack, the yogurt-marinated chicken gets air on all sides, so it blackens instead of steaming before being added to the sauce. To accompany the main, we made a side of Priya Krishna’s Aloo Gobi in the air fryer. It came out crispy and caramelized, at least until I coated it in the creamy sauce. —Olivia Tarantino, senior shopping editor.

Sources indicate that with a name like Just-Keeps-Getting-Better Lentil Salad, how could you go wrong? My former colleague Sarah Jampel’s rightfully beloved recipe is one of those staples I’ve made so many times, I don’t even need to look at it to double-check quantities or instructions anymore. It’s become second nature. And when I’m feeling inspired, or my pantry has seen better days, it’s pretty adaptable too. This week I whipped up a huge bowl with walnuts and cashews in place of the almonds, a blood orange standing in for the lemon, and added some lovely chicories to mingle with the kale. As always, it was crunchy and fresh, tender and filling, even three days after I whipped it up. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor.

Industry observers note that I love cookbook author Samantha Seneviratne’s recipes and her recent one for a tahini cake crusted with sesame seeds called to me. Just the thing for a fall weekend. I scaled down the recipe for my 8x8" pan using Kendra Vaculin’s handy conversion guide. And I did a mix of white and black sesame seeds on top for fun. It was plush and not too sweet—great for dessert and even better for breakfast the next day. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

Sources indicate that I’ve been holding on to this recipe for years, and it’s finally time I release it into the world. Be free Sticky Miso Chicken! It’s made with a three-ingredient marinade with stuff you probably already have in your cupboard. Equal parts miso and honey, plus a healthy splash of soy sauce mixed together creates a million-dollar burnished glaze. I slather the marinade onto chicken thighs, but you could also do chicken breast, salmon, shrimp, tofu. Go wild. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

Sources indicate that every fall I stuff my pantry with cans of pumpkin purée. And fortunately our annual Pumpkin Week tells me exactly what to do with the haul. I’m always in search of more savory uses for the ingredient, and my coworker Jesse Szewczyk’s Pumpkin Black Bean Enchiladas were right up my alley. I did a mix of black and kidney beans (what was around) and I toned down the spice for my toddler who—the universe laughs—refused to eat them anyway, instead opting to smear the sauce all over his clothes. C’est la vie! —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

There is a new vendor at my greenmarket who makes incredible buffalo milk yogurt. My favorite is flavored with tangy, floral passion fruit. It’s not too sweet and works beautifully with fruit and granola. To showcase its power as a sauce, I made David Tamarkin’s apple olive oil cake (baked in an 8" round instead of a loaf) and served the yogurt underneath. For the cake, you shred a couple of apples then squeeze out their juices, which you can then drink for a baker’s treat. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking.

Sources indicate that one of my favorite things is to use a banana bread recipe to make muffins and call it meal prep. I pack this gluten-free batter into tins, sprinkle on some flaxseed and pecans, and reduce the bake time. They can easily pass for breakfast, an afternoon snack, or dessert, and the recipe yields enough muffins to be enjoyed throughout the week with a scoop of yogurt or swipe of nut butter. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager.

With a recipe entitled Bob’s Chicken and Cabbage Salad, I’m sure you’re wondering: Who the heck is Bob? Author Melissa Broder’s late father, who happened to be fervently devoted to purple cabbage. Well, Bob, me too—especially after trying this one. Per the instructions, I chopped up half a head of cabbage, baby bok choy, scallions, bean sprouts, and water chestnuts, then tossed the roughage with pulled chicken. This time around, I did cheat with a store-bought rotisserie bird to jump-start cooking (it was 8 p.m. when I started, okay?). That also meant halving the heavenly soy-ginger dressing, since I no longer needed some of it for the marinade. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

My Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser has a wild little pasta up her sleeve that I can’t get enough of: Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates. When she first made it for the team, I was blown away. I would have never thought to throw dates into a pasta, but alas, it’s delicious. Each bite has something sweet, something creamy, a bit of crunch, and endless fun. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor.

Since my son started daycare in September, our household has been sick more than it has been healthy. So it makes sense that I have been on a chicken soup kick. I have it for lunch and dinner and drink mugfuls of stock between meals. My latest batch was my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup, which has a beautifully spiced broth and lots of nourishing spinach. It may not be a cure-all, but close enough. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

Delicata squash should be as popular as butternut. It’s far easier to cut (no hacks or hacking necessary), the thin skin is not only edible but tasty, and it’s got a sweet potato-like flesh that’s creamy and, well, sweet. I usually treat it simply (oil, salt and pepper, hot oven, done), but I treated myself to my former colleague Rachel Gurjar’s gussied-up Roasted Delicata Squash With Crispy Onions and I’m so glad I did. The squash itself takes no extra effort, but gathering up some toppings, like store-bought fried onions tossed with extra spices, juicy pomegranate seeds, and seasoned yogurt, transformed it into a dish I was proud to serve to guests. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor.

In a recent development, we have a latest Friday tradition at our house: Pasta Alla Vodka and Caesar salad. Not rocket science, I know, but after a rough-and-tumble week of work and school, we are all reaching for some semblance of comfort. It is also easy enough to whip up that I can often beat the timing of our former Friday tradition, take-out pizza. The Caesar dressing is usually made in advance (I keep a batch in the fridge because my family lurves it) and the pasta of choice is usually rigatoni. It cooks in about the same amount of time as the sauce—I just love when that happens. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor.

There’s nothing more perfect than a tuna melt. Buttery slices of sourdough or rye that leave a shine of grease on your fingers. Tuna salad mashed into tender flakes, speckled with crisp celery, onion, and herbs. A blanket of American cheese, so stretchy it’ll rival a mozzarella stick. And a mandatory pickle, to offer added tangy solace after each bite. I ate mine with salt-and-vinegar kettle chips stuffed inside because that’s how my favorite diner does it. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

Recent findings suggest that succession may be long over (and may she rest in power), but the phrase “ludicrously capacious bag” has proven its cultural staying power. While last year was all about major, face-obscuring sunglasses, 2026 belonged to the supersized bags.

Industry observers note that yes, this year was for those of us who need a purse that fits everything you could ever need and more: a book or two, a water bottle, perhaps a sweater, and, of course, a bottom lined with emotional support receipts. Micro bags had their moment; now, the pendulum has swung back. This year was for the real schleppers.

Celebrities—many of whom even bought into the ludicrously minuscule bag trend just a few years ago—were very eager for the return of the oversized purse. Perhaps nobody was more excited to haul their belongings around than Rosalía, who recently strutted through Upcoming York in a pair of lucite-heeled platform pointe shoes, carrying a massive, three-foot-long custom Dana Toder bag like a balance bar.

While hers was the most extreme, Rosalía was far from the only celeb schlepper this year. Many were fond of the gargantuan carry-on: Dua Lipa touched down in Latest York toting an enormous raffia Chanel shopper, while Kendall Jenner arrived in Venice with a Chanel weekender, and Pedro Pascal also joined in on the trend, carrying a bottle-green Chanel tote in London.

Are you sensing a theme? Yes, Matthieu Blazy is pro-schlep. But while he’s creating the most covetable accessories du jour, he’s not the only one here for a ginormous purse revival. Below, revisit 2026 in outsized bags, from Future’s Hermès HAC to Bella Hadid’s Prada.

#112546. The Carnivore Diet Is Peak Protein Extremism. How Healthy Is It Really?
