📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you blueprint to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

Industry observers note that we never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling).

According to recent reports, whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

According to recent reports, make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too promptly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

In a recent development, do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

It has been revealed that bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Industry observers note that transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

According to recent reports, spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

Which Thanksgiving Foods Belong in the Same Bite?

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

It has been revealed that some Thanksgiving food combinations are obvious. Others might earn you some questioning looks at the dinner table.

For years, my kids refused to let any two foods touch on their plates. I found this particularly maddening at Thanksgiving. There’s an entire table of food to fit onto a single plate and only so much room to negotiate separate territories for the mashed potatoes and green bean casserole! Thankfully, they’re a little more accommodating these days and, like me, have come to appreciate the occasional overlap between dishes.

Recent findings suggest that of course, plenty of adults also have strong opinions about which Thanksgiving foods should mingle. There are those who insist on keeping every dish separate, those who permit a little gravy to stray onto the stuffing but draw the line at cranberry sauce, and those who deliberately assemble the perfect combination on every forkful. Then there’s always the unhinged relative who stirs the entire contents of their plate into a single, gravy-saturated mass and eats it with the serene confidence of someone who has never once questioned their choices.

In a recent development, personally, I’m firmly in favor of combining foods, although I do believe a little discretion is in order. Thanksgiving dinner offers a wonderful assortment of rich, savory and tart flavors, and knowing which ones to bring together is part of what makes the meal so satisfying. There’s a culinary reason that cranberry sauce belongs alongside turkey, and that stuffing and mashed potatoes are particularly good together. And once you understand why those combinations work, you can start building some excellent bites of your own.

According to recent reports, absolutely. In fact, some of the most familiar food pairings are built around the idea that one ingredient can supply something another lacks. Think of a rich cut of meat served with a sharp, acidic sauce, or a creamy dish finished with something crisp. Neither component is necessarily lacking on its own, but the contrast makes the combination much more interesting.

Industry observers note that the same principle applies to Thanksgiving foods. Acidity helps balance richness, sweetness can temper salty or intensely savory flavors, and a change in texture can make a forkful more interesting. It’s not particularly complicated, but there’s a difference between understanding why two foods complement each other and simply hoping for the best.

Some combinations are simply better than others, though saying so at Thanksgiving dinner may invite more opinions than you bargained for.

Turkey and cranberry sauce: There’s a reason this pairing has endured for generations. Turkey, particularly the breast meat, is relatively mild, and the tartness of cranberry sauce gives it a welcome lift. It’s also an excellent remedy for turkey that’s spent a little too long in the oven, a situation that has befallen even the most conscientious Thanksgiving cooks.

Mashed potatoes, stuffing and gravy: I consider this one of Thanksgiving’s greatest achievements. The smooth, buttery potatoes and herbaceous stuffing are excellent together, and a generous spoonful of gravy makes the whole arrangement even better. There’s nothing particularly subtle about it, but Thanksgiving dinner isn’t generally celebrated for its subtlety.

Industry observers note that sweet potatoes and turkey: The natural sweetness of roasted sweet potatoes makes a lovely contrast to savory turkey, particularly the richer dark meat. A traditional sweet potato casserole can work, too, although I draw the line somewhere around the marshmallow topping. I have nothing against marshmallows, but I prefer to encounter them after dinner.

Green bean casserole and mashed potatoes: These are two of my Thanksgiving essentials, and I see no reason they shouldn’t share a fork. The creamy green beans and buttery potatoes are lovely together, but it’s the crispy fried onions that really make the combination work. That salty crunch is a welcome addition to the softer textures.

It has been revealed that turkey, stuffing and cranberry sauce: This is probably my favorite combo of the bunch. The savory turkey and seasoned stuffing are practically made for one another, while a little cranberry sauce cuts through the richness. It’s essentially a Thanksgiving leftover sandwich without the bread, although I wouldn’t object to adding a dinner roll to the equation.

Macaroni and cheese and cranberry sauce: I realize this combination may call my culinary credentials into question, but hear me out. Rich, creamy mac and cheese practically begs for something sharp and acidic to cut through it, and cranberry sauce does exactly that. It’s not so different from serving a sharp cheddar with fruit preserves on a charcuterie board, although I concede that putting cranberry sauce on macaroni and cheese is a considerably harder sell. But that’s half the fun of Thanksgiving dinner: discovering which combinations you’re willing to defend.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At first glance, these homemade cinnamon rolls have all the classics: buttery, golden-brown dough, a gooey cinnamon-and-brown-sugar filling, and a generous swoop of cream cheese frosting. But a couple of smart moves make them especially fluffy, with a tender crumb that stays soft well into the next day (assuming there are any left).

Sources indicate that one is tangzhong, a Chinese technique that cooks a small portion of flour and milk into a thick paste before it’s added to the dough. The precooked starch helps the dough hold on to more moisture, resulting in pillowy, supple cinnamon rolls.

The other is brown butter, which gives the filling a nutty, toasty edge. The tangy cream cheese frosting balances all that richness; add the optional lemon zest for extra brightness.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls the night before?

Yes. You can refrigerate the dough after its first rise or assemble the rolls in their baking pans and refrigerate them before the second rise. Cover tightly with plastic wrap to prevent the dough from drying out. The next day, let the chilled dough sit at room temperature for about an hour before proceeding with the recipe, making sure the shaped rolls have doubled in volume before baking.

Why is my cinnamon roll dough so sticky?

This is a soft, moisture-rich dough, but it should become smooth and elastic as you knead it. For the most consistent results, weigh your flour rather than measuring by volume. Also, make sure the tangzhong has thickened into a paste before adding it to the dough: You should be able to see the tracks of your whisk across the bottom of the saucepan. Avoid adding excessive extra flour, which can make the finished rolls dense.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls without a stand mixer?

Yes, though kneading this soft, enriched dough by hand takes considerable time and effort. Several readers have reported success doing so. If using a stand mixer, keep an eye on the motor during the extended kneading time. If it begins to strain or overheat, stop the machine and finish kneading by hand.

Can I use active dry yeast instead of instant yeast?

It has been revealed that this recipe calls for instant yeast, which can be mixed directly into the dough. Active dry yeast generally requires activation in warm liquid and may affect rising times, so we recommend sticking with instant yeast for the recipe as written. For more information, see our guide to the different types of yeast.

Whisk ¾ cup whole milk and ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour in a medium saucepan until smooth. Place saucepan over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture is thickened and whisk lines are visible on bottom of pan, about 2 minutes. Scrape tangzhong into the bowl of a stand mixer and let cool.

Add 1 large egg, one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), ⅓ cup (67 g) granulated sugar, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt,  and remaining 1½ cups whole milk to tangzhong and whisk to combine. Add remaining 5½ cups (688 g) all-purpose flour. Fit bowl onto stand mixer; fit mixer with dough hook attachment. Mix on low speed until combined, about 1 minute. Increase speed to medium-low and mix, scraping down sides of bowl occasionally, until dough is smooth and elastic, 18–24 minutes. Pinch off a golf-ball-size piece of dough and stretch between your fingers as thin as possible without breaking. If you can see light through the dough, it’s ready. If not, continue mixing a few more minutes, then try again.

Add ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, to dough and mix on medium speed until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Continue mixing until dough pulls away cleanly from sides of bowl and is no longer tacky to the touch, 5–7 minutes longer. Remove bowl from mixer and cover with a damp kitchen towel. Let sit in a warm spot until doubled in volume, 60–90 minutes.

While the dough is rising, cook ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until butter foams and milk solids turn dark amber, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a heatproof bowl and let cool slightly. Add 1 cup (packed; 200 g) dark brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. ground cinnamon, 2 Tbsp. heavy cream, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to butter and mix to combine.

Stretch dough into a rough rectangle; if dough feels stiff, let sit 5–10 minutes to allow gluten to relax. Arrange dough with short side facing you and roll out to a 24x13" rectangle. Spread filling over dough in an even layer.

Recent findings suggest that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Bake rolls until golden on top and puffed (don’t be alarmed if they rise dramatically in the center), 25–30 minutes.

Meanwhile, using an electric mixer on medium speed or a whisk, beat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, and 8 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, in a large bowl, scraping down sides of bowl as needed, until combined. Add 1¼ cups (138 g) powdered sugar, 1 Tbsp. heavy cream, 1 tsp. lemon zest (if using), and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt and beat until mixture is smooth and sugar is incorporated. Taste and beat in more powdered sugar (up to ¾ cup) if desired. Thin with more cream as needed, a teaspoonful at a time, until frosting is thick but spreadable.

Let cinnamon rolls cool in pan 5 minutes; spread frosting over.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, what a lark! What a plunge! Next up on the Vogue Book Club’s reading list is none other than Mrs. Dalloway, the classic 1925 novel by Virginia Woolf.

Our selection comes near the end of a year crowded with Woolf adaptations: Virginia Woolf’s Night and Day, based on her 1919 novel, directed by Tina Gharavi and written by Justine Waddell, and two retellings of Mrs. Dalloway—Rachel Rose’s The Last Day, starring Alicia Vikander, Victoria Pedretti, and Wagner Moura, and Clarissa from Arie Esiri and Chuko Esiri, starring Sophie Okonedo, David Oyelowo, and Ayo Edebiri.

In the September 15, 1925, issue of Vogue, our reviewer, Berenice Claire Skidelsky, compared the prose style employed in Mrs. Dalloway—fleet and fluid, drifting in and out of the minds and memories of its characters—to James Joyce’s in Ulysses, published three years earlier. “Both books have as their substance the odyssey of a group of persons through a day—not only their outward circumstances, but the intricate twistings and windings of their thoughts and the interplay of their lives, one with another,” Skidelsky wrote. “Both recognize the importance of the nuance in human significances; and both get arresting effects in an extremely novel manner.”.

In a recent development, on the subject of Mrs. Dalloway’s actual plot—Mrs. Dalloway prepares for a party while a veteran of World War I suffers from post-traumatic stress—Skidelsky noted, dryly: “No summary of the story can be given, for the simple reason that there isn’t any story.” Yet that isn’t, strictly speaking, a criticism. “A series of incidents move with sequence and with charm into the formation of a unity that has novelty and strength to recommend it,” she continued. “A faintly melancholy consciousness of the evanescence of youth, and, indeed, of life itself, that rings like an echo ever and again throughout the book…adds poignancy of appeal for readers to whom the essence of life reflected in literature is of more moment than a story.”.

Befitting, in a way, the book’s unusual structure, the Vogue Book Club is varying its format for Mrs. Dalloway. Instead of publishing a succession of stories on a weekly basis, we’ve declared December 14–18 Woolf Week here at Vogue. (Clarissa is in limited theaters December 18.) Every day that week will yield upcoming stories about Mrs. Dalloway and the life and work of Woolf more broadly.

Industry observers note that eager to follow along? Those who don’t already have a dog-eared copy of Mrs. Dalloway at home can pick up a (discounted!) paperback here. Then let the schedule below guide your reading—and when you’re done, meet us here (and on the Vogue app!) for Woolf Week. See you soon!

  • For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.
  • It has been revealed that whisk 1 tsp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

It has been revealed that whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Sources indicate that place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

According to recent reports, spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.).

According to recent reports, bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

  • This flavorful bowl reminds me of Dig Inn’s glory days—only I can enjoy it without elbowing my way through midtown lunchtime mobs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, most nights I try to hit up an exercise class after work, which means when I finally get home in the evening I’m tired, hungry, and craving something full of nutrients. With 26 grams of protein and just 25 minutes of prep-and-cook time, HelloFresh’s Garlicky Shrimp Couscous Bowl is a great solution for dinner.

This flavorful bowl reminds me of Dig Inn’s glory days—only I can enjoy it without elbowing my way through midtown lunchtime mobs. Roasted broccoli and shrimp sautéed with lemon and plenty of garlic are spooned on top of large couscous pearls. Chili flakes add an extra kick.

In a recent development, you’ll need to grab olive oil, butter, salt, and pepper from your own pantry; everything else is included in your delivery. The shrimp arrives fully cleaned and deveined, thank god. I love that a small pouch of veggie stock is included for cooking your couscous, a detail that many meal kits overlook.

True to the recipe card’s promise, the meal cooks in less than half an hour. Prep your mise (chop the broccoli, garlic, and parsley; slice your lemon; rinse the shrimp), then get your broccoli in the oven and couscous on the stove. While they do their thing, you cook the shrimp so that everything finishes around the same time.

I found the instructions incredibly clear to follow, including when to add water and butter to your shrimp, and when to reduce the pan’s heat. I don’t often cook shrimp at home, and I was pleasantly surprised how easy it was and how swiftly they pinked up.

In a word: delish! Garlic can cover a multitude of sins, and there’s a generous amount used when cooking both the couscous and shrimp, the latter also includes garlic powder, for good measure. Lemon and parsley give the dish a nice freshness; the flavors remind me of my favorite clam pie from a local Brooklyn pizzeria.

Sources indicate that this is a great dish for pescatarians, those looking to cut back on red meat, and health-conscious eaters. The small ingredient list is full of nutritional value: carbs, fats, and lean protein to help me refuel after a long day, plus five grams of fiber and vitamin K, calcium, and potassium from the broccoli (cruciferous veggies are super good for you).

Would make again. Sometimes you want to use your time in the kitchen to discover newly introduced flavors and learn new techniques, and sometimes your main goal is getting dinner on the table quickly. This recipe hits on the weeknight trifecta: It’s tasty, easy to make, and nutritious.

The Best Everyday Sneakers, According to Vogue Editors

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that whether you’re walking down Broadway to run weekend errands, hiking through the Adirondacks, or logging miles in preparation for a marathon, sneakers are the backbone of a modern wardrobe.
  • For some on the team, comfort and versatility matter most.
  • I love these Kallmeyer Nike sneakers as a fancy weekend shoe and these brown Asics for my fall palette.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that whether you’re walking down Broadway to run weekend errands, hiking through the Adirondacks, or logging miles in preparation for a marathon, sneakers are the backbone of a modern wardrobe. Designed to keep up with long days, busy schedules, and whatever the calendar throws your way, they’ve earned their place as true essentials—and our editors have strong opinions on which styles make the cut.

For some on the team, comfort and versatility matter most. For others, it’s about injecting color and personality into pared-back, off-duty looks. Sneakers that offer a sense of play—like Onitsuka Tiger’s Mexico 66 in silver or one of the ongoing Wales Bonner x Adidas designs—are among the favorites. After all, if the shoe doesn’t gel with the wearer’s personal style, it won’t stay in rotation for long. Our editors’ picks have earned their keep: They can go the distance.

I love these Kallmeyer Nike sneakers as a fancy weekend shoe and these brown Asics for my fall palette. For exercising, I have been running in Brooks Ghost sneakers for 20 years, and I’m not planning to stop anytime soon. I wear Alo Runners for other cardio.

When Phoebe Philo designed her take on an elevated Vans sneaker, I sourced the originals and have kept them in my sneaker rotation ever since. Paired with tailored wide-leg pants, they’re the perfect casual-cool shoes. Jamie Haller and Toteme are other favorites; I love minimalist sneakers from brands I regularly shop.

A Stan Smith is the definition of timeless style. Some might argue it’s no longer as relevant, since the Tokyo and Samba have overtaken it as Adidas’s bestselling styles, but I still reach for my Stan Smiths when I need a classic, chic, subtle sneaker for work. Forever engraved in my brain is the image of Phoebe Philo bowing at one of her Celine indicates in a gray sweater, gray pants, and Stan Smiths—chic.

Recent findings suggest that my favorite sneaker has to be the Adidas Taekwondo. The laceless design eliminates all unnecessary fuss, while the flat sole keeps the silhouette clean and streamlined. Lightweight and easy to pack, they have earned a permanent spot in my closet and carry-on!

I never felt that sneakers and real clothes looked great on me, so I’ve long been a fan of the understated, retro look that is so popular now. Slim in silhouette, they wear more like ballet flats than sneakers. My go-to white sneakers are a Marni pair I found on The RealReal ages ago. I was happy to see this latest iteration from the brand pop up at the end of last year. My other favorite pair is my original Loewe ballet runners; Vogue fashion editor Max Ortega inspired the purchase. They don’t produce the exact style anymore, but here they are in 2.0!

Industry observers note that I rarely feel moved by sneakers unless they’re of the running kind, but every so often I’ll reach for this all-white pair from Dries to wear on the weekend. I also have these Nike x Jacquemus Moon sneakers that, for lack of more weather-resistant options, have somehow become my rainy-day shoe of choice.

I’m really not the biggest sneaker wearer, but I’m a fan of Michael Rider’s Jazz sneaker for Celine. I know they’re somewhat controversial, but as someone who danced jazz in my youth, these shoes hold a lot of nostalgia for me. Otherwise, I love a sneaker that feels a bit more fancy, like the Nike x Jacquemus Moon satin trainers.

For the weekend, the Nike Air Max 90 Futura remains my go-to. The colorway I own (white, gray, and black) is sold out, but it’s still available in a variety of options.

I love an all-white sneaker for ease and versatility, and my go-to is the Tory Burch Howell Court sneaker. Its minimalist design takes the guesswork out of getting dressed, and it’s elevated enough for the office.

According to recent reports, I am not a major sneaker person, but I have developed an obsession with the ongoing Wales Bonner x Adidas sneaker collabs. They suit my style—slightly 1970s—while offering the comfort of a sneaker. Win-win!

It has been revealed that the evolution of my footwear needs to be studied, because I swore I was a heels girl, but then I found myself only wearing flats, and now I have a newfound interest in sneakers. Maybe it’s because I’m a runner and am always on the hunt for the best pair of running shoes, but I take my sneaker search seriously. Running shoes aside, the sneakers I wear for my long walks are equally important, and this pair of Nike Air Max Moto 2K sneakers has been a staple in my shoe rotation—especially as the weather gets colder. They’re pretty versatile, and I’ve even worn them to the office!

According to recent reports, my favorite sneaker has to be the Prada America’s Cup Original sneaker. Originally conceived in 1997 for the Luna Rossa sailing team, it refines the familiar classic with a rugged, functional design that stays true to its original proportions. I own this style in multiple colors, as well as vintage and reissued versions. It is the perfect sneaker to elevate a casual outfit and has become a symbol of the intersection of luxury and streetwear.

Sources indicate that I have a tough time with sneakers! Every time I try to make a fashion sneaker work, I end up not feeling like myself. Maybe one day I’ll find a more dressed-up sneaker I love, but for now my go-to is a more technical option: the Salomon XT-Whisper sneakers in all black. I wear them at the gym, for short hikes, or on the weekends while running errands around the city.

I’m both a longtime Converse fan and Vogue’s resident tennis nerd—well, our other tennis nerd—so you can imagine my delight when Palmes, the tennis-forward Copenhagen label run by my genius friend Nikolaj Hansson, collaborated with Converse on a killer version of the original court shoe, the Jack Purcell. If you can still find those, jump on them—they’re scarce. If you can’t—or if your tastes run a bit more uptown compared to the resolutely downtown feel of the Palmes collab—the more recent Converse First String Jack Purcells are essentially the most haute version of the Jacks that one could imagine. Both are the sturdiest, chunkiest, coziest sneakers I’ve found in years.

It has been revealed that I’m completely obsessed with my Adidas Japans (so obsessed that I have them in two colorways), and have gotten my entire family on board. They’re sleek, soft, and so comfortable—no break-in required. If you’re into the low-profile look but aren’t keen on a wacky sneakerina, this is the shoe for you.

It has been revealed that living in Brooklyn, I was skeptical about hopping onto the Salomon wave taking over the street style scene, but in the two years since I bought a pair, they’ve become my go-to sneakers—unseating my former true love, my Upcoming Balance 990v5s. They’re lightweight, comfortable enough to wear all day, and you don’t even have to tie the laces. Swoon!

The higher the platform, the more likely I am to make it mine. Of course, my first foray into Rick Owens footwear had to be one of the more dramatic offerings, not a standard-height sole. Initially testing them out on the ground at Vogue World: Milano, I found the shoe’s roomy toe box and comfortable leather insole carried me through the night on the cobblestone streets of Milano and all the way back to the United States—on the plane and in the airport.

Sources indicate that I wear Vans checkerboard slip-ons pretty much every day! They are the perfect sneaker; truly, they go with everything. They are so classic that they are neither trendy nor not cool. I’m from LA, and wearing them always makes me feel connected to Southern California. I love them!

Living in Latest York calls for a comfortable shoe, and personally I’m a huge fan of a good sneaker. I wear these Asics sneakers everywhere—to the gym, around town, and even to the office, depending on the look.

I am not a sneaker person, but my Latest Balance 574s have been in my wardrobe for years and are still my go-to travel shoes.

A sneaker, in my opinion, should keep a low profile. I’ve tried chunkier, sportier styles but found my footing with the Jacquemus The Tennis sneaker. The chocolate brown suede is impossible to resist.

In a recent development, few things excite me more than an unexpected fashion collaboration, and Hoka x Marni is a pairing I can wholeheartedly get behind. Where high performance meets high fashion, this duo strikes the perfect balance between function and flair. Hoka’s signature comfort meets Marni’s playful, offbeat design sensibility, transforming a performance sneaker into a bona fide fashion statement.

Back in Vogue’s earlier days, the idea that a sneaker could elevate any look would never have made it past the edit—yet here we are, celebrating the classic silhouette that can seamlessly carry you from desk to dinner. Recent runways inspired a desire for Vuitton’s Sneakerina!

Recent findings suggest that I am a huge sneakerhead. I have every Wales Bonner x Adidas collaboration sneaker because they’re the best shoes ever. They’re not only super comfortable, but they also come in great colorways and textiles. My favorite pair is a sequin-and-croc-leather style that I got two years ago. Tory Burch also makes a great pair of sneakers that feel comfy and look great. My favorite colorway has been the brown suede. The only downside is that I wear them so much, the flat soles are already wearing thin!

Industry observers note that the low-profile sneaker isn’t going anywhere, and I particularly love this sleek, Mary Jane–inspired silhouette from Zendaya’s On collab. I’m a longtime On fan for Barry’s workouts (Cloudpulse Pro to the end!) and was glad to add this put-together pair to my stomping-around-the-city rotation for when I’m not on the treadmill. They also fared pretty well on a recent trip I took to the Australian outback. Who notes you can’t traverse 500-million-year-old rock formations in your balletcore best?

While you might have spied Lili Curia’s ornamental, Victorian-style Isadora boots on the feet of all the pop stars this past summer, their sneaker version is the girl you need to know: all the same chic and sophisticated character, translated into a sportier shape. I love the contrasting black leather and brown suede upper, which makes it super versatile.

Industry observers note that it’s only recently come to my attention that I gravitate toward sneakers that look like little soccer cleats (pardon me, football boots!). For starters, nothing beats the arch support of an Onitsuka Tiger, even though they look anything but orthopedic. I completely understand why Uma Thurman sported these in Kill Bill.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that WNBA basketball player Cameron Brink and rower-turned-robotics founder Ben Felter were the rare college students who were able to find love at the height of Covid. Since they were athletes, the Stanford freshmen were in the tiny group allowed on campus during the fall of 2020. “The only people I socialized with were my basketball teammates—until the upperclassmen on my team had us fill out an ‘athlete mingle survey,’” Cameron claims.

She begrudgingly filled out the form, was matched with Ben, and later received an email with the subject, “attempting to mingle.” In the message, Ben wrote: “I wanted to chat you up but thought DMs were a bit creepy, so here’s my number.” Cameron—who goes by Cam—says she jumped up and down in her room, elated that he was gentlemanly enough to reach out with his number.

Industry observers note that “From there, we had three dates where Ben showed me his hometown of Palo Alto, and he asked me to be his girlfriend five days before we won a national championship,” says Cam. “He is my forever good luck charm.” She adds her friends and teammates Lexie and Lacie Hull were the ones who paired them together and is “forever grateful for their vision.”.

Recent findings suggest that their relationship grew as they graduated college and Cam had begun playing as the Los Angeles Sparks’ forward. On September 30, 2024, Cam was on a trip to Paris for fashion week, and Ben knew it was the perfect opportunity to propose. “I snuck over from California to surprise her with the ring,” he says. “She thought she was going to an important after-party, but really, it was just me waiting for her on the terrace of the Shangri-La Hotel overlooking the Eiffel Tower that was shining with pink lights that night.” At first, Cam was so stunned by the view that she didn’t realize there was no party. “I’ll never forget the expression of pure surprise on her face when it finally sank in that it was me standing in front of her,” remembers Ben. “I told her that it is my purpose to make her happy before getting on one knee and asking her to marry me. She fell to the ground crying and luckily noted ‘yes.’”.

In a recent development, the couple always knew they wanted to tie the knot at Stanford’s Memorial Church. “Walking past the ornate mosaics on my way to class was always the best part of my day,” notes Cam. At first, the bride was nervous that they would have to be on a waiting list for up to four years, but luckily, the university gives alumni a shorter waiting period. The couple set the date for November 14, 2026, with a reception at the Ritz-Carlton, Half Moon Bay, just 30 minutes away.

Industry observers note that cam says she took on the nickname “bridechilla” in her engagement period, attributing her details-focused planner Kristi Lee for making everything so seamless. “Other than working with the church’s clergy, daydreaming with my mom, and scrolling with Ben most nights on Pinterest for inspiration, we were lucky enough to have our family and wedding planner to carry most of the load,” she says. “I guess I always knew it would be beautiful because I have the best circle of humans imaginable that helped the vision come to life.”.

Another MVP on the wedding team? “My stylist Shiona Turini was our North Star when it came to what both Ben and I wore,” says Cam. “When she agreed to help me find my dream wedding dress, I never knew it would end with two custom looks from Danielle Frankel, the designer I have been bookmarking since my sophomore year of college.” Cam first tried on styles at Frankel’s Los Angeles salon and found two silhouettes she loved. Frankel herself helped collaborate on customizations. “We ended up perfectly mixing what I envisioned with Danielle’s additions and creating a gown that felt timeless yet extravagant,” the bride explains. For the ceremony, Cam would wear a silk wool deep-V column dress with crinkle organza godets that helped form a full, bubble skirt. Later at the reception, she would change into a column gown crafted with an exaggerated neckline and textural crinkle organza strips. Each gown was accessorized with Manolo Blahnik satin heels and desert diamond studs by Irena Jewels.

Sources indicate that frankel also helped dress the groom for his walk down the aisle with a custom single-breasted tuxedo jacket and bow tie. “The silk lapels were the same fabric as my dress, and it paired together so perfectly,” states Cam. The bow tie is now part of a fresh menswear offering by the designer. “Ben also wore the watch that I gifted him from our friend Eric Wind—a vintage Rolex Root Beer GMT-Master from the ’70s.”.

Sources indicate that A trip to Fresh York for fittings coincided with the city’s bridal fashion week, and Cam was invited to see Di Petsa’s first bridal collection. “I knew right away I had to wear the silk long dress with pearl details for my rehearsal dinner,” indicates the bride. “I adore pearls and wanted jewelry that played off of the pearl details of the back of the Di Petsa gown.” She eventually settled on jewelry from Mateo New York, and also had pearl details from Jennifer Behr added to her hair for the night. The bride also found another Di Petsa look with draped tulle and lace to wear at the after-party. “The discreet pearl at the belly button was so special,” Cam says. “We paired it with one of my favorite shoe designers—Amina Muaddi’s lace heels. But to be honest, I kicked off the shoes at the end of the night and ended up in a pair of New Balance sneakers!”.

To finish off every look with the right glam, Cam had her makeup artist Jocelyn Biga make a trip from Newly introduced York for the celebration. “The day wouldn’t have felt complete without her as she’s done my makeup for all of the biggest events in my life: the WNBA draft, our engagement, and now the wedding,” says the bride.

The wedding party was also outfitted for the major day. Amsale made custom dresses in deep blue for the bridesmaids, and groomsmen wore classic tuxedos. “For our entire group of children, Maison Ava created a bespoke wardrobe,” explains Cam. “The girls' looks had hand embroidery, hand-cut and hand-appliquéd floral motifs, crystals, beading, and 3D flowers, [while] the boys had custom velvet tuxedo jackets and wool trousers. It was so incredible to see all of the kids in their looks, and they also had tiny, custom New Balance sneakers at the end of the night!”.

Industry observers note that after a morning getting ready with their closest circles and taking portraits along the California coastline, the couple reunited at their alma mater to exchange vows at the Memorial Church. “The light was shining through the stained-glass windows so brightly all I could see was Cameron’s beautiful silhouette as she walked down the aisle with her parents, Greg and Michelle, and I tried to hold back tears,” remembers Ben. Cam admits she tripped right before walking down the aisle (and thankfully, her mom came to the rescue), but all her nerves washed away once Ben lifted her veil. “I felt overwhelmed by the support from our loved ones, and most of all I felt the deepest sense of gratitude and belonging looking into Ben’s eyes,” she claims. The bride’s godmother read scripture, the couple exchanged personal vows, and their pastor gave wishes for their future, including “a peaceful home filled with joy, laughter, and one day, the sound of little feet running around wearing number 22.”.

In a recent development, once the newlyweds paraded down the aisle and did the dip they practiced all week, they sped off to the Ritz-Carlton, Half Moon Bay in a 1957 Rolls-Royce. “I asked our driver for his best marriage advice since he’s been with his wife for 58 years,” recalls Ben. “He remarked, ‘It’s not that complicated. I just do what she says.’ Cameron elbowed me and got a kick out of that.” After portraits at sunset, the bride and groom joined their guests for cocktail hour on the grounds.

“The rest of the night was filled with so much joy, belly laughs, and dorky dance moves,” states Ben. The reception moved indoors to a space filled with florals and greenery curated with the help of Flowers by Edgar. Dinner kicked off with the couple’s first dance to “Until I Found You,” sung by their flower girl Ryan. The night was also peppered with speeches from the bride’s father and the groom’s brothers. As the dance floor lit up, guests could also head outdoors to indulge in a cigar lounge. “The energy in the ballroom was unmatched, erupting multiple times with cheers and toasts,” adds Ben. “We couldn’t be happier with how the best day of our lives concluded.”.

It has been revealed that now off on their honeymoon in Kyoto, the pair share they are in a bubble of newlywed bliss. Says Cam: “We couldn’t have dreamt of a better day and are feeling so incredibly blessed to have shared it with all of the people whom we love so dearly.”.

Dirty Spaghetti

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dirty rice has met its noodle match with our Louisiana-style dirty spaghetti.
  • Let the good times roll with this Louisiana-inspired dirty spaghetti dish!
  • The key it its flavor is Cajun seasoning, a blend cayenne pepper, garlic powder, black pepper, paprika and thyme.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recipe by Susan Bronson, Rhinelander, Wisconsin.

Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Dirty rice has met its noodle match with our Louisiana-style dirty spaghetti.

Let the good times roll with this Louisiana-inspired dirty spaghetti dish! It’s a riff on Cajun-Creole dirty rice that transforms the original into an easy one-pot pasta.

The key it its flavor is Cajun seasoning, a blend cayenne pepper, garlic powder, black pepper, paprika and thyme. And herein lies an important cooking tip: When using store-bought seasoning blends like this one, give them a little taste first before adding anything to the pot. Different brands rely on different ratios of ingredients, and a tablespoon of one product could be much milder (or pack way more heat!) than a tablespoon of another. Your personal preferences matter, too. So whether you are sensitive to spice or like to pack on the heat, make sure you’re adding the proper amount of spice for your taste.

It has been revealed that dirty spaghetti is a riff on dirty rice, a classic Cajun-Creole side dish. Traditional dirty rice is made with chopped organ meats such as chicken livers or gizzards, which, along with the herbs and seasonings, color the white rice and earn it its “dirty” moniker. This dish, however, has a meaty base that’s made with ground beef and diced andouille sausage. Like the original, it also features the “holy trinity” of Cajun and Creole cooking: chopped onion, bell pepper and celery. A healthy dose of Cajun seasoning ensures each bite is packed with bold flavor.

Sources indicate that heat the oil in a large Dutch oven or large high-sided skillet over medium-high heat. Add the ground beef and cook it until it’s browned, four to six minutes, using a wooden spoon or spatula to break it into small crumbles.

Editor’s Tip: If you use a skillet, make sure it has a lid.

In a recent development, add the chopped andouille sausage, onion, celery, red pepper and green pepper. Cook them until the vegetables are soft, about three to four minutes. Add the garlic and cook it until it’s fragrant, 30 to 60 seconds. Stir in the tomato paste and Cajun seasoning, and cook for one to two more minutes. Add 3 cups of broth and bring the mixture to a simmer.

Add the broken spaghetti to the pot, ensuring that the noodles are submerged in the liquid and separated as much as possible. Add more liquid if needed. Bring the mixture to a boil, then reduce the heat to medium-low. Cover the pot and simmer the pasta for six minutes.

Remove the lid and continue simmering until the spaghetti is al dente, stirring every two to three minutes. Add more broth as needed. Remove the pot from the heat, and season the pasta to taste with salt and pepper.

Leftover dirty spaghetti can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to four days.

Industry observers note that the best way to reheat a pasta dish like this one is either in the oven or on the stovetop. To reheat leftover dirty spaghetti in the oven, transfer it to an oven-safe baking dish, cover it tightly with foil, and cook it in an oven preheated to 350 degrees for about 20 minutes or until it’s heated through. To reheat it on the stovetop, heat a saucepan over medium heat and add a drizzle of olive oil. Add the leftover pasta and sauce and saute them for about two to three minutes or until they’re hot.

Sources indicate that yes, you can freeze dirty spaghetti. After allowing it to cool completely, transfer leftovers to a freezer-safe container and store them in the freezer for up to three months. Allow the dirty spaghetti to thaw overnight in the fridge before reheating it.

The best pan for making this one-pot pasta dish is a Dutch oven or a large, high-walled skillet or pot with a tight-fitting lid.

According to recent reports, first, be sure to give your Cajun seasoning a little taste first because seasoning blends like this one can vary widely in spiciness. Depending on how spicy your Cajun seasoning is, add more or less to taste. You could also make a homemade Cajun seasoning blend and customize the amount of cayenne pepper and chili powder to your personal taste. The andouille sausage also adds quite a bit of spice; for less heat, skip it entirely, or swap in sweet Italian sausage, breakfast sausage, chicken sausage or a milder smoked sausage like kielbasa.

You’ll definitely want to pair this dirty spaghetti with crusty French bread, garlic bread or cornbread to sop up any extra sauce. Southern-inspired side dishes to consider include southern green beans, collard greens or black-eyed pea tomato salad. Or, complement the pasta dish’s spicy flavor with a fresh and crisp green salad.

Breaking: Pear Salad With Honey-Roasted Seeds

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake.
  • Industry observers note that pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over.
  • For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Industry observers note that pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Sources indicate that preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

In a recent development, arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

When it comes to Black Friday, your local GQ Recommends editors operate from a fairly unique vantage point: we shop for a living, after all, so the chaotic nature of the weekend hardly phases us.

What they didn't tell us when we started here, though, is how easy it is to mistake professional life for play, shopping away the wee hours of the morning even when we're off the clock. And when you eyeball literally hundreds of items a day, you’re bound to encounter a few that you actually like—so much so that you’re willing to put your hard-earned salary towards 'em. That risk gets doubly dangerous around this time of year, when mentioned Black Friday deals start popping up like moles in the digital tundra.

So hear’s a rare peek into the truly sick minds—and truly sickening carts—of us GQ editors. From plush corduroy shirts to red-carpet-ready shades, these are the pre-Black Friday deals weighing heaviest on our fragile hearts and long-suffering bank accounts. Scroll on if you dare.

Japanese denim specialists: good for more than jeans!

I was perusing the digital aisles of the brands site the other day, as a commerce editor is one to do, and was struck by this studded belt. Of course, I had to pull the trigger, it doesn’t hurt that it also happens to be on sale right now for 30% off.

This is the type of jacket I will buy and it will eventually become my entire personality. Someone is going to be talking about geopolitics and the AI bubble and all I’ll be thinking about is shoehorning in the fact that this is a Kaptain Sunshine suede trucker that I got on sale for Black Friday.

I think Mase’s 2004, seminal hit, “Welcome Back,” sums it up best. And the usage of seminal here is purely meant to reflect my own enthusiasm, so bare with me. But really, welcome back baby.

If you know me, you know that I’m being so for real right now about this silly hat. This one is like an earworm that I can’t get out of my head and the only remedy is to just buy the damn thing.

Industry observers note that gap’s recent line of handbags went semi-viral thanks to the affordable prices and designs which borrow obvious inspiration from a certain French luxury house. While the B*rkin denim dupe has sold out, this simpler version also bears a striking resemblance to what some might call a Garden Party bag from the same house, albeit for less than 1% of the price.

It has been revealed that had I known these were gonna go on sale, I would’ve waited another week to pull the trigger. Alas, I might have to cop these in another colorway because I ran a PB straight out of the box.

I’ve blogged about this probably every year since working at GQ and I might just have to do it because I’m tired of writing about the same product and I’m tired of not having juicy delicious poulet roti every day.

It has been revealed that this week I swore off any more corduroy on this very website but there’s also a 98% chance (give or take) that I disregard all of that and buy this all-time, elbow-patched shirt. Life is short or whatever, I want more corduroy.

In a recent development, I have once again put a hole in my Boston’s and can no longer wear them in good conscience. What I can do in good conscience, however, is save myself $40 on their replacements.

I went five years without losing a pair of sunglasses and then lost two this past week, so the only reasonable thing to do—by my calculations, at least—is to buy another nice pair and roll them dice.

If all my picks were practical, I’d be doing wishlists wrong.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The chaos doesn’t seem to be getting to the cookbook author, chef, and aspiring empire-builder.
  • What Roman has built has grown beyond recipes and bean propaganda.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With only weeks before opening, Alison Roman’s Brooklyn brick-and-mortar is still unfinished. “Today they’re doing up the walls and putting in the floors,” Roman claims. In short, it does not yet look like a dreamy European-inspired grocer. There are still a mountain of calls to be made, meetings to be had, speed bumps to overcome.

The chaos doesn’t seem to be getting to the cookbook author, chef, and aspiring empire-builder. “It’s been so fun,” Roman, a Bon Appétit alum, states of the process. Perhaps that shouldn’t be a surprise; this breezy effortlessness is at the bedrock of the Alison Roman universe. You know the kind of nonchalant magic I’m talking about: chilling wine bottles in a bathtub of ice, buckets of take-out fried chicken at dinner parties—I mean, this woman was one of the foremost proponents of brothy beans.

What Roman has built has grown beyond recipes and bean propaganda. The ever-creeping edges of her lifestyle brand now encompass a jarred tomato sauce brand, once cheekily titled A Very Good Sauce, now renamed Roman’s. There’s also the upcoming podcast, Having People Over, where she hosts guests for a meal and a yap, plus the speaking tour she’s calling “Food, Life and Other Strong Opinions.” There are the shoes (sleek mules and chunky clogs) she made in collaboration with New York–based footwear brand Margaux. And now First Bloom, the grocery store–slash–wine bar–slash–café that—as of mid-November—is on track to open in December.

Industry observers note that the Brooklyn shop is an extension of the original Catskill’s location of the same name. Roman says this fresh outpost is “a totally different proposition of what we are offering people.” There’s more budget to work with, there’s more staff, there’s more space, and there’s more food.

In a recent development, whereas the upstate location’s function is closer to utility—meat and produce from local farms are a major feature—in Brooklyn (where specialty grocers abound) Roman is focusing on something more akin to world-building. But do not call First Bloom a shoppy shop, those whimsically designed boutiques that seem to pop up everywhere selling the same $45 squiggly candlesticks and squeeze-bottle olive oils everyone seems to have. “I think ‘shoppy shop’ is derogatory,” Roman notes. “In a world where you can buy anything from anywhere, sometimes it’s nice to be told what to do.”.

In a recent development, at Brooklyn’s First Bloom, the shelves will be stocked with products that Roman herself deems “hyper-defensible.” There’s a reason they’re stocked, and a reason for how they’re priced. They’re best in class or a personal favorite of Roman’s. “Perspective and curation is a really special thing to be able to convey,” she notes.

The vision for First Bloom is set, but with the opening just a month out, Roman doesn’t have all the details nailed down. “We are going to have a rotisserie chicken,” she notes. “I don’t know how much it’s going to cost yet,” she follows up promptly, before I can ask. There will also be a couple salads and a couple sandwiches on offer—plus another secret off-menu sandwich for the neighborhood regulars and the real Roman-heads who know to ask for it. “I’m very if-you-know-you know,’” she says. But Brooklyn’s First Bloom isn’t just for popping into—you’ll be able to lounge with a glass of wine or relax with a snack and a coffee.

Alison Roman’s world is organic, craft-centered, and easy but considered. To step into it is an enticing foil to the AI-fueled tasteslop tilt-a-whirl on which we find ourselves. It’s a vision of a slow, steady, wabi-sabi life that many of us only aspire to. A life where one can even somehow enjoy, say, a monthslong commercial renovation project in one of America’s most competitive real estate markets. That’s the draw of First Bloom. The hard-to-find tinned fish, yes, but also the ease of living in Alison’s world if only for an hour.

And if not, well, it seems like there’ll be a pretty good rotisserie chicken, at least.

#112496. “Do You Like It? Would You Wear It? Would You Buy It?”—An Oral History of Marc by Marc Jacobs

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (4058 w)
📖 Baca
