“Do You Like It? Would You Wear It? Would You Buy It?”—An Oral History of Marc by Marc Jacobs

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in the 2000s, Marc Jacobs was the high-low king of fashion.
  • Industry observers note that behind Marc by Marc was a small team encouraged to follow its instincts, with creative direction by legendary stylist and photographer Venetia Scott, who had been consulting on the main line since 1997.
  • Industry observers note that and, oh, the stores.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in the 2000s, Marc Jacobs was the high-low king of fashion. A decade after he propelled grunge onto the runway with his landmark collection for Perry Ellis, he was the first creative director at Louis Vuitton, and LVMH owned a majority share of his business. Meanwhile, he was selling $2 condoms in matchbooks alongside wares in every category: rarefied lace-trimmed cocktail dresses for the well-heeled, shrunken denim military jackets for downtown girls, and of course, those ubiquitously irreverent tchotchkes on Bleecker Street for everyone in between. Ineffable cool across all price points was the name of the game, especially with the launch of Marc by Marc Jacobs in 2001, which loomed large over the booming contemporary market of the era. It was so Kirsten Dunst. It was so Alexa Chung. And at the same time it was so me circa my first trip to NYC with a five-dollar lipstick pen and not much else in a branded shopping bag.

Industry observers note that behind Marc by Marc was a small team encouraged to follow its instincts, with creative direction by legendary stylist and photographer Venetia Scott, who had been consulting on the main line since 1997. Together, they trawled vintage shops and film costume warehouses for inspiration. But, perhaps most of all, there was Robert Duffy, the shrewd fashion executive who was Jacobs’ co-founder and longtime consigliere, tasked with turning the designer’s whimsical runway impulses into dollars and cents. They were the Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé of a new generation, and together they built a company that was both creative and commercially viable. Introducing Marc by Marc Jacobs was a perfect example of their dualities coming together to produce harmonious results.

Industry observers note that and, oh, the stores. Jacobs’s shops helped transform a once sleepy stretch of the West Village into a destination, with six outposts within walking distance of each other. Among them was the Marc by Marc Jacobs accessories store, the pièce de résistance for tourists and broke fashion kids alike. Whether it was your first trip to New York or your tenth, you lined up on Bleecker. Tote bags came stamped with the most iconic run-on sentence in fashion history: Jacobs by Marc Jacobs for Marc by Marc Jacobs in Collaboration with Marc Jacobs for Marc by Marc Jacobs. With a simple tongue-twister, Jacobs let us all in on the joke.

Marc by Marc Jacobs was folded into Marc Jacobs in 2015, but it lives on as a moment of accessible cool that can’t be replicated. For those who worked on it, its magic was in the freedom they were given to create. Twenty-five years after it was first rolled out, we spoke with members of its creative team about the vintage hunts, the last-minute fittings, and how they were able to recreate the downtown cool around them for the runway.

Sources indicate that in a serendipitous turn of events, Vogue learned that there are looks underway by to revive the Marc by Marc Jacobs label, sometime next year. While details are currently under wraps, this is the place for updates on the beloved brand that had an outsize imprint on fashion in the early aughts.

Lauren (the Marc by Marc fit model), Frederic Tremblay, and designer Susanne Deeken.

Backstage at the London show held at Claridge’s.

Venetia Scott began working with Marc Jacobs on the main collection in 1997. By the time Marc by Marc was taking shape, she had become a central creative collaborator and operated as the creative director on a day-to-day basis with the team.

Recent findings suggest that venetia Scott, Creative Director (2001-2015)Joe McKenna had been [styling] the Marc Jacobs runway. He suggested that I would be good to take it over, and Nian [Fish] from KCD also thought so. I had just had my daughter about three weeks before, and had gone down to Cornwall. And then my agent rang and stated, “Will you go and meet Marc Jacobs and Robert Duffy?” They ended up coming to London, and then that was it. I started that September. When I was assembling my team, I brought Alister Mackie to style men’s. Frederic Tremblay and Aude Tabet were already on the team. Fred was focused on the army aesthetic and denim. Susanne Deeken came in to do summer dresses. Irene Chung did the shoes.

We needed accessories for the show. I knew Katie Hillier from London, and she had been doing necklaces and stuff for Luella’s reveals. So I got her to come out to make stuff, strings and beads. Eventually we’d put a small run in the Marc by Marc shop, and then later, it grew into bags.

Sources indicate that alister Mackie, Menswear Consultant (2003-2014)I started on the Marc Jacobs main line around 2001, when they showed men and women together. In spring 2003, we started putting men into the Marc by Marc show. Venetia would set the narrative. At the first meeting, she would have spoken to Marc, and this story of who these kids were would be laid out by Venetia. We would then have to go off and find a boy that was relevant to that. This was really driven by character, which made it unusual, and it made it a lot of fun.

Sources indicate that venetia ScottThere was not really a strategy behind a lot of it. It sort of evolved as it went along. [Co-founder] Robert Duffy was very much like, “Let Marc do what he needs to do, and he will do it.” We never hit our deadlines. I remember Marc saying, “It’s great, we do what we want to do, and it seems like people like it.” I think we were lucky to be able to work in that vacuum without a lot of people dictating what the needs were of the line.

Recent findings suggest that frederic Tremblay, Senior Design Director (1999-2008)LVMH was seeing the contemporary market brewing. Our price point was a fraction of the main collection, but we took the essence of what Marc was. There was this big opportunity for department stores, who were also telling us, “We’ll give you tons of square footage because this is what we’re seeing as the next thing, but there’s nobody there.” Co-op was happening at Barneys, so we were one of the first big brands.

Backstage at the spring 2006 Marc by Marc Jacobs show.

Sources indicate that venetia ScottMarc was the author of the collection, and so we would have conversations, decide where we were going with it, and then I would work doing the research on fabrics or prints. And then I would go to Paris or to New York, and take him the research that I had done. Marc by Marc was a little group of us, and it was much more like a collaboration.

Sources indicate that camille Bidault Waddington, stylist (2000-2014)Venetia was styling the Marc Jacobs show and was working on the Marc by Marc collection through the season. I was coming for the last two weeks to style the show with her and the team. I was doing looks, but she had the final word. Sometimes it was a fight, but a gentle one. Marc was obviously coming to see us, also to have a breather in the middle of the sophisticated [main collection] prep. We were the kids.

Frederic TremblayMarc would review the collection ahead of the show and suggest pieces we were missing. It was always a great little thing that maybe when we were in the moment, we weren’t necessarily thinking about it, but he would come out and be like, "You know, you need this now." And we were looking at it, we were like, “Yep!”.

Senior design director Frederic Tremblay and Venetia Scott trying on clothes during a research trip in London.

According to recent reports, venetia ScottWe’d go to L.A. for the Rose Bowl Flea and the costume houses, or we’d go to Paris, Antwerp… We’d choose a different place every season. Our thing was always, as a group, “Do you like it? Would you wear it? Would you buy it?”.

In a recent development, camille Bidault-WaddingtonAt the beginning, we were customizing stuff to accessorize the looks, and invented crazy bits and bobs with Katie Hillier, or used things from markets and punk shops. It was very, very free.

Recent findings suggest that frederic TremblayWe amassed these amazing vintage pieces, and then we had a model coming in to try on pretty much everything. We started doing a bit of a look with the vintage, and that was our starting point. Those amazing costume rental places are truly magical. You’ve got to see Home Depot-size warehouses where you have to go on those industrial ladders, and there’s three, four rows of clothes, rows and rows. I think we just let our gut tell us where to go in the aisles.

Aude Tabet, Design Director and Director of Product Design, Little Marc Jacobs and Marc by Marc Jacobs Swimwear (1999-2015)We reworked prints, color, and artwork based on the vintage pieces we’d found, either internally or using a print studio. I still go by the Marc by Marc color palette we developed. It’s ingrained.

Backstage at the fall 2005 Marc by Marc Jacobs fashion show.

Industry observers note that venetia ScottIn the beginning, it wasn’t an idea to do a cheaper line. It was, let’s make some things that we all want. Marc’s always liked that high and low mishmash of things. Marc and Sofia Coppola were good friends, and other people around him would do this good mix of wearing the bouclé jacket with a silk shirt, with a pair of jeans, with a pair of flats. So that was natural.

According to recent reports, what was great was building this gang of cool girls. One might be in a jumpsuit, one might be in jeans and a T-shirt, one girl’s in a summer dress, but they all look like the same gang.

Industry observers note that camille Bidault-WaddingtonThe point was to represent what cool girls would wear. Models at the time had supercool style, and we were inspired by them, from Kirsten Owen to Angela Lindvall and Tasha Tilberg. They were super-stylish, and we wanted to capture the Upcoming York streets too—the musicians and the It girls.

Recent findings suggest that alister MackieSometimes it’s quite hard to fit the men into a women’s story, but it was a fun challenge to make it believable that these girls and boys were together. Fall 2007 (above) was these sorts of winter college kids who were also really grungy. It was very much that character that we kept going back to.

In a recent development, camille Bidault-WaddingtonSince I’m French, sometimes I thought we were a bit much, but I was then going downstairs with Alister Mackie, who was styling the boys, and actually noticed people in Newly introduced York were pretty daring. So that was the kick to go back up and add a hat here or a triple sock there.

Alister Mackie[Marc Jacobs HQ on] Spring Street was like the kingdom, and everyone was always there. There was a whole floor of ladies sewing, like a factory, so loud and intense. The whole thing was vibrating. Military coats were getting made up to the last minute, all this food arriving, and all these shoes in the corridors.

Irene Chung, who did the shoes, would fly from Italy with batches. Then she’d fly back and get more because Marc wanted to see all the options, and everything had to be just so perfect. It was this very theatrical experience to be part of.

Sources indicate that aude TabetOur first show was for spring 2001, but our first fall show (above) was my favorite: Dark denim, the coolest girls, slightly English styling, and very Bohemian. It felt almost like the American version of Katharine Hamnett [the English designer known for her mix of tailoring and a vintage-inspired look that was revolutionary at the time].

Recent findings suggest that camille Bidault-WaddingtonThe music was very experimental, indie, and daring. Frédéric Sanchez was coming up with upcoming bands or weird choirs or film soundtracks. And we were blasting them. Some journalists got annoyed, but it was very fun.

For fall 2007, the brand presented its collection at London Fashion Week. Here, behind-the-scenes shots from the show, held at Claridge’s Hotel.

Another backstage shot from the Marc by Marc Jacobs fall 2007 collection.

Marc by Marc Jacobs’ legacy lives on in some of its most ubiquitous products, like the Moonboots and the Souris mouse flats, first launched in 2002 and soon a cult favorite that would live on for decades and have recently found a newly introduced life with a new wave of whimsy enthusiasts.

Hillary Duff seen wearing the Marc by Marc Jacobs signature mouse slipper in 2008.

Industry observers note that venetia ScottThe original mouse shoe is a pointy one, which was done for the Marc Jacobs collection around 1998 with a [bow] that potentially looked like whiskers. And so Marc called it the mouse shoe. The more literal mousey thing with whiskers is what it later became.

Tote bags emblazoned with “Jacobs by Marc Jacobs for Marc by Marc Jacobs in Collaboration with Marc Jacobs for Marc by Marc Jacobs” became another signifier of Jacobs’s tongue-in-cheek approach to the brand.

Frederic TremblayThat was Marc realizing the repetition of his name and the number of lines was getting a little silly. It was just something, kind of, funny, you know? Marc has that ironic thing. He just came up with that, him and Robert.

Amid the designer denim boom of the 2000s bolstered by the likes of Diesel, True Religion, and 7 For All Mankind, Marc by Marc denim launched alongside the first collection for spring 2001. The following February, Vogue reported that its creased jeans were flying off retailers’ shelves.

Industry observers note that aude TabetWe did a creased pair of jeans for our denim launch. The jeans were creased as if they had been folded always on the side, like this forever. That was what we called our “San Francisco SF” wash. It was a mid-pale blue with a gray cast, developed in L.A. And we did all those drummer boy jackets with it.

The main collection and Marc by Marc shared a photographic and visual language, shaped by photographer Juergen Teller and Scott, and later Mackie.

Recent findings suggest that venetia ScottRight at the beginning, when I worked on Marc Jacobs, Juergen and I were together. Juergen would come over and stay in Newly introduced York. The conversation came up that there wasn’t any budget, but “maybe when you go back to London, you could photograph Kim Gordon?” And “Venetia, you could take a dress, and you could go to the Shepherd’s Bush Empire, where she’s performing, and she’ll put the dress on,” and “Juergen, you take some pictures of her up on stage or backstage in the dress.” It was just a conversation that didn’t ever really go through lots of tiers of people to be able to get any permission. We just did it.

Sources indicate that early on, there wasn’t any money for those ads. It was just something that we wanted to do. And then it carried on like that, really, as a conversation of who it could be, who’d be a good person this time. Sometimes Juergen would come up with an idea [or see a newly introduced actress], like, “Who is she? Oh, I think the girl who’s just been in that film.” And it would be Samantha Morton. Or Dakota Fanning, who I’d just seen in a film when she was tiny, and thought she was the most amazing thing. “Maybe we could shoot her?” We’d just say, “Yes, let’s do that.”.

It has been revealed that often Juergen would go off and do the Marc Jacobs campaigns on his own. And then Marc by Marc, we usually used who we thought had been the best girls in the show, or who seemed the most right for it. It’d be maybe three or four of those girls, and they’d often do the shoots. It was more models that had been used on the runway.

Sources indicate that alister MackieSometimes I went with Juergen on trips, and they were phenomenal. We were going to Milan, to Venice, to upstate New York, and we went on these very, very lo-fi trips with him and the models.

In 2010, the New York Times called Jacobs’ West Village retail footprint a monopoly. In other cities, from L.A. to Lisbon, the stores felt like anchors of cool, devoted to a high-low mix that epitomized fashion at the time. Under Duffy’s leadership, Jacobs’s world opened up to the masses via the accessible “junk” operation: an ever-changing assortment of novelties for people who couldn’t afford the clothes.

Industry observers note that aude TabetI moved to the West Village in ’92. The Mercer Street store was the nucleus—this crazy, beautiful, minimal location in that former garage. You would just want to be there, sit in a corner, and people-watch. Before Marc was there, Bleecker was very sleepy. There were a couple of antique stores. Then Marc went there and ended up opening a few stores, and that changed all of Bleecker. Every place where Marc went and opened up retail, everyone followed.

In a recent development, frederic TremblayA lot of the ideas for the trinkets came from Fiorucci [the popular 1970s brand and store known for carrying an eclectic mix of high-end clothes alongside novelty trinkets and small gifts and where Jacobs worked as a teenager]. Marc would often talk to us about that reference. He would go to the Fiorucci store by Bloomingdale’s, and they had a lot of that stuff too—products that were satellite to the main brand of clothing or accessories, those little things that anyone could afford.

Industry observers note that alister MackieWhat we made was really for the show, but Robert and the merchandising team made all these products, which were really fun and successful, and then they put them together in the stores. Somehow, one elevated the other, and one made the other more fun. The people who worked in the shop represented Marc as much as we did, or the people in the office and the models. Everybody had the same kind of positivity and welcoming spirit.

Camille Bidault-WaddingtonIt was very, very cool to sit on the bench at Balthazar and see so many people walking by, wearing Marc by Marc. It was very cool because it was a collection on its own, not a variation of the other line. It was deep, not just a commercial version.

In a recent development, venetia ScottYou’ve got your little haul of a tote, and this and that and the other, all for under 50 bucks. It was a fun idea, a bit like Biba in the ’70s, where you could get a T-shirt for very little money or buy a poster to stick up in your room at school. But I think the cheap products that were Marc by Marc, in the long run, probably didn’t do us any good. What we were doing was something very different. We were doing boots that you could sit on the pavement, kick about, and have fun in. They’d get better and better. It wasn’t meant to be a cheap version of something expensive. It was meant to be what it was.

Recent findings suggest that alister MackieMarc threw these huge parties, and it was very early on for that kind of branding, having these great parties and everybody wanting to be part of it. Chloë Sevigny and all these fabulous women were around—all that was part of the magic of the brand.

Marc’s parties were the talk of the town, and he took it to the extreme. In Venice, he was a pigeon. And then the Arabian Nights, he was camel toe. He took it to this other kind of level of surrealism.

Industry observers note that those parties were also part of the myth of the brand, because everybody was going. It wasn’t exclusive. Everyone in town wanted to be there. That was part of the expansionist generosity of Robert and Marc at that time.

Heidi Bivens, Justin Theroux and Marc Jacobs’ then-boyfriend Lorenzo Martone front row at the spring 2010 Marc by Marc Jacobs show.

Rachel Zoe, Lorenzo Martone and Brad Goreski at the spring 2009 Marc by Marc Jacobs show.

Marc by Marc Jacobs, spring 2009.

By 2013, the contemporary market that Marc by Marc Jacobs had helped define was crowded with competitors, including Alexander Wang, 3.1 Phillip Lim, and Rag & Bone. That year, as Katie Hillier and Luella Bartley were appointed to lead its next chapter, Duffy acknowledged that the line had lost some momentum. “The competition has become too great,” he told WWD. “We rested on our laurels, and it hurt us.”.

According to recent reports, venetia ScottWhen it got really big, then we were asked to do things like, “Oh, somebody’s got, you know, this brand’s got some [legging trousers called] treggings.” And we’d all think, “Well, we don’t want to do treggings.” And I think that was, for me, that was sort of maybe where it lost its way a little bit, and the identity was not as clear as it had been in the beginning. Before, when we were just doing what we wanted to do, that seemed to sell well.

Sources indicate that frederic TremblayAround 2006, 2007, Topshop became a thing. Zara and H&M started to get more momentum. They took a lot of our market. We started feeling like, okay, we really need to offer something different. We weren’t the only ones in contemporary to feel that. We couldn’t really compete.

Venetia ScottOther brands could do that army jacket in a second, and have it out in the shop at the same time that we would. So I think all that contributed to it probably not having the sales that it had once had. I think it was time for a refresh. Katie and Luella came in, and I continued with them to consult on the process. They set up a London studio, and we all worked together on the show and the styling.

In May 2013, Katie Hillier was named creative director of Marc by Marc Jacobs, with Luella Bartley joining as women’s ready-to-wear design director. Their debut for fall 2014 brought an edgier, London-inspired vision to the brand, but it didn’t last long. In March 2015, it was unveiled that Marc by Marc Jacobs would be absorbed into Marc Jacobs, bringing contemporary and luxury products together under one name. “We believed that fashion could exist at lots of different prices,” Jacobs told WWD at the time.

Beginning with spring 2016, the consolidated label incorporated lower-priced pieces alongside its runway collection, a strategy Jacobs later acknowledged “didn’t really work.” Given the extensive retail footprint of the Marc by Marc Jacobs line, rather than the main line, much of its exposure was lost to customers, leaving space for other brands to replace it.

Sources indicate that venetia ScottThe [pieces] have a character that you don’t find if you go to a high street store. They still are around, what is it, 20 years later? They still look great.

Industry observers note that they had all these extra details that you discovered as you wore them. You’d have a piping on the inside of the cuff, which was some little candy cane stripe. They were quite honest clothes, I think.

Aude TabetI wear those pieces from time to time, and I love the emotional connection. I love how disruptive it was. In a good way, positive, disruptive.

Industry observers note that frederic TremblayI’ve been doing mentoring at SCAD, and there are students who will have picked something in a vintage store that’s Marc by Marc. They kind of know what it is, but they don’t really have the whole story about it. They don’t know about the real impact it had when it was made. So it’s always fun when one of the students wears one of those pieces, and I can tell them a little bit about it.

Julia Child’s Controversial Thanksgiving Turkey Method Isn’t As Crazy As It Sounds

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Julia Child's solution to a common turkey dilemma was equal parts culinary brilliance and holiday theater.
  • According to recent reports, julia Child had a marvelous way of making even the most intimidating cooking techniques seem entirely within reach.
  • According to recent reports, take Thanksgiving turkey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Julia Child's solution to a common turkey dilemma was equal parts culinary brilliance and holiday theater.

According to recent reports, julia Child had a marvelous way of making even the most intimidating cooking techniques seem entirely within reach. She was a brilliant cook, a gifted teacher, and a woman who understood that a little butter could solve an astonishing number of problems. But perhaps her greatest talent was her willingness to question the rules, even when those rules involved one of America’s most beloved holiday traditions.

According to recent reports, take Thanksgiving turkey. Most of us have spent our lives roasting the bird whole, partly because that’s how it’s always been done and partly because a beautifully browned turkey makes such a magnificent centerpiece on a holiday table. Julia, however, recognized a rather inconvenient flaw in this arrangement: A whole turkey is not well designed for even cooking.

According to recent reports, her solution was ingenious. She took the turkey apart, cooked its individual pieces, and then put the whole thing back together again for presentation. It was a triumph of culinary common sense, with just enough theatrical flair to make the whole thing unmistakably Julia.

Sources indicate that julia called her creation the “re-assembled roast turkey,” a technique she shared in her cookbook, The Way to Cook. Rather than wrestling an entire bird into the oven and hoping for the best, she removed the backbone, separated the leg and thigh portions, and roasted the breast on a bed of stuffing while the dark meat cooked in another pan.

In a recent development, once everything was properly cooked, she arranged the pieces together on a serving platter, restoring the turkey to something resembling its original form. In her recipe, Julia cheerfully suggested that nobody would ever know the difference.

It has been revealed that in a 2012 NPR Thanksgiving segment, Christopher Kimball, who had cooked alongside Julia, demonstrated the method with host Renee Montagne. The two had a wonderful time discussing the reconstructed bird, which they affectionately dubbed “Frankenturkey.” It wasn’t quite traditional, but that was rather the point. Julia had found a way to preserve the spectacle of a whole roasted turkey without actually having to cook one.

Industry observers note that the trouble with roasting a whole turkey is that its various parts have very different needs. The breast is lean and can become dry and stringy when overcooked, while the legs and thighs contain more fat and connective tissue, and generally benefit from cooking to a higher internal temperature. Getting everything just right at the same time is a challenge, even for experienced cooks.

Breaking down the turkey solves much of that problem. With the pieces separated, you can monitor their temperatures individually and remove them as they finish cooking. The dark meat has time to become tender without drying out the breast, and heat circulates more efficiently around the smaller pieces, reducing the overall roasting time.

It’s a method we’ve championed at Taste of Home. Our guide to cooking a deconstructed turkey outlines the process of breaking down the bird, roasting the individual pieces and getting beautifully crisp skin. You can even ask your butcher to handle the disassembly if you’d rather not begin Thanksgiving morning with a pair of poultry shears.

And there’s another advantage Julia certainly appreciated: With the backbone removed, you’ve already got a head start on making a rich turkey stock for the gravy.

Sources indicate that of course, there’s no requirement that you follow Julia all the way through to the reconstruction. You can simply arrange the carved meat on a serving platter and bring it to the table. But I do love that Julia went to the trouble of putting her turkey back together. She understood that Thanksgiving dinner is as much about tradition and presentation as it is about good cooking, and she found a wonderfully clever way to have both.

The result was better-tasting turkey that still got its moment of glory on the table. And if anyone could make taking a turkey apart and putting it back together seem like the most sensible thing in the world, it was Julia Child.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

Recent findings suggest that bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

Recent findings suggest that do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

It has been revealed that making a truly excellent bowl of mac and cheese shouldn't take an entire afternoon. Here's the one ingredient I rely on to get the creamiest cheese sauce every time.

I’ve made enough macaroni and cheese over the years to have developed some fairly strong opinions about it. Having two kids has given me plenty of opportunities to experiment, from throwing together the familiar blue box to baking versions that require several kinds of cheese and a considerable amount of attention. I appreciate a proper cheese sauce as much as anyone, but there are evenings when dirtying another saucepan to make a roux and standing over the stove with a whisk feels like an unreasonable amount of ceremony for a bowl of macaroni.

It has been revealed that which is why I’m particularly fond of a method that requires just three ingredients: pasta, grated cheese and evaporated milk. It produces an exceptionally creamy mac and cheese without butter, flour or any of the usual fuss, and it’s so simple that even boxed mac begins to look complicated.

Evaporated milk is regular milk that’s been heated until about 60% of its water is gone. The result is thicker and more concentrated than ordinary milk, with a richness that makes it especially useful for cheese sauces.

It has been revealed that more importantly, those concentrated milk proteins help the cheese melt into a smooth, cohesive sauce. Ordinarily, adding cheese directly to hot liquid can be a temperamental business. The fat may separate, the proteins can tighten up, and the sauce can become grainy instead of silky. Evaporated milk helps keep everything together, doing much of the work that a traditional flour-and-butter roux would otherwise accomplish.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

In a recent development, one of the things I like most about this method is how little precision it demands. If you’re cooking a pound of macaroni, start with a 12-ounce can of evaporated milk and roughly 12 to 16 ounces of grated cheese. Sharp cheddar provides plenty of flavor, while Monterey Jack or fontina will give you a smooth melt. I generally prefer a combination, but there’s no reason to make a special trip to the store if you already have a perfectly good block of cheese in the refrigerator.

I do recommend grating the cheese yourself, since the anti-caking ingredients in bagged shredded cheese can keep it from melting smoothly. Beyond that, there’s plenty of room for flexibility. There’s no need to measure everything down to the last ounce, which is part of what makes this method so wonderful.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

In a recent development, boil the pasta in generously salted water as you normally would, then strain it and return it to the pot, reserving about a cup of pasta water. Add the cheese and evaporated milk, warming them gently over low heat. Keep stirring until everything melts into a smooth sauce, adding splashes of pasta water as you go until it reaches your desired consistency.

Recent findings suggest that the same trick works beautifully in more elaborate recipes, whether you’re making a baked southern mac and cheese, a big pan of potluck mac and cheese or a comforting crockpot mac and cheese. All have their merits, but for an ordinary weeknight, I rather like knowing that one pot, three ingredients, and about as much time as it takes to boil pasta are all I need.

I Tested Peloton's Upcoming, More Affordable Folding Treadmill

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1674 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In my mind and, I think the minds of many others, Peloton has always been a stationary bike brand.
  • Industry observers note that nevertheless, Peloton actually has been making treadmills since 2018.
  • The new Tread Flex, however, heads in a slightly different direction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In my mind and, I think the minds of many others, Peloton has always been a stationary bike brand. The Bike, after all, was its first product, turning the Peloton name into a catch-all term for at-home cycling that we now hear everywhere, from broadcasts of the Tour de France and Giro d'Italia to television sitcoms. (A running gag online is that Peloton's upscale, soothing video workout content is worlds away from The Office's Dwight Schrute leading a group of stationary riders off an imaginary cliff.).

Industry observers note that nevertheless, Peloton actually has been making treadmills since 2018. The first Tread delivered the same proposition as the Bike: premium hardware that looks good enough to bring out of the basement, as well as access to interactive, instructor-led runs and HIIT classes on a major, immersive screen. Over the years, Peloton has brought improvements to that first Tread: larger screens, voice controls, AI-informed movement tracking for form analysis and coaching.

The new Tread Flex, however, heads in a slightly different direction. It has a simpler belt, simpler speakers, a smaller screen. It's $1,300 cheaper than the next step up, and $4,500 cheaper (!) than Peloton's slat belt-equipped Tread+ Vision. Its affordability isn't even its main selling point, however, because the Tread Flex has a nifty final trick: it folds up to save space.

Sources indicate that could these space and money-saving tactics make the Tread as popular as the Bike? Well, I run nearly every day, and ever since a tester Tread Flex highlighted up at my door, I've been doing it indoors much more frequently. In my experience, here's what makes Peloton's latest worth considering.

Treadmills tend to have a problem that stationary bikes don't: the nicer they get, the bigger they get. Premium models have larger motors and roomier running platforms. In short, they're heavy. (The Tread+ Vision is a hefty 460 pounds.) The Tread Flex is 170 pounds less, and that's crucial to its ability to fold up, because that feature wouldn't be much of a selling point if it felt like adding a power clean to the end of every run.

In reality, stowing the Tread Flex is quite easy. You just lift up the running deck from the end and push it forward until a hydraulic cylinder locks into place. There's a pin clip to lock it. To drop it down, you push forward on the deck and then on the hydraulic support, then walk it back. At about 45 degrees, the hydraulics take over completely; you can go put on your running shoes while a gentle thump lets you know the deck is back on the ground.

Folding up the Tread Flex drops its area from about 16.5 square feet to half that. (The Tread+ Vision is around 19.25.) Just as importantly, I've discovered, is that lifting the deck brings the machine up onto a set of locking wheels. I've kept mine in a designated corner, but it's so easy to move that it wouldn't be much hassle to wheel it out and lower it for every workout, if your space required it. Get your cardio out of the way, then get your cardio out of the way.

Okay, so folding and moving a treadmill might be a pain if you're using it every day. But I suspect if you're running that often, you're doing some of it outside. I live less than an hour away from the Canadian border, and run on roads and trails five or six times a week all year round. Good layers get you pretty far, and there's a reason why run clubs continue to boom while SoulCycle-adjacent Mile High Run Club closed all its studios this year.

Treadmills are for something else. They're for a warm-up prior to lifting, or for bootcamp-style HIIT workouts that combine sprinting intervals with weight intervals. The prioritization value of time spent doing these doesn't seem to align with the space investment a treadmill requires if you don't have a pool house or big garage. (I have a sun porch-slash-mudroom where I keep firewood and ski boots in the winter and a napping couch in the summer.).

This is how, I think, the Tread Flex makes the ultimate proposition as the ideal home treadmill. A treadmill doesn't replace a usual running routine; it adds to it. On Monday I do my usual seven miles down the road and back on the river trails; on Tuesday I let Andy Speer kick my ass with sprints and kickstand deadlifts. (And, sure, when it's -10° and blowing in late January, I might run inside, now that I have the option.).

None of the above would matter as much if it came at the cost of quality. I've run on hotel treadmills that sound like your grandma's washing machine and feel similar to how they look, i.e., stomping around on hollow plastic. The Tread Flex may not have the cushioned slat belt the Tread+ Vision has, but it's definitely not that.

In a recent development, what it does have is a spec that's right in line with top-notch treadmills. Its max speed is 12.5 miles per hour (a 4:48 mile, in runner's units), a 12.5% max incline grade (but no decline), and a 20-inch by 59-inch running surface that, though not cushioned, feels good to run on. The swiveling screen is nice and substantial at 21.5 inches, with HD resolution and a touchscreen interface. I particularly like how adjusting speed and incline is done with rolling knobs, which feel much better—and more natural—to engage with than buttons when you're gasping at threshold pace.

Recent findings suggest that on top of that is Peloton's interactive experience: You can take live classes where you can pit yourself against others and get kudos from the instructor. The pre-recorded catalogue includes thousands of classes for yoga, Pilates, and meditation, in addition to strength and the running, cycling, and rowing the organization makes machines for.

According to recent reports, the Tread Flex also provides personalized training plans, smart pacing guidance based on where you're at, automatically adjusting incline for classes, and of course leaderboards and an entire ecosystem of badges and achievements to earn, if you're into all that. For $50 per year, that is.

In a recent development, oh, and did I mention it's a good-looking machine? It's sleek; an attractive, soft-edged Z with a minimal screen instead of a board of colorful buttons. Nobody's throwing around the word "console" to describe this thing. That's good; home gym setups deserve different consideration than gym rigs. If images of Crunch Fitness flash through your head every time you glance into the corner, something has missed the mark.

Where Peloton's Tread Vision treadmills are clearly high-end, the Tread Flex toes the line against mainstream consumer models. Its features match up with some of the most popular machines, and its price, while at the higher end of the spectrum, does too. But the Tread Flex gets there with more style, and with Peloton's huge ecosystem of live and archived class content.

Sources indicate that so, if we're looking at other treadmills out there, my quick answer is yes. The Tread Flex is the utilitarian Peloton Treadmill, but it's still a Peloton treadmill.

In a recent development, how you answer this question really requires asking yourself a series of other questions first. What do you want a treadmill for? How much do you want to invest? Do you want access to fitness classes—especially ones other than running—and are you okay with the $50/month subscription fee?

Form factor and access to classes and content are non-negotiables. The Tread Flex might be Peloton's fresh entry-level treadmill, but it's far from a simple running machine. Flex refers to that nifty fold-up feature, but also to this treadmill's ability to integrate into an exercise program that also includes strength training, HIIT workouts, yoga, and on and on.

As a runner who prefers to log miles outside whenever possible, I was encouraged by how much I enjoyed running on the Tread Flex. The classes are fun, and Peloton's instructors are real pros, but even in Just Run mode, the Tread Flex proved responsive and comfy. It's getting dark around 4:30 PM these days, and my daylight windows for running on the well-used roads around me have narrowed like a Death Star trash compactor. It's nice to know I can snag seven miles after sundown if need be.

Industry observers note that well, if you aren't limited by space or cash, the Tread Vision and Tread+ Vision get you bigger screens, AI-enabled running form feedback and coaching, and a more cushioned, broader running area. If you just prefer running or walking on a treadmill to doing it outside, investing more heavily in a treadmill is worth considering (though the Tread Flex will still be great).

Sources indicate that the Tread Flex's real competition is the NordicTrack Commercial 1750, which you'll find recommended on just about every treadmill buying guide on the internet. The machines are similar in function and specs, but there are some differences. The NordicTrack's running surface is two inches wider and one inch longer; it has a slightly more powerful motor; it can decline to -3% grade; its belt is slightly cushioned; it has a built-in fan; and NordicTrack's class and entertainment platform, iFit, is cheaper at $39 a month.

In comparison, the Tread Flex takes up slightly less space, has a higher max speed (12.5 mph over 12 mph), a steeper incline (12.5% over 12%), and a larger screen (21.5 inches over 16 inches). The rolling knobs to adjust speed and incline are nicer to use. My partner, who designs commercial and residential interior spaces, agrees with me that the Tread Flex is a better-looking machine.

According to recent reports, list price for the Tread Flex is $300 cheaper, but the NordicTrack seems to be perpetually on sale. So it might come down to looks, that 3% decline, or what class platform you'd like to buy into.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

The secret to a beautifully golden Thanksgiving pie might be the simplest ingredient in your kitchen.

Thanksgiving pies have a way of bringing out the perfectionist in even the most relaxed bakers. Yet you might spend half an hour creating the perfect pie dough design, carefully crimping the edges or cutting little leaves from scraps of pastry, only to pull the finished pie from the oven and discover that your beautiful handiwork has browned unevenly. It’s a small disappointment in the grand scheme of things, but after all that effort, a little indignation is understandable.

An egg wash is supposed to give pastry a lovely golden color and delicate sheen, but getting it to cooperate isn’t always as simple as beating an egg and picking up a pastry brush. Fortunately, there’s an easy trick that makes a noticeable difference, and it comes courtesy of a familiar face in the baking world: Great British Baking Show judge Paul Hollywood.

According to recent reports, paul’s secret is simply to add a pinch of salt to the beaten egg. He lets it sit for about five minutes before brushing it onto pastry dough. In a BBC Food demonstration, Paul uses the technique to glaze scones, but it works just as well for giving pie crusts a beautiful, even finish.

Industry observers note that beat an egg with a small pinch of salt until they’re well combined, then set the mixture aside for a few minutes. Give it another quick stir before brushing a thin, even layer over the pastry. The amount of salt won’t affect the flavor, and there’s no reason to make any other adjustments to your favorite pie recipe.

Sources indicate that the difference is subtle but useful. Instead of clinging stubbornly to your pastry brush or collecting in the little crevices of a crimped edge, the egg wash spreads more easily.

Emiko Franzen For Taste Of Home.

If you’ve ever tried brushing a plain beaten egg onto pastry, you’ve probably noticed that it can be surprisingly thick and stringy. That’s because the proteins in the egg give it structure—a nuisance if you need to spread it evenly. Adding salt loosens those proteins, making the egg wash thinner and more fluid after a few minutes. It glides over the pastry more smoothly, leaving a light, even coating rather than stringy puddles.

Sources indicate that the egg itself is what gives pastry its golden color and glossy sheen. Salt doesn’t make the crust magically browner; it simply helps the egg wash do its job better. The result is a more consistent finish, particularly around the edges and decorative details where egg wash tends to collect.

It has been revealed that A pinch of salt won’t turn a lopsided pie into a masterpiece, but it can help a well-made crust look its best. And after we’ve spent an unreasonable amount of time weaving strips of pastry into a lattice for a Thanksgiving pie, I think we’re entitled to a little help with the finishing touches.

Charred Cabbage With Yogurt and Hot Sauce

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a blender, combine 9 pickled Fresnos, stems removed and roughly chopped, plus 2 Tbsp.
  • Preheat the oven to 425°F and set racks in the center and top of the oven.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you think cabbage is boring, this dish will absolutely change your mind. Charred aggressively, it takes on a smoky, almost meaty quality—it’s the main event. A drizzle of hot sauce, crispy breadcrumbs, and a cooling yogurt sauce round it out. Treat cabbage like a protein, and it will reward you.

More showstopping cabbage recipes here.

In a blender, combine 9 pickled Fresnos, stems removed and roughly chopped, plus 2 Tbsp. brine, 1 small shallot, roughly chopped, 3 garlic cloves, 3 Tbsp. red wine vinegar, juice of 1 navel orange, and 1 tsp. kosher salt. Blend on high, taking a pause to scrape the sides, until smooth. With the blender running on low, slowly pour in 1 cup extra-virgin olive oil until the sauce is silky and runny. Transfer the sauce to a bottle or jar and refrigerate for up to 2 weeks.

Preheat the oven to 425°F and set racks in the center and top of the oven. Line a sheet tray with parchment paper.

Make the Cabbage: Cut 1 large head green cabbage in half, then slice each half into four wedges. Arrange on the prepared sheet tray, drizzle generously with extra-virgin olive oil and kosher salt, and massage it into all those craggy layers. Roast on the center rack for 20–25 minutes, until a knife slides through easily. Set the broiler to high and slide the cabbage to the top rack. Broil for 2–4 minutes, until the edges are deeply charred and irresistibly crispy.

Sources indicate that while the Cabbage Roasts, Make the Breadcrumbs: In a small skillet over medium heat, melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter with 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Stir in ½ cup panko breadcrumbs, 1 garlic clove, finely grated, and ½ tsp. kosher salt, then toast, stirring constantly, until golden and fragrant. Remove from the heat and mix in ¼ preserved lemon, store-bought or homemade, peel only, finely diced, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh dill, and 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh parsley. Set aside to cool.

It has been revealed that make the Yogurt: In a small bowl, whisk together 1 cup full-fat Greek yogurt or labne, zest and juice ½ lemon, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh dill, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh parsley, and 1 tsp. kosher salt until smooth and creamy.

When the cabbage is ready, swoop the yogurt across a serving plate. Arrange the cabbage wedges at dramatic angles. Drizzle generously with hot sauce, letting it seep into the leaves. Finish with the golden breadcrumbs, fresh dill fronds, and a few extra grates of lemon zest. Serve immediately.

In a recent development, place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.).

Sources indicate that add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Industry observers note that add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Industry observers note that nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.).

Industry News: This Is What Was on the Menu at the First Thanksgiving in 1621

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Somehow, turkey has spent the last four centuries getting all the glory.
  • In a recent development, for a meal that has been discussed, depicted and reenacted for more than four centuries, the first Thanksgiving has left us surprisingly few details about what anyone actually ate.
  • The gathering took place in Plymouth in the fall of 1621, when about 50 English colonists celebrated their first successful harvest alongside 90 Wampanoag, including their leader, Ousamequin, better known to history as Massasoit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Somehow, turkey has spent the last four centuries getting all the glory.

In a recent development, for a meal that has been discussed, depicted and reenacted for more than four centuries, the first Thanksgiving has left us surprisingly few details about what anyone actually ate. We know there were roughly 140 people, three days of feasting and exactly five deer. Beyond that, the historical record is rather unhelpful. Apparently, nobody thought to write down the menu.

The gathering took place in Plymouth in the fall of 1621, when about 50 English colonists celebrated their first successful harvest alongside 90 Wampanoag, including their leader, Ousamequin, better known to history as Massasoit. It was a meeting between two communities whose relationship was far more complicated than the cheerful scene that would eventually find its way into American classrooms. Although they had formed an alliance earlier that year, cultural differences and tensions of an English settlement on Wampanoag land were hardly going to disappear over dinner.

And while the English had much to celebrate in bringing in their first harvest, they owed a great deal of that success to Indigenous knowledge. The Wampanoag understood the region’s growing seasons, its waterways and the foods that could be grown and gathered in the surrounding landscape. Their traditions had helped sustain communities there long before the colonists arrived.

The two surviving English accounts of the gathering offer only a few details about the feast itself, but taken together with what historians know about the food traditions of both communities, they give us a rather interesting picture of what may have been on the table.

Edward Winslow, one of the English colonists who attended the gathering, recorded that the Wampanoag went hunting and returned with five deer, which they presented to the colony’s leaders. It’s one of the few specific foods mentioned in his account and an especially substantial contribution to a celebration that lasted three days.

Recent findings suggest that deer were an important source of food for the Wampanoag, who also made use of their hides, bones and other materials. In England, however, deer hunting was largely reserved for the wealthy, making venison something most ordinary people rarely got to enjoy. The meat may have been roasted over a fire or simmered in a hearty venison stew, although Winslow neglected to tell us how it was prepared. We know exactly how many deer arrived, but what became of them in the kitchen remains a mystery.

According to recent reports, roast turkey has become so thoroughly associated with Thanksgiving that it’s difficult to imagine the holiday without one occupying the center of the table. The trouble is, we don’t actually know whether turkey was served at the original celebration.

Winslow wrote that four Englishmen went hunting for wildfowl and returned with enough to feed the colonists for nearly a week. What he didn’t do was tell us which birds they shot. Wild turkeys were present in the region, but so were ducks, geese and other game birds, all perfectly suitable for roasting over a fire. There’s every possibility that turkey was on the menu, but nothing to suggest it enjoyed the distinction we’ve since bestowed upon it. For all we know, the centerpiece was a duck, and we’ve spent the last few centuries giving credit to the wrong bird.

Corn was one of the most important foods available to both communities, although the English were relatively new to growing it. The Wampanoag had cultivated maize for generations, developing agricultural practices suited to the region’s soil and growing seasons. Their knowledge was enormously valuable to the colonists, whose first attempts at establishing a food supply had been anything but fruitful.

One traditional Wampanoag preparation was nasaump, a thick porridge made from ground corn, sometimes cooked with other ingredients. Corn could also be ground into meal for simple breads, early relatives of the cornbread we bake today, or used to thicken stews and make other hearty dishes.

Sources indicate that the waters around Plymouth were full of food, provided you knew where to look and how to catch it. The Wampanoag had long fished the region’s rivers and coastline, gathering shellfish and catching everything from bass and cod to eels. Clams, mussels and lobsters were plentiful too.

The English were beginning to take advantage of these resources by 1621. William Bradford, the Plymouth colony’s governor, wrote of the colonists catching substantial quantities of cod and bass during the summer. A freshly caught fish could be roasted or boiled, while clams and mussels might be cooked over a fire. Lobster was another plentiful local catch that was enjoyed regularly. The variety of ocean fare available might have made for a Thanksgiving spread that looked rather more like a seafood boil than the feast we know today.

Squash and pumpkin were notable crops in Wampanoag agriculture, and their ability to keep well after harvest made them especially useful as the colder weather set in. Both could be roasted, boiled or added to stews, much like we still prepare winter squash today, though without the benefit of a balsamic glaze.

In a recent development, the English called pumpkins pompions, a name I think we abandoned prematurely. They were familiar with the vegetable, although the varieties growing in Fresh England differed from those they might have seen at home. A pumpkin dish would have been entirely plausible at the harvest celebration, but anyone hoping for a slice of pumpkin pie would have to wait almost two centuries. The colonists had limited supplies of wheat flour, butter and sugar, and the familiar custard-filled pie wouldn’t appear in American cookbooks until 1796.

Industry observers note that the Wampanoag grew beans alongside corn and squash, three crops that complemented each other remarkably well. Cornstalks supported climbing beans, while squash vines spread across the ground and helped shade the soil. The combination was as useful in the garden as it was on the plate.

A traditional Wampanoag stew called sobaheg combines ingredients like corn, beans, squash and meat or fish, depending on what’s available or in season. The combination of corn and beans also appears in succotash, another dish with Indigenous New England roots that remains an American favorite.

The forests and wetlands of New England offered plenty beyond cultivated crops. Chestnuts, walnuts, hazelnuts, acorns, wild grapes and cranberries were among the foods the Wampanoag knew how to gather and prepare, each with its own season and uses.

Nuts could be eaten plain, stored or ground into meal, while fruits could be enjoyed fresh or preserved for later. Acorns required particular attention, since their natural bitterness had to be leached out with water before they could be used in cooking. It’s one of the few ingredients we’ve more or less surrendered entirely to the squirrels.

Of all the wild fruits available, cranberries have perhaps the most recognizable place on a modern Thanksgiving table. Their natural tartness eventually found a friend in sugar, giving rise to the cranberry sauce that’s become nearly as much a part of the holiday as the turkey itself.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Recent findings suggest that place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve ever scraped a black fleck off a melted spatula into your pasta and wondered what exactly you just ate, congratulations: You’ve already arrived at the case for nontoxic utensils. Swapping out your plastic-handled, mystery-material kitchen tools is one of the easiest upgrades you can make.

More difficult is choosing a material to commit to. Walk through any kitchen store and you'll encounter wood, silicone, stainless steel, bamboo, and any number of hybrid constructions. Each has its advocates and its limitations. But after thinking through the tradeoffs and cross-referencing what professionals actually reach for day to day, we landed on a clear answer: Silicone is the best material for a nontoxic utensil set, and a five- to six-piece core collection is all most home cooks need to start.

Newly introduced in this update: We added more information about the pros and cons of each of our winning non-toxic utensil sets.

Sources indicate that food-grade silicone is heat-resistant up to around 450°–600°, depending on the manufacturer, which means it’s unlikely to melt against the side of a hot pan or leach chemicals into your food the way that plastic utensils can when exposed to prolonged heat. It's also nonreactive, meaning it won't interact with acidic ingredients like tomato sauce or citrus the way that some metals can. Unlike wood, it's fully dishwasher-safe and nonporous and it won't harbor bacteria or crack over time with repeated washing. And—critically—it won't scratch your enameled cast iron.

There are some things silicone doesn't do especially well. It can feel slightly grippy or drag-heavy compared to a thin fish spatula, for instance, and some silicone utensils pick up odors over time. (The odor issue is real—I've had cheaper silicone spatulas that smelled faintly of dish soap for months.) One other issue you might find is that you can’t scrape a pan very effectively with silicone in a situation where you might want to blend fond into a sauce for flavor (that’s a case for keeping a wooden spoon around). But for the vast majority of everyday cooking tasks—stirring, folding, sautéing, serving—high-quality silicone outperforms the competition on the merits that matter most.

Material: Platinum-cured siliconeSet size: 5 pieces (also available in 3- and 10-piece sets)Heat resistance: Up to 425°FDishwasher safe: Yes.

According to recent reports, what we love: GIR (Get It Right) makes some of the best silicone utensils on the market. Its tools are made from 100% platinum silicone, which among other things, is a method that keeps odors off the utensils. It also makes them fully heat-safe and more durable than most other sets. That matters more than it might sound: Many budget silicone utensils use a nylon or fiberglass core to add rigidity, which can become a problem if the silicone outer layer ever cracks or peels. With GIR, what you see is what you get all the way through.

In a recent development, the handles are weighted and ergonomic without being bulky, and the heads are thin enough to actually get under food—like a delicate omelet—which is a genuine problem with thicker silicone spatulas. GIR's tools also hold up unusually well over time. The silicone doesn't discolor, doesn't absorb odors the way cheaper versions can, and doesn't degrade with repeated dishwasher cycles.

In a recent development, the brand offers a range of set configurations, but its core five-piece collection gives you exactly what you need without the extras: a spatula, a flip turner, a spoon, a ladle, and GIR's signature spoonula—a hybrid tool that functions as both spoon and spatula that’s particularly useful for scraping the sides of a pan or transferring food cleanly from pot to bowl. The spoonula in particular gets more use in my kitchen than I expected—it's become the default tool for anything that needs to be scraped, scooped, or transferred.

What we'd leave: It's a bit pricier than other silicone sets, but we think it's well worth it.

The set includes a ladle, a cooking spoon, and a turner, with flexible edges designed to get every last bit from pans and bowls. The handles are comfortable and grippy even when wet, and the one-piece silicone construction makes cleanup straightforward.

What we'd leave: It's a leaner starting point than our top pick, but that's not necessarily a bad thing—if you're building a collection piece by piece, this is a smart, low-commitment way to start with utensils you'll actually use.

Industry observers note that what we'd leave: The wood requires more upkeep (and will eventually crack or warp) compared to silicone, but a quick hand-wash and occasional wipe-down with wax takes about 30 seconds. It's not cheap, but it's a premium product. Just keep it out of the dishwasher. For cooks who prefer the feel of wood, Jonathan's Spoons makes some of the most thoughtfully crafted wooden utensil sets available.

5-Piece Stainless Steel Kitchen Utensil Set.

Material: Stainless steelSet size: 5 piecesHeat resistance: 600°FDishwasher safe: Yes.

What we love: Stainless-steel utensils are indestructible and oven-safe to high temperatures, and they look sharp hanging from a rail or stored in a stylish crock. So why make silicone the top recommendation instead? Bare stainless can scratch nonstick and enameled surfaces, so these are best suited for cooks who primarily use uncoated cookware (carbon steel, stainless steel, cast iron). All-Clad's 5-piece set includes a ladle, a solid spoon, a slotted spoon, a turner, and a storage caddy, all crafted from heavy-gauge stainless steel with ergonomic handles long enough to reach into deep pots. The set is heat-safe up to 600°, dishwasher-safe, and backed by All-Clad's limited lifetime warranty. If you're already cooking on All-Clad stainless-steel pans, this is the obvious companion set.

What we'd leave: If you don't have uncoated cookware, this isn't the set for you.

Recent findings suggest that once you have your core set, it's worth considering what other tools you'd need. Whether you're pescatarian, a deep-fryer, or an avid wok user, there's a tool out there that'll help you achieve your highest cooking goals. None of these need to come from the same brand—this is where building piece by piece, based on what you actually cook, makes more sense than buying a bigger bundle. Here are a few of our favorites.

Sources indicate that if crisping salmon skin is your game, a fish spatula is a must. The Lamson Flexible Stainless-Steel Slotted Turner ($53) is a longtime favorite, but Winco’s Fish Spatula ($10) is an inexpensive alternative with a wooden handle that's still flexible enough for delicate fillets.

Medium Stainless Steel Fish Spatula.

If steak is more up your alley, you can't be without a pair of tongs. Of course it's great for turning the steak in a skillet and holding in steady while you slice, but this tool is also helpful for a boatload of other tasks, like removing corn cobs from a pot of boiling water and shifting sheet pans around your oven. Oxo’s 12" Locking Tongs ($20) with silicone tips are gentle on nonstick and enameled surfaces while still giving you a confident grip.

Sources indicate that whether you're a deep-fry fanatic or a dumpling enthusiast, a spider strainer is a great tool for removing crisped or boiled items from hot pots and pans. We like this stainless-steel version for its sturdiness and extra-long handle.

Open Kitchen by Williams Sonoma.

It has been revealed that A from-scratch dressing, a silky cream sauce, or a fluffy whipped cream is made possible because of a good whisk. You can splurge on the editor-favorite Matfer Bourgeat Piano Whisk or opt for a silicone-coated Oxo Good Grips version.

In a recent development, the same logic that makes a 7-piece cookware set a better starting point than a 15-piece one applies here: More isn't always better, and the average home cook will reach for the same handful of tools repeatedly. A well-considered five-piece silicone set typically covers a large spoon (for stirring sauces, soups, and grains), a slotted spoon (for draining and serving), a flexible spatula (the workhorse for eggs, fish, and pancakes), a turner or solid spatula (for heavier tasks like flipping burgers or moving proteins), and a ladle or tongs, depending on what you cook most.

With five tools, you can execute most stovetop and baking tasks without reaching for anything else. That remarked, not every set breaks down exactly this way—and that's fine. A three-piece set that covers your everyday tools beats a five-piece set with two pieces you never touch. Think of five as the target, not a hard rule.

Are silicone utensils actually nontoxic?

According to recent reports, high-quality, food-grade silicone is considered one of the safest materials for kitchen utensils, with FDA-approved versions specifically tested to ensure they don’t leach harmful substances into food. It's nonreactive, doesn't leach chemicals into food, and is stable at high temperatures. However, the quality of silicone utensils is much more all over the place. Cheaper sets often use filler materials or nylon cores that can degrade over time. Look for utensils made from 100% platinum-cured or pharmaceutical-grade silicone—the kind GIR uses—and you can feel confident about what's touching your food.

How do I take care of my utensils so they last?

It depends on the material. Silicone is the lowest maintenance—most sets are dishwasher-safe and require no special treatment. Wood needs more attention: hand-washing, drying thoroughly after each use, and oiling periodically with food-safe mineral oil or wax. Stainless steel is virtually indestructible, but hand-washing will keep it looking better longer. Regardless of material, avoid soaking utensils for extended periods and store them somewhere with good airflow rather than sealed in a drawer while still damp.

Do I need to match my utensils to my cookware?

Not exactly—but it's worth thinking about. If you cook primarily on nonstick or enameled cookware, silicone is your safest bet since it won't scratch delicate surfaces. If you cook mainly on stainless steel or cast iron, you have more flexibility and can use metal utensils without worry. Also, you may need a little more leverage to get food off, and metal can help with that. Wood works well across the board but comes with its own maintenance tradeoffs. The most practical approach for most home cooks: Start with a silicone set as your everyday workhorse, then add a stainless fish spatula or tongs as your cooking demands them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that after years of over-packing, under-packing, and everything in between, I’d like to think I’ve finally mastered the art of packing for a work trip. Most of my work trips take me to the fashion capitals, where I can more or less anticipate what my itinerary–and, naturally, my personal lookbook–will entail. After countless fashion months, I have a fairly reliable formula down–but every now and then, a destination comes along that throws my blueprint for a loop. My latest challenge? Las Vegas for the F1 Grand Prix.

According to recent reports, why is packing for Vegas so difficult? Mainly because dressing for the glitz of Sin City falls rather outside my usual minimalist style. But, as a devoted F1 fan, I decided to embrace the challenge.

In a recent development, I was headed out there to celebrate the launch of the fresh, limited edition Wynn Las Vegas x Olivia Von Halle collection, so I knew there were a few event-specific outfits I needed to prepare. My action-packed itinerary (and hyper-glam Las Vegas alter ego) required sparkles, velvet, and more than a few statement jackets, so I started there, but generally my packing philosophy for all work trips is fairly simple. I start with understanding my itinerary, then work in outfits. I like to scribble my packing list by hand, try on the full look before it makes it to my suitcase (unless I have worn it before), and sometimes commit to a mirror selfie as a reminder. Once I have the key looks figured out, I typically throw a few wardrobe staples in as back-ups. A great pair of denim, black pointed-toe heels, a few white t-shirts, and a black clutch always come with me.

According to recent reports, my first stop on this trip was brunch at the recently opened Zero Bond, hosted by Olivia Von Halle and Kelly Piquet. They brought together a mix of familiar faces from the worlds of fashion and Formula 1, including Susie Wolff, CEO of F1 Academy, Bianca Bustamante, racing driver, and jewelry designer Isabela Gruttman. Beyond the collection launch, there was no shortage of entertainment. From being able to look out my window and see the race track, to race cars installed between blackjack tables, to a host of driver pop-up activations, Formula 1 truly took over the city and the energy was incredible.

Ahead, everything I packed and wore for a long weekend work trip to Las Vegas.

Sources indicate that simple, comfortable, and practical is always my philosophy when it comes to a travel outfit. My Away luggage comes with me on every trip, and my travel uniform remains the same as always: a white t-shirt, Agolde denim, Nike sneakers, and in this case, my largest coat that simply could not fit in my suitcase.

I picked up this custom pearl-embroidered Róhe jacket during Paris Fashion Week this past season. It’s heavy and added several pounds to my suitcase, but felt brunch-appropriate styled with a simple black slip skirt and Chanel pumps.

Sources indicate that this festive velvet red jacket from Liberowe was certainly on-theme. By day, I wore the jacket with a simple white tee, jeans, and a faux fur snood; then, for an evening at the casino, I switched it up with the matching mini skirt, sheer tights, and patent heels.

It has been revealed that race night was just incredible; but the dressing brief was tough. I needed a statement-making outfit that was appropriate for the Wynn Skybox but warm enough to spend a few hours outdoors. With 352 overtakes and 31 lead changes, it was nearly impossible to take my eyes off the track… thankfully, I stayed cozy in the Maeve shearling jacket from Ducie. Then came a swift change for my after-party look, where I traded denim for sequins with this semi-sheer Alfie dress, and styled it out with the same giant shearling and a Julietta collar necklace.

In a recent development, there are a few things I never leave behind when traveling for work; good skincare, luxurious pajamas, and jewelry are at the top of that list. I’m quite particular about keeping to my usual morning and evening routines, even when I’m away. My travel skincare is an extension of what I use at home, with a few indulgences that make the end of a long day feel slightly more familiar. The same goes for sleepwear; I almost exclusively travel with a pajama set from Olivia von Halle, this time in an on-theme casino print!

Great jewelry is truly what makes every look your own, and thanks to Michael Rider at Celine my collection has been growing recently… including a dice charm I purchased on this trip as a very chic souvenir.
